articles.title: Colorado transfer tax: the $0.01 per $100 documentary fee
articles.description: Colorado's only statewide charge on a sale is a documentary fee of $0.01 per $100: $62.50 on a $625,000 home. Who pays it, exemptions, Denver.

articles.title: How to verify a real estate license in Colorado
articles.description: Colorado licenses brokers, loan originators, appraisers and land surveyors; the statutes I read do not license home inspectors. Who to check and where.

real-estate-agent.regulator: Colorado Real Estate Commission, Division of Real Estate (DORA)
real-estate-agent.lookup_name: DRE eLicense Search for a Licensee
real-estate-agent.note: C.R.S. 12-10-202. The DRE also offers downloadable licensee rosters (GenerateRoster page); I did not open them or read their conditions. Lookup page and DORA accessibility page read; no terms-of-use page found.

mortgage-loan-officer.regulator: Board of Mortgage Loan Originators, Division of Real Estate (DORA); NMLS
mortgage-loan-officer.lookup_name: DRE eLicense Search for a Licensee (NMLS Consumer Access also lists originators)
mortgage-loan-officer.note: C.R.S. 12-10-704 requires the state license and an NMLS identifier. NMLS Consumer Access is behind a 403 block for scripted access (not opened); URL kept because official state pages link to it. Terms page unreadable.

home-inspector.regulator: None found
home-inspector.note: The statutes read do not license home inspectors (home inspection services appear only in 12-10-218). Nothing to look up.

closing-attorney.regulator: Colorado Supreme Court, Office of Attorney Regulation Counsel
closing-attorney.note: Page read; it says an attorney must be active and in good standing to practice. Its Privacy Policy link was not opened and no terms-of-use clause was read, so bulk_compilation is marked unreadable.

appraiser.regulator: Board of Real Estate Appraisers, Division of Real Estate (DORA)
appraiser.lookup_name: DRE eLicense Search for a Licensee
appraiser.note: C.R.S. 12-10-616. Federal check: ASC Appraiser Registry (https://www.asc.gov/appraiser). ASC Appraiser Registry opens, but its terms of use (ffiec.gov/disclaimer) returned 403, so bulk-use rules are unreadable.

facts.fact: State deed tax of 0.33% paid by the seller and mortgage registry tax of 0.23%; Hennepin County adds 0.01% to each
Homesteads are classed at 1% of the first $500,000 of value and 1.25% above, after a homestead exclusion of up to $38,000
Written disclosure before the purchase agreement is signed; claims within 2 years of closing
Mostly non-judicial sheriff’s sale after 6 weeks of published notice, then a 6-month redemption period for most homes

articles.title: Closing costs in Minnesota: what buyers and sellers pay
articles.description: Minnesota's closing taxes are fixed: on a $400,000 Minneapolis sale, the deed tax is $1,360 and the mortgage tax on a $320,000 loan is $768.

articles.title: First-time home buyer programs in Minnesota and Minneapolis
articles.description: Minnesota Housing's Start Up loan allows incomes to $151,200 in Hennepin County and up to $18,000 in down payment help. Minneapolis adds up to $20,000.

articles.title: Foreclosure in Minnesota: process, timeline and your rights
articles.description: Most Minnesota foreclosures are non-judicial: 6 weeks of published notice, then a sheriff's sale and a 6-month redemption period. Deficiency rules differ.

articles.title: Home prices in Minnesota and Minneapolis: median value
articles.description: Median owner-occupied home value: $344,600 in Minnesota and $368,300 in Minneapolis (Census ACS 2024). FHFA: Minnesota prices up 2.5% in a year.

articles.title: Buying a home in Minneapolis, Minnesota
articles.description: Minneapolis median home value: $368,300 (Census ACS 2024). Sellers need a city Truth in Sale of Housing report; city down payment loans reach $20,000.

articles.title: How Minnesota property tax works and what the homestead saves
articles.description: Minnesota taxes homesteads at 1% of value after a market value exclusion of up to $38,000. A $400,000 Minneapolis homestead owes about $5,723 at 2025 rates.

articles.title: Do you need a real estate attorney to close in Minnesota?
articles.description: Minnesota law lets attorneys, brokers or licensed closing agents run a home closing. Closing fees must be disclosed in writing 5 business days before closing.

articles.title: Minnesota seller disclosure: what sellers must tell buyers
articles.description: Minnesota sellers must give buyers a written disclosure before signing. Buyers have 2 years after closing to sue; pre-1978 homes add a 10-day lead test window.

articles.title: Buying a rental property in Minnesota: tenant rules to know
articles.description: Minnesota law sets no cap in ch. 504B, but St. Paul limits rent hikes to 3%. Deposits come back in 3 weeks; a nonpayment eviction needs 14 days' notice.

articles.title: Minnesota deed tax and mortgage registry tax explained
articles.description: Minnesota charges a 0.33% state deed tax on sales and a 0.23% mortgage registry tax on new loans. Hennepin County adds 0.01% to each: $1,360 on a $400,000 sale.

articles.title: How to verify a real estate license in Minnesota
articles.description: Minnesota licenses agents, closing agents, appraisers, mortgage originators and surveyors; the laws reviewed show no home inspector license. How to check each.

real-estate-agent.regulator: Minnesota Department of Commerce (Commissioner of Commerce)
real-estate-agent.note: Minn. Stat. 82.81. The Commerce website blocked my scripted requests (bot-protection page); the lookup URL comes from an official search listing and from the home page link, and was not opened by me. Terms unreadable.

mortgage-loan-officer.regulator: Minnesota Department of Commerce, through NMLS
mortgage-loan-officer.note: Minn. Stat. 58A.03. NMLS Consumer Access is behind a 403 block for scripted access (not opened); URL kept because official state pages link to it. Terms page unreadable.

home-inspector.regulator: None found
home-inspector.note: Chapters 82, 82B, 58, 326, 326B and 325F as previously searched contain no home inspector license. Nothing to look up.

facts.fact: $1.85 per $500 ($1.30 state plus $0.55 county), paid by the seller with the buyer secondarily liable
A legal residence is assessed at 4% of value, other property at 6%; owner-occupants are exempt from school operating millage
Required: the South Carolina Supreme Court holds that all real estate and mortgage closings must be supervised by an attorney
Judicial in practice, with bidding left open 30 days after the sale when a deficiency is sought

articles.title: Closing costs in South Carolina: what buyers and sellers pay
articles.description: On a $400,000 Greenville sale, the seller owes $1,480 in deed recording fees by law; the buyer pays $15 to file the deed and $25 for the mortgage. Line by line.

articles.title: First-time home buyer programs in South Carolina: SC Housing
articles.description: SC Housing gives $10,000 forgivable down payment help; Palmetto Home Advantage gives up to 4% of the loan. Greenville County limits and local aid.

articles.title: South Carolina foreclosure: court process, timeline, your rights
articles.description: South Carolina foreclosures go through court. Bidding stays open 30 days after the sale, and a lender may seek a deficiency judgment for what is still owed.

articles.title: Buying a home in Greenville, South Carolina
articles.description: Greenville median home value: $553,700 (Census ACS 2024); Greenville County $339,800. SC Housing offers $10,000 forgivable down payment help.

articles.title: Home prices in South Carolina and Greenville: median and trend
articles.description: Median owner-occupied home value: $299,500 in South Carolina and $553,700 in Greenville (Census ACS 2024). FHFA: state prices up 2.4% in a year.

articles.title: Natural hazards and home insurance in South Carolina
articles.description: Home policies in South Carolina exclude flood and earthquake. NFIP flood cover starts 30 days after purchase; coastal wind may need the state wind pool.

articles.title: Property tax in South Carolina: 4% ratio, rates, appeals
articles.description: South Carolina assesses a primary residence at 4% of value. In the City of Greenville, 2025 millage is 331.5, or about $3,045 on a $400,000 home after the school exemption.

articles.title: Do you need a real estate attorney to close in South Carolina?
articles.description: Yes. The South Carolina Supreme Court says real estate and mortgage closings must be supervised by a licensed attorney. What that covers, and what it does not.

articles.title: South Carolina seller disclosure: what the state form requires
articles.description: South Carolina sellers must give buyers the state disclosure form before signing. A missing form does not void the sale; knowingly false answers cost damages.

articles.title: South Carolina deed transfer tax: $3.70 per $1,000
articles.description: South Carolina charges a deed recording fee of $3.70 per $1,000 of value ($1,480 on a $400,000 Greenville home). The seller owes it by law. Exemptions and examples.

articles.title: How to verify a real estate license in South Carolina
articles.description: Check a South Carolina agent, loan originator, home inspector, appraiser or surveyor using the state board lookups and the national registries.

real-estate-agent.regulator: South Carolina Real Estate Commission (LLR)
real-estate-agent.note: S.C. Code 40-57-20. LLR disclaimer of liability read (no clause on lists or commercial use). Note the SC.GOV privacy policy cites the Family Privacy Protection Act of 2002 on commercial solicitation, which may also apply; not confirmed for LLR.

mortgage-loan-officer.regulator: Department of Consumer Affairs (mortgage brokers) and State Board of Financial Institutions, Consumer Finance Division (lenders); NMLS
mortgage-loan-officer.lookup_name: Consumer Affairs Licensee Lookup (mortgage brokers); NMLS Consumer Access
mortgage-loan-officer.note: Two regulators depending on employer. Terms: SC.GOV privacy policy, which the Consumer Affairs page links. NMLS Consumer Access is behind a 403 block for scripted access (not opened); URL kept because official state pages link to it. Terms page unreadable.

home-inspector.regulator: Residential Builders Commission (LLR)
home-inspector.note: S.C. Code 40-59-520. LLR disclaimer of liability read (no clause on lists or commercial use). Note the SC.GOV privacy policy cites the Family Privacy Protection Act of 2002 on commercial solicitation, which may also apply; not confirmed for LLR.

closing-attorney.regulator: South Carolina Supreme Court; South Carolina Bar
closing-attorney.note: Directory pages open. The Judicial Branch /attorneys/ page returned 406 to scripted access. No terms clause read.

appraiser.note: S.C. Code 40-60-30. LLR disclaimer of liability read (no clause on lists or commercial use). Note the SC.GOV privacy policy cites the Family Privacy Protection Act of 2002 on commercial solicitation, which may also apply; not confirmed for LLR. ASC Appraiser Registry opens, but its terms of use (ffiec.gov/disclaimer) returned 403, so bulk-use rules are unreadable.

facts.fact: Deed tax of $0.50 per $500 and mortgage tax of $0.15 per $100 (Code of Alabama §§ 40-22-1, 40-22-2)
Homes (Class III) assessed at 10% of value; 72.5 mills in Birmingham for October 2025
No statutory form in the sections read; licensees face fines for hiding known latent defects
Non-judicial sale after 3 weeks of published notice; redemption within 180 days for a homestead

articles.title: Buying a home in Birmingham, Alabama
articles.description: Birmingham median home value: $189,800 (Census ACS 2024). Prices up 0.6% in a year (FHFA). The city offers up to $10,000 in down payment help.

articles.title: Closing costs in Alabama: what buyers and sellers pay
articles.description: Alabama's closing taxes are set by law: $0.50 per $500 deed tax and $0.15 per $100 mortgage tax. On a $250,000 Birmingham sale with a $200,000 loan, $550.

articles.title: First-time home buyer programs in Alabama and Birmingham
articles.description: AHFA offers down payment help of 4% of the price, up to $10,000, and Birmingham adds up to $10,000 more. Income limits as of Oct. 2026.

articles.title: Foreclosure process in Alabama: steps, timeline, redemption
articles.description: Alabama lenders can foreclose without a court: 3 weekly notices, a courthouse-door sale, then 180 days to redeem a homestead (1 year for other property).

articles.title: Home prices in Alabama and Birmingham: median value, trend
articles.description: Median owner-occupied home value: $233,300 in Alabama and $189,800 in Birmingham (Census ACS 2024). FHFA: Alabama prices up 2.8% in a year.

articles.title: Natural hazards and home insurance in Alabama
articles.description: Flood is not covered by home policies; NFIP covers up to $250,000. AIUA insures Baldwin and Mobile counties; Strengthen Alabama Homes pays up to $10,000.

articles.title: Alabama property tax: how it works and the homestead exemption
articles.description: Alabama assesses homes at 10% of market value. In Birmingham the October 2025 millage totals 72.5 mills, about $1,760 a year on a $250,000 home.

articles.title: Do you need a real estate attorney to close in Alabama?
articles.description: No Alabama statute I read requires an attorney at closing, but only lawyers may prepare deeds and mortgages for others (Ala. Code § 34-3-6). Who does what.

articles.title: Seller disclosure in Alabama: what a seller must tell
articles.description: No Alabama statute I read requires a seller disclosure form. Agents must disclose known defects ($100 to $5,000 fines); federal lead rule covers pre-1978 homes.

articles.title: Alabama deed tax and mortgage tax: rates and who pays
articles.description: Alabama charges a deed tax of $0.50 per $500 of price and a mortgage tax of $0.15 per $100 borrowed. On a $250,000 sale with a $200,000 loan: $250 and $300.

articles.title: How to verify a real estate license in Alabama
articles.description: Check Alabama agents, loan originators, home inspectors, appraisers and surveyors in free public lookups. AREC fines for violations run $100 to $5,000.

real-estate-agent.regulator: Alabama Real Estate Commission (AREC)
real-estate-agent.note: Code of Alabama 34-27-30. The search page has a 'Policy' item that is only a mailto link; no terms page found.

mortgage-loan-officer.regulator: Alabama State Banking Department, Bureau of Loans; NMLS
mortgage-loan-officer.note: Code of Alabama 5-26-4. The Bureau's own licensee search is listed as temporarily unavailable and points to NMLS. NMLS Consumer Access is behind a 403 block for scripted access (not opened); URL kept because official state pages link to it. Terms page unreadable.

home-inspector.regulator: Alabama Department of Finance, Division of Construction Management
home-inspector.note: Home Inspectors Registration Act, Title 34 Chapter 14B; the act speaks of registration and a certificate of licensure; I classed it as registration. Page links a 'Legal' item (finance.alabama.gov/about) that I did not read.

closing-attorney.regulator: Alabama State Bar
closing-attorney.note: Page opens (200). Alabama attorneys are admitted by the Supreme Court and regulated through the State Bar; no terms page read.

appraiser.regulator: Alabama Real Estate Appraisers Board
appraiser.note: Code of Alabama 34-27A-3. The portal itself is reached from the REAB home page. ASC Appraiser Registry opens, but its terms of use (ffiec.gov/disclaimer) returned 403, so bulk-use rules are unreadable.

facts.fact: No new transfer tax since 2011 (Louisiana Constitution, Art. VII, § 2.3); New Orleans charges a documentary tax of $300 to $325 per sale
Homes assessed at 10% of market value; homestead exemption of $7,500 of assessed value ($75,000 of market value)
Yes: community of acquets and gains; both spouses must agree to sell or mortgage a community immovable (Civil Code art. 2347)
Property disclosure document due by the time of the offer; 72 hours to cancel if it comes later
Judicial executory process: the first sale at least 60 days after the writ, at a minimum bid of two-thirds of the appraisal

articles.title: Closing costs in Louisiana: what buyers and sellers pay
articles.description: No state deed tax, but New Orleans sellers pay a $300 documentary tax. Recording an act costs $100 to $300, plus $35 in portal and building fees.

articles.title: Louisiana community property and buying a home as a couple
articles.description: Louisiana's default regime is community of acquets and gains: each spouse owns half of what is acquired in marriage, and both must sign to sell a community home.

articles.title: First-time home buyer programs in Louisiana: LHC and New Orleans
articles.description: Louisiana Housing Corporation HomeStart: 4% forgivable assistance, up to $55,000 under HomeStart Plus, plus up to $55,000 from New Orleans.

articles.title: Foreclosure process in Louisiana: executory process explained
articles.description: Louisiana forecloses through a court-ordered sheriff's sale, usually by executory process. The first sale is set no sooner than 60 days after the writ.

articles.title: Home prices in Louisiana and New Orleans: median value and trend
articles.description: Median owner-occupied home value: $223,200 in Louisiana and $305,100 in New Orleans (Census ACS 2024). FHFA: Louisiana prices up 1.6% in a year.

articles.title: Hurricanes, flood and home insurance in Louisiana
articles.description: Homeowners policies exclude flood. NFIP covers up to $250,000 for a house; Fortify Homes grants up to $10,000 for a roof; Citizens is the insurer of last resort.

articles.title: Buying a home in New Orleans, Louisiana
articles.description: New Orleans median home value: $305,100 (Census ACS 2024). Up to $55,000 in city down payment help and up to $55,000 from the state's HomeStart Plus.

articles.title: Louisiana property tax: 10% assessment and homestead exemption
articles.description: Louisiana assesses homes at 10% of market value; the homestead exemption removes $7,500 of assessed value ($75,000 of value). New Orleans 2026 rates inside.

articles.title: Do you need an attorney or notary to close in Louisiana?
articles.description: Louisiana sales are passed before a notary, and preparing an act of sale for pay counts as practicing law. Here is what the code requires and who does what.

articles.title: Seller disclosure requirements in Louisiana
articles.description: Louisiana sellers of 1-4 unit homes must give buyers a property disclosure document by the time of the offer; a late one gives 72 hours to cancel.

articles.title: Real estate transfer tax in Louisiana and New Orleans
articles.description: Louisiana has no state deed tax. New Orleans charges a documentary transaction tax of $300 on a house sale under its Code, paid by the seller.

articles.title: How to verify a real estate license in Louisiana
articles.description: Check Louisiana agents and appraisers on the LREC portal, loan originators on NMLS, inspectors with their state board and surveyors on lapels.com.

real-estate-agent.note: LREC disclaimer read: public-service information, no clause on lists or commercial use.

home-inspector.note: R.S. 37:1476. The board's own site (lahomeinspectors.com) returned 522 when I tried; no online lookup URL confirmed.

closing-attorney.regulator: Louisiana Supreme Court; Louisiana State Bar Association
closing-attorney.note: LSBA Disclaimer of Liability read; no clause on lists or commercial use. Louisiana notaries also close sales; not covered here.

appraiser.regulator: Louisiana Real Estate Appraisers Board (administered with LREC)
appraiser.note: LREC disclaimer read, no clause found. ASC Appraiser Registry opens, but its terms of use (ffiec.gov/disclaimer) returned 403, so bulk-use rules are unreadable.

$1.260 per $100 inside the Urban Services District; homestead exemption of $49,100 for 2025-2026, only for owners 65 or older or totally disabled
No, but since 2020 couples can opt into a Kentucky community property trust (KRS 386.620 and following)
Judicial; a 6-month redemption right only if the sale brings less than two-thirds of the appraised value

articles.title: Closing costs in Kentucky: what buyers and sellers pay
articles.description: Kentucky's transfer tax is $0.50 per $500, paid by the seller: $242 on a $241,700 Louisville sale. Recording a deed costs $33 plus a $4 state tax.

articles.title: Community property and buying a home in Kentucky
articles.description: Kentucky is not a community property state: courts divide marital property under KRS 403.190. Since July 2020, spouses can opt in with a trust (KRS 386.620).

articles.title: First-time home buyer programs in Kentucky: KHC and Louisville
articles.description: KHC down payment assistance is up to $12,500; Louisville Metro gives up to 20% of the price (cap $30,000) to households at 80% of area income or less.

articles.title: Foreclosure in Kentucky: court process and 6-month redemption
articles.description: Kentucky forecloses through the courts. If a sale brings under two-thirds of the appraised value, the owner has six months to redeem, by statute (KRS 426.530).

articles.title: Home prices in Kentucky and Louisville: median value and trend
articles.description: Median owner-occupied home value: $226,000 in Kentucky and $241,700 in Louisville (Census ACS 2024). FHFA: Kentucky prices up 4.3% in a year.

articles.title: Buying a home in Louisville, Kentucky
articles.description: Louisville median home value: $241,700 (Census ACS 2024). 2025 property tax: $1.26 per $100 in the Urban Services District. Transfer tax: $0.50 per $500.

articles.title: Kentucky property tax: rates, homestead exemption, appeals
articles.description: Kentucky's 2026 state real estate rate is 10.3 cents per $100. In Louisville's Urban Services District the 2025 total was $1.26 per $100. Homestead: $49,100 (65+).

articles.title: Do you need a real estate attorney to close in Kentucky?
articles.description: No Kentucky statute I read requires an attorney at closing, but every deed must name its preparer (KRS 382.335) and drafting one for others is the practice of law.

articles.title: Seller disclosure requirements in Kentucky (KREC Form 402)
articles.description: Kentucky requires a seller's disclosure form (KREC Form 402) when a paid licensee is involved; the listing agent must deliver it within 72 hours of a signed offer.

articles.title: Real estate transfer tax in Kentucky: rate, payer, exemptions
articles.description: Kentucky's transfer tax is $0.50 per $500 of value, charged to the seller: $242 on a $241,700 sale, $400 on $400,000. Foreclosure and divorce transfers are exempt.

articles.title: How to verify a real estate license in Kentucky
articles.description: Kentucky licenses agents, loan originators, home inspectors, appraisers and land surveyors. Where to check each one, and what unlicensed work can cost.

Measure 50: maximum assessed value grows at most 3% a year, and a sale does not reset it

Non-judicial trustee sale at least 120 days after the notice of sale; no redemption and no deficiency after a trustee’s sale

articles.title: Closing costs in Oregon: what buyers and sellers pay
articles.description: Oregon has no transfer tax. Recording a deed in Multnomah County costs $86 for the first page, $5 per extra page. Line-by-line costs for buyers and sellers.

articles.title: First-time home buyer programs in Oregon and Portland
articles.description: Oregon's FirstHome loan adds 4% or 5% down payment aid; Portland's DPAL offers up to $80,000-$100,000. Income and price limits for Multnomah County.

articles.title: Foreclosure process in Oregon: steps, timeline and help
articles.description: Oregon lenders can foreclose without court. Notice of sale must go out 120+ days before the auction (ORS 86.764), with no redemption after it.

articles.title: Home prices in Oregon and Portland: median value and trend
articles.description: Median owner-occupied home value: $497,500 in Oregon and $588,200 in Portland (Census ACS 2024). FHFA: Oregon prices up 0.3% in a year.

articles.title: Natural hazards and home insurance in Oregon
articles.description: Oregon home policies cover wildfire but not quakes or floods; only about 20% of Oregonians carry earthquake cover, with deductibles of 10% or 15%.

articles.title: Buying a home in Portland, Oregon
articles.description: Portland median home value: $588,200 (Census ACS 2024). The city's DPAL offers up to $80,000-$100,000 to first-time buyers inside city limits.

articles.title: Oregon property tax: Measure 50, rates and who gets relief
articles.description: Oregon taxes assessed value, capped at 3% growth a year. Portland's code area 001 paid $26.92 per $1,000 in 2025-26. No general homestead exemption.

articles.title: Do you need a real estate attorney to close in Oregon?
articles.description: No Oregon statute read here requires an attorney at closing. Escrow agents must be licensed (ORS 696.511); see what each party may and may not do.

articles.title: Seller disclosure in Oregon: what sellers must tell buyers
articles.description: Oregon requires a signed property disclosure on most home sales. Buyers get 5 business days to revoke after delivery (ORS 105.475). Exemptions and lead rules.

articles.title: Buying a rental property in Oregon: tenant rules
articles.description: Oregon caps rent hikes at 7% plus inflation or 10%: 9.5% for 2026, 10% for 2027. After year one, landlords need a legal reason to end a tenancy.

articles.title: Real estate transfer tax in Oregon: none, with one old exception
articles.description: Oregon's Constitution bans transfer taxes on real property except those in place on Dec. 31, 2009. Portland charges none; you pay recording fees.

articles.title: Buying a home in Cheyenne, Wyoming
articles.description: Cheyenne median home value: $360,800 (Census ACS 2024). Laramie County first-time buyer price limit: $566,354 (WCDA, June 2026).

articles.title: Closing costs in Wyoming: what buyers and sellers pay
articles.description: Wyoming has no transfer tax. Recording costs $12 for the first page and $3 after; title premiums are set by each insurer's filed schedule.

articles.title: First-time home buyer programs in Wyoming (WCDA)
articles.description: WCDA offers up to $15,000 in down payment assistance and a 2026 Laramie County price limit of $566,354. Programs, limits and how to apply.

articles.title: How does foreclosure work in Wyoming?
articles.description: Wyoming forecloses mostly by advertisement: 4 weeks of published notice, then a sheriff's sale and a 3-month redemption period (12 for farmland).

articles.title: Home prices in Wyoming and Cheyenne: median value and trend
articles.description: Median owner-occupied home value: $339,500 in Wyoming and $360,800 in Cheyenne (Census ACS 2024). FHFA: Wyoming prices up 3.2% in a year.

articles.title: Wyoming property tax: how it works and the 25% exemption
articles.description: Wyoming taxes 9.5% of market value. In Cheyenne's main school district the 2025 levy is 70.54 mills; a 25% homeowner exemption trims the bill.

articles.title: Do you need a real estate attorney to close in Wyoming?
articles.description: Wyoming statutes do not require an attorney at closing. Licensed title agents may run escrow and closings (W.S. 26-23-314), but may not practice law.

articles.title: What must a home seller disclose in Wyoming?
articles.description: Wyoming has no statutory condition form for houses; W.S. 34-1-151 covers vacant land only. Agents must disclose known adverse material facts.

articles.title: Real estate transfer tax in Wyoming: is there one?
articles.description: The Wyoming statutes we read impose no transfer tax on deeds. Buyers file a sworn statement and pay $12 for the first recorded page, then $3 a page.

articles.title: How to verify a real estate license in Wyoming
articles.description: Check Wyoming agents, loan originators, appraisers and surveyors in state lookups. Wyoming statutes show no state license for home inspectors.

alabama.answer: Alabama has no official typical closing-cost total; the state fixes a deed tax of $0.50 per $500 of price and a mortgage tax of $0.15 per $100 borrowed, which come to $250 and $300 on a $250,000 sale with a $200,000 loan.
alabama.recording_fees: Jefferson County Probate Court: $16 for the first page and $3 for each additional page (schedule effective June 1, 2012), plus an $11 indexing and filing fee per instrument (Code of Alabama 45-37-84.43).
alabama.biggest_items: Deed tax ($0.50 per $500 of price), mortgage tax ($0.15 per $100 borrowed), title insurance (insurer's filed rate), lender charges.
alabama.example: $250,000 Birmingham home with a $200,000 loan: deed tax $250, mortgage tax $300, recording $33 (deed) and $69 (mortgage); fixed lines total $652, before title premium and lender charges.
alabama.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Statutes do not say who pays the deed or mortgage tax; the contract decides.

alaska.answer: Alaska has no official typical closing-cost total; it charges no transfer tax (AS 43.98.035), and recording a deed costs $20 for the first page and $5 for each additional page.
alaska.recording_fees: $20 for the first page, $5 for each additional page, and $2 for each name indexed over six (11 AAC 05.200, Alaska DNR).
alaska.biggest_items: Title insurance (insurer's filed rate), escrow and closing charges (filed schedule), lender charges. No transfer tax.
alaska.example: $400,000 Anchorage home with a $320,000 loan: transfer tax $0, recording a 5-page deed $40, recording a 20-page deed of trust $115.
alaska.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No statute read sets who pays each cost; the contract decides.

arizona.answer: Arizona has no official typical closing-cost total; it charges no transfer tax, the county recorder charges $30 per instrument, and title insurers must charge their filed rates.
arizona.recording_fees: $30 per instrument ($15 if a government body is a party and requests it), A.R.S. 11-475; the $2 transfer fee is included in the $30.
arizona.biggest_items: Lender fees, title premium (insurer's filed rate), escrow fee, prorated property tax. No transfer tax.
arizona.example: $400,000 Phoenix home: transfer tax $0, recording the deed $30 and the deed of trust $30, fixed recording total $60.
arizona.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Statutes read do not divide costs between buyer and seller.

arkansas.answer: Arkansas has no official typical closing-cost total; the state transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration ($660 on a $200,000 sale) and Pulaski County recording is $15 for the first page plus $5 per added page.
arkansas.recording_fees: Pulaski County: $15 for the first page (one side) and $5 for each additional page, $15 per extra instrument in the same document up to $300; schedule dated 2019, confirm with the clerk.
arkansas.biggest_items: State transfer tax ($3.30 per $1,000), title insurance and escrow (no official schedule read), lender charges.
arkansas.example: $200,000 Little Rock home: transfer tax $660, deed recording $35, deed of trust recording $70; public lines total $765.
arkansas.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. DFA pages do not say whether buyer or seller bears the transfer tax.

california.answer: California has no official typical closing-cost total; transfer taxes are set by county and city, for example $1.10 per $1,000 in Los Angeles County plus $4.50 per $1,000 in the City of Los Angeles, or $5,600 on a $1,000,000 home.
california.recording_fees: Los Angeles County grant deed: $15 base fee, $7 fraud notification fee, $2 restrictive covenant modification fee and $3 per additional page; $10 survey monument fee if the legal description is not on a recorded tract map; $20 if no Preliminary Change of Ownership Report is filed.
california.biggest_items: Transfer taxes (county and some cities), title insurance (insurer's filed rate), escrow fee, lender charges, supplemental property tax bill about six months after purchase.
california.example: $1,000,000 City of Los Angeles home with an $800,000 loan: county transfer tax $1,100, city transfer tax $4,500, recording $30 and $69; fixed lines total $5,699.
california.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No official source sets a default buyer/seller split; the contract and escrow instructions do.

colorado.answer: Colorado has no official typical closing-cost total; the state documentary fee is $0.01 per $100 of price ($62.50 on $625,000) and Denver charges a flat $43 to record each real estate document.
colorado.recording_fees: Denver Clerk and Recorder: flat $43 per real estate document (as of October 2026); since July 1, 2025 county clerks charge a flat $40 instead of per-page fees (HB24-1269).
colorado.biggest_items: Owner's title policy (seller if seller selects the title company, buyer if buyer does), closing services fee, lender charges, prorated property tax.
colorado.example: $625,000 Denver purchase: documentary fee $62.50, deed recording $43, deed of trust recording $43; fixed fees total $148.50.
colorado.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Standard contract CBS1 section 15.1 says buyer and seller each pay their respective closing costs unless the contract says otherwise.

connecticut.answer: Connecticut has no official typical closing-cost total; by law the seller pays the conveyance tax (0.75% state plus 0.25% or 0.5% municipal, 1.25% state above $800,000), and recording a deed costs $70 for the first page.
connecticut.seller_text: Seller owes the conveyance tax by statute: $3,750 on a $300,000 Hartford sale, before any commission or payoff (commission not included).
connecticut.recording_fees: Town clerk: $10 for the first page and $5 for each later page, plus $10 per document and a $50 community investment fee per document; first page of a deed costs $70. Add-ons: $2 (documents under 10-261b), $5 (no grantee mailing address), $1 (names not typed).
connecticut.biggest_items: Conveyance tax (seller), lender charges, title insurance and attorney fees (no official rate table read), recording fees.
connecticut.example: $300,000 Hartford sale with a 3-page deed: state conveyance tax $2,250 plus Hartford tax $1,500 equals $3,750 (seller); deed recording $80.
connecticut.note: The article gives no typical total or percentage for buyer or seller; seller_text is the statutory conveyance tax from the worked example, not a typical total. Hartford's 0.5% municipal rate is from a 2020 state report.

delaware.answer: Delaware has no official typical closing-cost total; the realty transfer tax is 4% of the price (2.5% state plus 1.5% county or municipal), with the state share apportioned equally between buyer and seller, and each recorded document carries $30 in state add-ons.
delaware.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: buyer's half of the 2.5% state transfer tax is $3,750 on a $300,000 sale ($2,250 for a first-time buyer); local tax payer set by ordinance.
delaware.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: seller's half of the 2.5% state transfer tax is $3,750 on a $300,000 sale (commission not included); between the parties the grantor bears the burden absent agreement (30 Del. C. 5412).
delaware.recording_fees: County recording fees are set by county ordinance (check with the Recorder); plus a $5 Housing Development Fund surcharge and a $25 Delaware Cultural Access Fund fee per document (9 Del. C. 9607(b)).
delaware.biggest_items: Realty transfer tax (4% total), title insurance (rates filed with the Department of Insurance), lender charges, attorney and settlement fees.
delaware.example: $300,000 sale with a 1.5% local tax: state tax $7,500, local tax $4,500, each side's half of the state tax $3,750 (first-time buyer reduction $1,500 for a $2,250 share); state recording add-ons $30 per deed.
delaware.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. State transfer tax is split equally by statute; local tax payer is set by the city or county ordinance.

florida.answer: Florida has no official typical closing-cost total; the deed carries documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 (60 cents in Miami-Dade), a new mortgage adds 35 cents per $100 and a 2-mill intangible tax, and the owner's title premium is $2,575 at $500,000.
florida.recording_fees: Miami-Dade Clerk: $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page of most documents, and $1 per name over four (as of October 2026).
florida.biggest_items: Deed documentary stamp tax (70 cents per $100), owner's title premium (state-set rate), mortgage stamp tax (35 cents per $100), intangible tax (2 mills of the loan).
florida.example: $500,000 Miami home with a $400,000 mortgage: deed stamp tax $3,000, mortgage stamp tax $1,400, intangible tax $800, owner's title policy $2,575, lender's policy $25, recording $27 and $129; government and title lines total $7,956.
florida.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Florida law does not assign most costs; all parties to a stamp-taxed document are liable, and the contract decides who pays.

georgia.answer: Georgia has no official typical closing-cost total; the transfer tax is $1 per $1,000 of price ($400 on $400,000) and the intangible recording tax is $1.50 per $500 borrowed ($960 on $320,000).
georgia.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: intangible recording tax is owed by the lender and may be passed to the borrower, $960 on a $320,000 loan.
georgia.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: transfer tax is the seller's by law (contract may shift it), $400 on a $400,000 home (commission not included).
georgia.recording_fees: Fulton County clerk: $25.00 for deeds or any instrument pertaining to real estate (as of October 2026); each county sets its own schedule.
georgia.biggest_items: Intangible recording tax on the loan, transfer tax, lender charges, title insurance and closing attorney fee (set by providers).
georgia.example: $400,000 Atlanta home with a $320,000 loan: transfer tax $400, intangible recording tax $960, deed recording $25.
georgia.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Transfer tax is the seller's by law but the contract may shift it to the buyer; the intangible tax is owed by the lender and may be passed to the borrower.

hawaii.answer: Hawaii has no official typical closing-cost total; the seller pays the conveyance tax by state rule ($1,600 on an $800,000 sale at the 2025 schedule) and recording a deed in the Regular System costs $41 per document up to 50 pages.
hawaii.seller_text: Seller pays the conveyance tax by state rule: $1,600 on an $800,000 sale if the buyer can claim the county homeowner's exemption, $2,000 if not (commission not included).
hawaii.recording_fees: Bureau of Conveyances: $41 per document up to 50 pages in the Regular System, $36 in the Land Court system (as of October 2026).
hawaii.biggest_items: Conveyance tax (seller, $0.10 to $1.00 per $100, higher rates if buyer lacks homeowner's exemption), escrow fee, title insurance, lender charges.
hawaii.example: $800,000 Honolulu sale to an owner-occupier: conveyance tax $1,600 (seller), deed recording $41, mortgage recording $41.
hawaii.note: The article gives no typical total or percentage for buyer or seller; seller_text is the conveyance tax from the worked example. Buyer pays the conveyance tax only if a government agency is the seller.

idaho.answer: Idaho has no official typical closing-cost total; no transfer tax was found, recording costs $15 for a deed and $45 for a deed of trust in Ada County, and title premiums and escrow fees are filed with the state.
idaho.recording_fees: Ada County Clerk (as of October 2026): $15 for a deed, $45 for a deed of trust, $15 for a reconveyance, each up to 30 pages, then $3 per page beyond 30.
idaho.biggest_items: Owner's and lender's title policies (filed rates), escrow fee (filed with the Department of Insurance), lender charges, survey and inspection.
idaho.example: $500,000 Boise home: deed recording $15, deed of trust $45, reconveyance of the seller's loan $15, transfer tax $0; a buyer with a mortgage paying both buyer-side recordings owes $60.
idaho.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax found in the sources read. Statutes read do not assign costs between buyer and seller.

illinois.answer: Illinois has no official typical closing-cost total; the Cook County Clerk charges $107 to record a deed or mortgage, and Chicago transfer taxes total $6.00 per $500 of price (state $0.50, county $0.25, city $5.25).
illinois.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: by default the buyer owes the Chicago city transfer tax portion ($3.75 per $500), $2,561.25 on a $341,200 home, plus recording the mortgage ($107).
illinois.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: by default the seller owes the state, county and CTA transfer taxes, $1,536.75 on a $341,200 Chicago home (commission not included).
illinois.recording_fees: Cook County Clerk (effective April 1, 2024): $107 per deed, mortgage, release, easement or miscellaneous document; $19 less for documents not subject to the state rental housing fee; $5 for mail return.
illinois.biggest_items: Chicago transfer taxes ($6.00 per $500), title premium and settlement fee (no state schedule), lender charges.
illinois.example: Chicago home at the $341,200 median value: transfer taxes total $4,098 (buyer owes $2,561.25 city portion, seller $1,536.75 by default), deed recording $107, mortgage recording $107.
illinois.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. By default the Chicago city portion ($3.75) falls on the buyer and the CTA portion ($1.50) plus state and county taxes on the seller.

indiana.answer: Indiana has no real estate transfer tax and no official typical closing-cost total; Marion County deed fees total $65, and filed title charges run $700 to $1,035 for a $250,000 purchase with a loan.
indiana.recording_fees: Marion County: Assessor $10 per parcel per document and $20 per sales disclosure form, Recorder $35 per document; $65 for one parcel and one deed. No separate mortgage fee found; other counties set their own.
indiana.biggest_items: Owner's title policy ($600 to $800 base rate at $250,000, median $755), lender charges, prepaids and escrow, separate title search and closing fees.
indiana.example: $250,000 Indianapolis purchase: transfer tax $0, Marion County deed fees $65, filed title charges $700 to $1,035 (median $1,000).
indiana.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The purchase contract decides who pays county and title charges.

iowa.answer: Iowa has no official typical closing-cost total; the transfer tax is $0.80 per $500 of price above $500, Iowa Title Guaranty charges a flat $175 up to $750,000, and Polk County charges $12 for a deed's first page.
iowa.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller is liable for the transfer tax, $340.80 on a $213,300 Des Moines home (commission not included).
iowa.recording_fees: Polk County: $12 for a deed's first page (includes a $5 transfer fee per parcel), $7 for a mortgage, $5 for each added page. Statewide base in 331.604 is $5 per page plus $1 and $1 add-on fees.
iowa.biggest_items: Iowa Title Guaranty certificate ($175 flat), transfer tax ($0.80 per $500, seller by statute), lender fees (origination capped at 2% of principal), abstract and attorney opinion.
iowa.example: Des Moines home at the $213,300 median value: transfer tax $340.80, title guaranty $175 (owner free if lender coverage issued at the same time), deed recording $22, mortgage recording $77.
iowa.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Seller is liable for the transfer tax by statute; the contract can allocate it.

kansas.recording_fees: Johnson County Register of Deeds (October 2026): $21 for the first page and $17 for each additional page of a deed or mortgage; includes Heritage Trust Fund and technology fees (K.S.A. 28-115).
kansas.biggest_items: Lender charges, title premium (each company's filed rate), survey and inspection, prorated property tax.

kentucky.answer: Kentucky has no official typical closing-cost total; the seller pays a transfer tax of $0.50 per $500 of value ($242 on a $241,700 sale) and recording a deed costs $33 for up to five pages plus a $4 state tax.
kentucky.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller (grantor) owes the transfer tax, $242 on a $241,700 Louisville home (commission not included).
kentucky.recording_fees: KRS 64.012: $33 for a deed or deed of trust of up to five pages, $3 per additional page, $4 per additional reference; $63 for a real estate mortgage up to 30 pages; $10 clerk storage reimbursement; plus a $4 state tax on each conveyance and each mortgage (KRS 142.010).
kentucky.biggest_items: Transfer tax ($0.50 per $500, seller), title insurance (filed rates, no table read), lender charges, appraisal, survey and inspection.

louisiana.answer: Louisiana has no official typical closing-cost total; the Civil Code puts the expenses of the act of sale on the buyer by default, recording in Orleans Parish costs $100 to $300 by page count plus a $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee, and New Orleans levies a $300 documentary tax on the seller.
louisiana.buyer_text: Civil Code art. 2463 says the expenses of the act and other expenses incidental to the sale must be borne by the buyer (no amount given).
louisiana.seller_text: Statutory item only, not a total: the New Orleans documentary tax of $300 on a single-family sale is the seller's by ordinance (the Clerk's page says $325); commission not included.
louisiana.recording_fees: Orleans Parish Clerk (schedule effective April 1, 2021): $100 for 1 to 5 pages, $200 for 6 to 25 pages, $300 for 26 to 50 pages then $5 per page, plus a $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee per recording; conveyance certificate $35, mortgage certificate $20, cancelling a mortgage $50.
louisiana.biggest_items: Notary and closing fees (no official schedule), title insurance (filed rates, none read), recording fees, New Orleans documentary tax ($300, seller).
louisiana.example: Financed New Orleans purchase with a 12-page act of sale and a 25-page mortgage: recording $235 plus $235 equals $470; documentary tax paid by the seller $300.
louisiana.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The Clerk's page says the documentary tax is $325 while the City Code says $300.

maine.answer: Maine has no official typical closing-cost total; the transfer tax is $2.20 per $500 of price, split half and half between buyer and seller by law, and registries charge $35 per recorded instrument.
maine.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the buyer owes half the transfer tax, $1,100 on a $500,000 sale, plus lender charges.
maine.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller owes half the transfer tax, $1,100 on a $500,000 sale (commission not included).
maine.recording_fees: $35 per instrument recorded (33 M.R.S. 751(1)(B)); plans cost $45. A deed and a mortgage are two instruments.
maine.biggest_items: Transfer tax ($2.20 per $500; extra $3.80 per $500 above $1 million from November 1, 2025), lender charges, title work and insurance (no official table read).
maine.example: $500,000 sale: transfer tax $2,200 ($1,100 each side), deed recording $35, mortgage recording $35.
maine.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage.

maryland.answer: Maryland has no official typical closing-cost total; the State transfer tax is 0.5% of the price, Baltimore City adds a 1.5% transfer tax and $5 per $500 recordation tax, and recording a residential instrument costs $60.
maryland.recording_fees: Circuit Court clerk (schedule effective September 2, 2026): $60 per instrument involving solely a principal residence other than a release; release of 9 pages or fewer $50; other instruments $60 under 9 pages and $115 over 10 pages.
maryland.biggest_items: Transfer and recordation taxes (State 0.5%, Baltimore City 1.5% plus $5 per $500), title premium (regulated), settlement fees (not regulated), lender charges.
maryland.example: $350,000 Baltimore home with an $280,000 loan: State transfer tax $1,750, city transfer tax $5,250, city recordation tax $3,280, recording $120; taxes total $10,280.
maryland.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. If the contract is silent, transfer and recordation taxes are shared equally; for a first-time Maryland buyer occupying the home, the seller pays the State tax (0.25%) and, unless the contract says otherwise, the local taxes.

massachusetts.answer: Massachusetts has no official typical closing-cost total; the seller pays the deeds excise of $2.28 per $500 of price outside Barnstable County ($3,648 on $800,000), and recording a deed costs $100 plus a $50 surcharge.
massachusetts.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller (person who signs the deed) owes the deeds excise, $3,648 on an $800,000 Boston sale; the seller must also equip the home with approved smoke detectors (commission not included).
massachusetts.recording_fees: Deed $100 plus $50 community preservation surcharge; mortgage $150 plus $50 surcharge; declaration of homestead $30 (G.L. c. 262, 38; c. 44B, 8). The registry may add charges for extra pages or copies.
massachusetts.biggest_items: Deeds excise ($2.28 per $500, seller), lender charges, title work and insurance (no premium set), legal fees.
massachusetts.example: $800,000 Boston purchase: deeds excise $3,648 (seller), deed recording $150, mortgage recording $200.
massachusetts.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Barnstable County has a higher excise rate.

michigan.answer: Michigan has no official typical closing-cost total; in Wayne County the seller owes transfer tax of $8.60 per $1,000 of value ($1,720 on $200,000) and recording a deed costs $30 per document.
michigan.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller owes state and county transfer tax of $1,720 on a $200,000 Wayne County sale, which the article states equals 0.86% of the price (commission not included).
michigan.recording_fees: Wayne County Register of Deeds (schedule effective January 1, 2026): $26 plus a $4 state survey and remonumentation fee where it applies, $30 per document whatever the page count; a purchase with a mortgage usually records two documents, about $60.
michigan.biggest_items: Transfer tax (state $3.75 plus county $0.55 per $500 in Wayne County, seller), title premium and closing fees (no schedule read), lender charges, prorated property tax.
michigan.example: $200,000 Wayne County sale: state transfer tax $1,500, county transfer tax $220, total $1,720 (seller); deed recording $30, mortgage recording $30.
michigan.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The buyer must notify the local assessor within 45 days; the sale lifts the taxable value cap.

minnesota.answer: Minnesota has no official typical closing-cost total; in Hennepin County the seller owes a 0.34% deed tax and a borrower owes a 0.24% mortgage registry tax, plus a $46 recording fee per document and a $5 conservation fee.
minnesota.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the borrower owes the mortgage registry tax, $768 on a $320,000 loan in Hennepin County (0.24%), plus recording fees.
minnesota.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller owes the deed tax, $1,360 on a $400,000 Minneapolis sale (0.34%), commission not included; a $54 well disclosure certificate applies if the seller knows of a well.
minnesota.recording_fees: Hennepin County: $46 per deed or other instrument (Minn. Stat. 357.18), $5 conservation fee on each deed or mortgage that pays tax, $54 well disclosure certificate when a well is known.
minnesota.biggest_items: Deed tax (0.34% of price, seller), mortgage registry tax (0.24% of loan, borrower), lender charges, title and closing services.
minnesota.example: $400,000 Minneapolis home with a $320,000 loan: deed tax $1,360, mortgage registry tax $768, conservation fees $10, recording $92; taxes total $2,128 before fees.
minnesota.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Minneapolis requires a Truth in Sale of Housing evaluation by the seller before showing the home.

mississippi.answer: Mississippi has no official typical closing-cost total; the Department of Revenue lists no tax on deed transfers, and recording a deed costs $25 for the first five pages and $1 for each extra page.
mississippi.recording_fees: Chancery clerk (Miss. Code 25-7-9, in force through December 31, 2027): $25 for the first five pages and $1 per extra page for a deed, deed of trust, release or cancellation; certifying a copy $1.
mississippi.biggest_items: Lender charges, title work and owner's policy (no official schedule), appraisal, survey and inspection.
mississippi.example: $150,000 Jackson home: transfer tax $0, deed recording $25, deed of trust recording $32, release of seller's old mortgage $25.
mississippi.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax found. Sources read do not assign costs between buyer and seller.

missouri.answer: Missouri has no official typical closing-cost total; no transfer tax was found (the Constitution bars new ones since December 2, 2010) and in the City of St. Louis a standard deed costs $25 for the first page plus $5 per extra page to record.
missouri.recording_fees: City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds: standard deed $25 for the first page and $5 per additional page; nonstandard deed $50 for the first page plus $5 per page. State base (RSMo 59.310): $5 first page, $3 per extra page, plus $25 for a document not meeting format rules.
missouri.biggest_items: Lender charges, title insurance and settlement fees (no premium table), St. Louis Certificate of Inspection ($120), appraisal and inspection.
missouri.example: $214,500 St. Louis home: transfer tax $0, recording a 3-page deed $35, City Certificate of Inspection $120 if required.
missouri.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax found. The contract decides who pays the $120 St. Louis inspection application.

montana.answer: Montana has no official typical closing-cost total; it has no transfer tax, recording costs $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page, and title insurers may charge only their filed rates.
montana.recording_fees: MCA 7-4-2632: $20 for the first page and $10 for each additional page for documents recorded by a photographic or similar process; the deed and the security instrument are recorded separately.
montana.biggest_items: Owner's and lender's title policies (insurer's filed rate), escrow fee (not set by statute), lender charges, survey and inspection.
montana.example: $400,000 Billings home: transfer tax $0, 3-page deed recording $40, 15-page deed of trust recording $160; statutory lines total $200.
montana.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax. Statutes read do not assign costs between buyer and seller.

nebraska.answer: Nebraska has no official typical closing-cost total; the documentary stamp tax is $3.32 per $1,000 of value since July 18, 2026 ($996 on a $300,000 sale), placed on the seller by statute, and recording costs $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page.
nebraska.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller (grantor) owes the documentary stamp tax, $996 on a $300,000 sale (commission not included).
nebraska.recording_fees: Register of deeds (Neb. Rev. Stat. 33-109): $10 for the first page and $6 for each additional page of a deed, mortgage or release.
nebraska.biggest_items: Documentary stamp tax ($3.32 per $1,000, seller), title insurance (one all-inclusive fee under filed rates), lender charges, closing fee.
nebraska.example: $300,000 sale: documentary stamp tax $996, 2-page deed recording $16, 15-page mortgage recording $94.
nebraska.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The tax rate was $2.32 from September 3, 2025 to July 17, 2026.

nevada.answer: Nevada has no official typical closing-cost total; in Clark County the transfer tax is $2.55 per $500 of value ($2,550 on $500,000), the Recorder charges $42 per document, and the State Bar says transfer tax, recording and escrow fees are often split equally.
nevada.buyer_text: Custom per State Bar of Nevada, not a total: buyer commonly pays the lender's title policy and new loan costs, and shares transfer tax, recording and escrow fees often split equally (transfer tax $1,275 each on a $500,000 Las Vegas sale).
nevada.seller_text: Custom per State Bar of Nevada, not a total: seller commonly pays the buyer's owner title policy and usually the broker's fee, and shares transfer tax equally ($1,275 on a $500,000 Las Vegas sale).
nevada.recording_fees: Clark County Recorder: $42.00 per document (schedule effective January 1, 2020); a deed plus a deed of trust is about $84; card payments carry a 2% fee plus $1.25 per transaction.
nevada.biggest_items: Transfer tax ($2.55 per $500 in Las Vegas), title insurance and escrow fees (filed with the Division of Insurance), lender charges.
nevada.example: $500,000 Las Vegas sale: transfer tax $2,550 ($1,275 each if split equally), recording a deed and a deed of trust about $84.
nevada.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The State Bar describes custom, not a statute; the contract and escrow instructions decide.

new-hampshire.answer: New Hampshire has no official typical closing-cost total; the state transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of price for the buyer and again for the seller ($3,000 each on a $400,000 home), and recording costs $10 for the first page and $4 per added page plus a $25 charge on deeds and mortgages.
new-hampshire.buyer_text: Fixed by law, not a total: $3,162 on a $400,000 Manchester home with a $320,000 loan (transfer tax $3,000, deed recording $51, mortgage recording $111); lender, title, attorney and inspection costs are extra.
new-hampshire.seller_text: Fixed by law, not a total: $3,000 transfer tax on a $400,000 home plus the cost of discharging the old mortgage (commission not included).
new-hampshire.recording_fees: Register of deeds: $10 for the first page plus $4 per added page; discharge of mortgage $15 for the first page plus $4 per added page; plus a $25 charge on each deed, mortgage, discharge or plan (RSA 478:17-g), paid by the grantee on a deed, the borrower on a mortgage, and the party discharging on a discharge.
new-hampshire.biggest_items: Transfer tax ($0.75 per $100, each side), lender charges, title insurance and attorney fees (no figure read).
new-hampshire.example: $400,000 Manchester home with a $320,000 loan and a 5-page deed and 20-page mortgage: buyer fixed costs $3,162, seller fixed costs $3,000 plus the mortgage discharge.
new-hampshire.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The Insurance Department's title page was not accessible, so no title premium or attorney fee is given.

new-jersey.answer: New Jersey's Department of Banking and Insurance tells buyers to expect one-time closing costs of about 3% to 4% of the sale price, and sellers owe the State Realty Transfer Fee, $4,655 on a $550,000 sale.
new-jersey.buyer_text: About 3% to 4% of the total sale price in one-time closing costs (NJ Department of Banking and Insurance guide), on top of the down payment, escrow deposits and prepaid insurance.
new-jersey.seller_text: Realty Transfer Fee of $4,655 on a $550,000 sale, imposed on the seller; plus a Graduated Percent Fee of 1% to 3.5% if the price is above $1 million (commission not included).
new-jersey.biggest_items: Buyer: loan application, credit report, appraisal, commitment and lock-in fees, inspections, title insurance, survey, escrow deposits, points. Seller: Realty Transfer Fee, Graduated Percent Fee above $1 million, brokerage compensation, mortgage payoff.
new-jersey.example: $550,000 Newark sale: buyer one-time costs $16,500 to $22,000 (3% to 4%); seller's Realty Transfer Fee $4,655.
new-jersey.note: Recording fees not given. Seller percent is null because the article gives a dollar fee on a $550,000 sale, not a percent of price. At $1,500,000 the seller would owe $15,625 in Realty Transfer Fee plus $15,000 in Graduated Percent Fee.

new-mexico.answer: New Mexico has no official typical closing-cost total; it has no transfer tax, recording in Bernalillo County costs $25 per document, and the Superintendent of Insurance sets title prices, such as $100 for a lender's policy issued with an owner's policy.
new-mexico.recording_fees: Bernalillo County Clerk (October 2026): $25 per document for up to 10 entries, and another $25 for each additional group of 10 or fewer.
new-mexico.biggest_items: Owner's title premium (state-set table, not retrieved), lender fees, escrow and settlement fees, appraisal, inspection and survey.
new-mexico.example: $400,000 Albuquerque purchase with a $320,000 loan: lender's title policy $100, title commitment $100, recording deed and mortgage $50, transfer tax $0; fixed lines subtotal $250.
new-mexico.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax found. A seller's broker commission is subject to gross receipts tax; the homeowner's own sale is exempt.

new-york.answer: New York has no official typical closing-cost total; on a $640,000 loan in New York City the mortgage recording tax is $13,890 (buyer about $12,290, lender $1,600), and sellers pay the 0.4% state transfer tax.
new-york.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: on a $640,000 New York City loan the borrower owes about $12,290 of mortgage recording tax; the buyer also owes the 1% mansion tax on prices of $1 million and up and generally pays both title policies.
new-york.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller owes the 0.4% state transfer tax, $3,200 on an $800,000 house; the NYC transfer tax of $11,400 on that price is assigned by contract (commission not included).
new-york.recording_fees: New York City: $32 plus $5 per page plus a $5 cover page for a deed or mortgage (a two-page document costs $42); mortgage tax affidavit $8. Counties outside the city set their own fees.
new-york.biggest_items: Mortgage recording tax (NYC combined $13,890 on a $640,000 loan), NYC transfer tax (1.425% above $500,000), state transfer tax (0.4%), mansion tax (1% from $1M), title policies.
new-york.example: $800,000 New York City house with a $640,000 loan: state transfer tax $3,200, NYC transfer tax $11,400, mortgage tax $13,890 (buyer $12,290, lender $1,600); total transfer tax on the sale $14,600.
new-york.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The article says rounding can shift results by a few dollars.

north-carolina.answer: North Carolina has no official typical closing-cost total; the seller owes the state excise tax of $1 per $500 ($864 on $431,900), recording a deed costs $26 and a deed of trust $64 in the county schedules read, and a North Carolina attorney handles the closing.
north-carolina.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller owes the state excise tax, $864 on a $431,900 Charlotte home, and pays off the existing mortgage from proceeds (commission not included).
north-carolina.recording_fees: Brunswick and Craven counties: $26 for the first 15 pages of an ordinary instrument then $4 per added page; $64 for a deed of trust for the first 35 pages then $4 per added page; no fee for a satisfaction of a deed of trust; $25 extra for nonstandard documents. Mecklenburg's own schedule was not read.
north-carolina.biggest_items: Excise tax ($1 per $500, seller), closing attorney fee (no rate table read), lender charges, lender's title policy.
north-carolina.example: $431,900 Charlotte home: excise tax $864 (seller), deed recording $26, deed of trust recording $64, local transfer tax $0.
north-carolina.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. County fees come from Brunswick and Craven schedules, not Mecklenburg.

north-dakota.answer: North Dakota has no official typical closing-cost total; it has no transfer tax and the county recorder charges $20 to record a deed or mortgage of one to six pages.
north-dakota.recording_fees: N.D.C.C. 11-18-05: $20 for one to six pages, or $65 for more than six pages plus $3 for each page after the first 25; $10 extra for a document without the required margins.
north-dakota.biggest_items: Lender charges, title insurance and escrow (no premium table), survey, inspection, prorated property tax.
north-dakota.example: Fargo purchase recording a 4-page deed ($20) and an 8-page mortgage ($65), transfer tax $0.
north-dakota.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax. The Insurance Department says the owner's title policy payer is negotiable and in many areas sellers pay.

ohio.answer: Ohio has no official typical closing-cost total; in Franklin County the deed carries a conveyance fee of $3 per $1,000 of price plus a $0.50 transfer tax, and the Recorder charges $34 for the first two pages and $8 per extra page.
ohio.recording_fees: Franklin County Recorder (October 2026): $34 for the first two pages and $8 for each additional page, plus $20 for a nonstandard document and $4 per marginal reference indexed (ORC 317.32).
ohio.biggest_items: Conveyance fee ($3 per $1,000 in Franklin County), lender charges, title insurance and escrow (no official schedule), survey and inspection.
ohio.example: $300,000 Franklin County sale with a 3-page deed: conveyance fee $900 ($300 state plus $600 county; $300 if the seller has the homestead exemption), transfer tax $0.50, deed recording $42.
ohio.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. The article does not say who pays the conveyance fee; the county's reduced rate for a seller with the homestead exemption points to the seller.

oklahoma.answer: Oklahoma has no official typical closing-cost total; the state fixes a documentary stamp tax of $0.75 per $500 on the deed, a mortgage tax of $0.10 per $100 borrowed (five years or more), and county recording fees of $8 for the first page plus $2 per extra page and a $10 preservation fee.
oklahoma.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: mortgage tax, $200 plus a $10 treasurer's certification on a $200,000 mortgage (payable by the borrower, lender or another interested party), recording fees, and the buyer's title commitment at buyer's expense.
oklahoma.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the documentary stamps, $375 on a $250,000 sale, fall on the person who makes, signs or sells the deed, normally the seller; the day of closing is the seller's day for tax proration (commission not included).
oklahoma.recording_fees: County clerk (28 O.S. 32): $8 for the first page of a deed or mortgage, $2 per additional page, and $10 per instrument for records preservation; nonconforming instruments cost $25 for the first page and $10 per additional page.
oklahoma.biggest_items: Documentary stamp tax ($0.75 per $500), mortgage tax ($0.10 per $100), title commitment or policy (no premium schedule), lender charges, prorated property tax.
oklahoma.example: $250,000 Oklahoma City sale with a $200,000 mortgage: documentary stamps $375, mortgage tax $200, treasurer's certification $10, deed recording $22, mortgage recording $46; fixed lines total $653.
oklahoma.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage.

oregon.answer: Oregon has no official typical closing-cost total; it has no transfer tax (Constitution Art. IX, section 15) and Multnomah County charges $86 to record the first page of a deed and $5 for each additional page.
oregon.recording_fees: Multnomah County (October 2026): $86 for the first page and $5 for each additional page for deeds and deeds of trust; $5 more for a cover page and $5 more for a document with a second transaction. State law sets $5 per page (ORS 205.320) plus fixed state amounts of $1, $10 and $60 per instrument (ORS 205.323).
oregon.biggest_items: Owner's and lender's title policies (filed rates, no table), escrow fee (rate schedule filed by each agent), lender charges.
oregon.example: $500,000 Portland home with a $400,000 loan: deed recording $96, deed of trust recording $181, transfer tax $0; recording lines total $277.
oregon.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax. Statutes read do not say who pays the title policy, escrow fee or recording fees. Nonresident sellers face income tax withholding from proceeds unless an exception applies.

pennsylvania.answer: Pennsylvania has no official typical closing-cost total; the realty transfer tax is 1% to the state plus local tax, 4.578% in Philadelphia ($11,610 on $253,600), usually split between buyer and seller, and Philadelphia charges $278.75 to record a deed.
pennsylvania.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: if the Philadelphia transfer tax is split evenly the buyer's half is $5,805 on a $253,600 home, plus recording the mortgage ($248.75).
pennsylvania.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: if the Philadelphia transfer tax is split evenly the seller's half is $5,805 on a $253,600 home (commission not included).
pennsylvania.recording_fees: Philadelphia Department of Records (October 2026): $278.75 for a deed and $248.75 for a mortgage; the city raised these fees by $3 on July 1, 2025. Other counties set their own fees.
pennsylvania.biggest_items: Realty transfer tax (4.578% in Philadelphia: 3.578% city plus 1% state), title insurance (no premium table), lender charges.
pennsylvania.example: $253,600 Philadelphia home: city transfer tax $9,074, state transfer tax $2,536, total $11,610 ($5,805 each if split), deed recording $278.75, mortgage recording $248.75.
pennsylvania.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Both buyer and seller are liable to the state; the city says the tax is usually split evenly but this is not required.

rhode-island.answer: Rhode Island has no official typical closing-cost total; the conveyance tax is $3.75 per $500 of price ($3,000 on a $400,000 sale), paid by the seller unless the contract says otherwise, and recording a warranty deed costs $80 and a mortgage $60.
rhode-island.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller normally owes the conveyance tax, $3,000 on a $400,000 sale (second $3.75 per $500 on residential value above $800,000), plus $45 to record a mortgage discharge (commission not included).
rhode-island.recording_fees: R.I. Gen. Laws 34-13-7: warranty or quitclaim deed $80, mortgage $60, discharge of mortgage $45, assignment or partial release $45, and $1 per additional page. Recording is in the city or town where the property sits.
rhode-island.biggest_items: Conveyance tax ($3.75 per $500, seller), lender charges, title insurance and attorney fees (no premium schedule read), recording fees.
rhode-island.example: $400,000 Providence sale with a $320,000 loan: conveyance tax $3,000, deed recording $80, mortgage recording $60, seller's mortgage discharge $45 (plus $1 per extra page).
rhode-island.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage.

south-carolina.answer: South Carolina has no official typical closing-cost total; the deed recording fee is $3.70 per $1,000 ($1,480 on $400,000) with the seller liable, and Greenville County charges $15 to file a deed and $25 to file a mortgage.
south-carolina.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller (grantor) is liable for the deed recording fee, $1,480 on a $400,000 sale ($1,040 state, $440 county), plus $10 to record a satisfaction of the existing mortgage; the buyer is liable only if the seller does not pay (commission not included).
south-carolina.recording_fees: Uniform filing fees (S.C. Code 8-21-310): $15 for a deed and $25 for a mortgage (Greenville County schedule matches); $10 for a satisfaction or release of mortgage.
south-carolina.biggest_items: Deed recording fee ($1.85 per $500, seller), lender charges, title search, policies and closing fee (no premium table), attorney fee.
south-carolina.example: $400,000 Greenville County sale with a $320,000 loan: deed recording fee $1,480, deed filing $15, mortgage filing $25, satisfaction of the seller's mortgage $10.
south-carolina.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage.

south-dakota.answer: South Dakota has no official typical closing-cost total; the seller pays a transfer fee of $0.50 per $500 of value ($400 on a $400,000 sale) and Minnehaha County charges $30 to record a deed and $30 to record a mortgage.
south-dakota.seller_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the seller (grantor) pays the transfer fee, $400 on a $400,000 sale, plus $30 to record a satisfaction of the old mortgage in Minnehaha County (commission not included).
south-dakota.recording_fees: Minnehaha County (October 2026): $30 for a deed, $30 for a mortgage, $30 for a satisfaction of mortgage, $2 more per page beyond 50.
south-dakota.biggest_items: Transfer fee ($0.50 per $500, seller), title insurance premium (insurer's filed rates), lender charges, survey and inspection.
south-dakota.example: $400,000 Sioux Falls home with a $320,000 loan: transfer fee $400, deed recording $30, mortgage recording $30, satisfaction of the seller's old mortgage $30.
south-dakota.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage.

tennessee.answer: Tennessee has no official typical closing-cost total; the buyer owes a realty transfer tax of $0.37 per $100 of price and the borrower a mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 after the first $2,000, which is $1,480 and $365.70 on a $400,000 home with a $320,000 loan.
tennessee.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the buyer (grantee) owes the transfer tax, $1,480 on a $400,000 home, and the borrower owes the mortgage tax, $365.70 on a $320,000 loan, plus recording fees and lender charges.
tennessee.recording_fees: Davidson County Register of Deeds (page last updated August 2021, confirm before closing): $5 per page, a $10 minimum and a $2 data-processing fee for deeds and deeds of trust, plus a $1 probate fee collected when state tax is paid.
tennessee.biggest_items: Realty transfer tax ($0.37 per $100, buyer), mortgage tax ($0.115 per $100, borrower), lender charges, title insurance (no state rate table read).
tennessee.example: $400,000 Nashville purchase with a $320,000 loan: transfer tax $1,480, mortgage tax $365.70, deed recording $27, deed of trust recording $77.
tennessee.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Seller costs generally come from the contract, such as releasing the existing loan and any commission.

texas.answer: Texas has no official typical closing-cost total; it charges no transfer tax, the owner's title policy on a $400,000 home costs $2,262 at Texas Department of Insurance rates effective March 1, 2026, and a simultaneous loan policy costs $100.
texas.buyer_text: Not a total: under the TREC resale contract the buyer pays the loan title policy ($100 when issued with the owner's policy), recording fees, lender charges, prepaid taxes and insurance, and half the escrow fee.
texas.seller_text: Not a total: under the TREC resale contract the seller pays to release existing liens, deed preparation, tax certificates, half the escrow fee, and the owner's title policy ($2,262 on $400,000) if paragraph 6A is checked for the seller (commission not included).
texas.recording_fees: Dallas County Clerk (as of October 2026): $25 for the first page and $4 for each additional page of a real property document.
texas.biggest_items: Owner's title policy ($2,262 on $400,000, state-set), lender charges, escrow fee (not set by TDI), prepaid taxes and insurance.
texas.example: $400,000 Dallas home with a $320,000 loan: owner's title policy $2,262, loan title policy $100, optional area and boundary amendment $113, 5-page deed recording $41, transfer tax $0.
texas.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. Title premium is set by the state and identical at every company; escrow fee is not set. The $2,262 owner's policy goes to whoever is checked in paragraph 6A of the contract.

utah.answer: Utah has no official typical closing-cost total; the state contract has the seller pay for the buyer's owner's title policy by default, each county recorder charges $40 per recorded document, and no transfer tax was found.
utah.buyer_text: Not a total: under the Utah REPC the buyer usually pays the lender's title policy, own escrow fees and lender charges (no amounts given).
utah.seller_text: Not a total: under REPC section 6.2 the seller pays the buyer's owner's title policy by default (no premium given); in the example the seller's share of property tax is $1,260.06 for a June 30 closing (commission not included).
utah.recording_fees: Utah Code 17-71-407: $40 per instrument plus $2 for each description beyond ten; Salt Lake County lists a flat $40 as of October 2026; some smaller counties add $5 in certain cases.
utah.biggest_items: Owner's title policy (seller by default, filed rates, no state table), lender charges, escrow fees, prorated property tax.
utah.example: $500,000 Salt Lake City home bought with a mortgage and closing June 30: deed recording $40, deed of trust recording $40, seller's property tax share $1,260.06, transfer tax $0.
utah.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. No transfer tax found in the sources read.

vermont.answer: Vermont has no official typical closing-cost total; the buyer owes the property transfer tax by statute, $3,940 on a $400,000 primary home, and the clerk charges $15 per page to record plus $15 for the tax return.
vermont.buyer_text: Statutory items only, not a total: the buyer owes the property transfer tax and Clean Water Surcharge, $3,940 on a $400,000 primary home, plus recording; total government charges are $4,210 in the example, before lender, title and attorney charges.
vermont.recording_fees: $15 per page to record any document (32 V.S.A. 1671), $15 for each previously recorded instrument a document affects, and $15 for the transfer tax return; collected by the town or city clerk (Burlington Clerk's schedule).
vermont.biggest_items: Property transfer tax (0.5% of first $200,000 and 1.25% above for a primary residence, 3.4% for a non-primary year-round home), Clean Water Surcharge (0.22%), lender charges, title and attorney fees.
vermont.example: $400,000 Burlington primary home with a 2-page deed and 15-page mortgage: transfer tax $3,500, Clean Water Surcharge $440, recording $255, return filing $15; total government charges $4,210.
vermont.note: The article gives no typical buyer or seller total or percentage. By statute the seller does not owe the transfer tax (contract can shift it). A nonresident seller faces 2.5% withholding by the buyer unless a Commissioner's Certificate exists.
