florida.answer: Florida taxes a home's assessed value minus exemptions at local millage rates; the 2026 homestead exemption removes $25,000 from all taxes plus up to $26,411 from non-school taxes, and Save Our Homes caps yearly assessment increases at the lower of 3% or inflation (2.7% for 2026). To appeal, file a petition with the Value Adjustment Board within 25 days after the TRIM notice is mailed.
florida.assessment_basis: County property appraiser values each home at just value as of January 1 (Fla. Stat. 192.042). Tax = (assessed value minus exemptions) x millage / 1,000 for each taxing body; school and non-school taxable values can differ.
florida.effective_rate_text: Miami (City of Miami, tax district 0100), 2025 adopted millage: 19.9878 mills total; $11,149.48 on a $600,000 home with homestead, $11,992.68 without.
florida.homestead_exemption: 2026: $25,000 off all taxes including school, plus an additional exemption of $26,411 off non-school taxes on value above $50,000 (indexed to inflation since 2025); maximum total $51,411. Must hold title and make the home your permanent residence on January 1; file with the property appraiser on or before March 1. CS/HJR 1F on the November 3, 2026 ballot would raise the non-school exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 if 60% of voters approve.
florida.assessment_cap: Homestead (Save Our Homes): lower of 3% or the CPI change a year (2.7% for 2026); resets to just value after a change of ownership; up to $500,000 portable to a new Florida homestead within three years. Non-homestead property: 10% a year for non-school taxes, no cap for school taxes.
florida.appeal_body: Value Adjustment Board (informal conference with the property appraiser is available first)
florida.appeal_deadline: 25 days after the TRIM notice is mailed (mailed each August)
florida.appeal_answer: In Florida, file a petition with the county Value Adjustment Board within 25 days after the August TRIM notice is mailed (Fla. Stat. 194.011(3)(d)); you can first ask the property appraiser for an informal conference.

georgia.answer: Georgia has no state property tax levy since 2016; counties, cities and school systems tax 40% of fair market value, and the state standard homestead exemption is $2,000 of assessed value. On a $400,000 Atlanta home the 2025 millage of 39.909 gives about $6,385 before exemptions, and in Fulton County you have 45 days from the assessment notice to appeal.
georgia.assessment_basis: County Board of Tax Assessors values property at fair market value; assessed value is 40% of fair market value (O.C.G.A. 48-5-7). Tax = (fair market value x 40% minus exemptions) x millage / 1,000.
georgia.effective_rate_text: City of Atlanta (Fulton County, Atlanta Public Schools), 2025: 39.909 mills total (9.039 county + 10.370 city + 20.500 schools); about $6,385.44 on a $400,000 home before exemptions, roughly 1.6% of market value.
georgia.homestead_exemption: State standard homestead: $2,000 off assessed value for county and school taxes. Fulton County and City of Atlanta basic: $30,000 off county (and $2,000 off school; $30,000 off City Operations, Park Fund and City School for Atlanta residents). Must own the home and have it as legal residence on January 1; apply by April 1 (the Department of Revenue also says you may apply until the end of your 45-day appeal window). Renews automatically. Age, income and disability exemptions also exist. A one-time 2026 grant reduces assessed value of homesteads by $18,000 (HB 439).
georgia.assessment_cap: Floating homestead exemptions: Fulton County base value rises each year by the lesser of CPI or 3% (2.6% a year for the City of Atlanta); statewide exemption (HB 581) set the 2026 inflation index at 2.7%, and the 2026 HOME Act (SB 33) makes it mandatory for local governments from January 1, 2027.
georgia.appeal_body: County Board of Assessors, then Board of Equalization, non-binding arbitration or hearing officer (Fulton County)
georgia.appeal_deadline: 45 days from the date of the notice of assessment (the deadline printed on your notice controls)
georgia.appeal_answer: In Georgia (Fulton County), you have 45 days from the date of the notice of assessment to appeal the value, online, in person or by mail, and you can choose a Board of Equalization hearing, non-binding arbitration or a hearing officer.
georgia.note: Appeal details are from Fulton County. Value can be appealed, not the tax.

hawaii.answer: In Honolulu, Hawaii, an owner with the home exemption pays $3.50 per $1,000 of net taxable value for July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, and the home exemption removes $120,000 of assessed value ($160,000 if 65 or older). To appeal, file with the Board of Review by January 15.
hawaii.assessment_basis: Property is taxed on 100% of fair market value, assessed in its entirety as fee simple; the date of assessment is October 1 before the tax year. Value comes from sales of similar properties and, where needed, a cost approach. Tax = (assessed value minus exemptions) / 1,000 x rate; $300 minimum per taxable parcel.
hawaii.effective_rate_text: Honolulu 2026-27: $3.50 per $1,000 of net taxable value for Residential; Residential A (assessed $1,000,000 or more, no home exemption) $4.00 per $1,000 on the first $1,000,000 and $11.40 above it. Example: $3,780 on a $1,200,000 home with the exemption.
hawaii.homestead_exemption: Home exemption for 2026-27: $120,000 of assessed value (owners under 65) or $160,000 (65 or older by June 30); rising to $140,000 and $180,000 from July 1, 2027. Must own and occupy as principal home on October 1, one exemption per taxpayer, ownership recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances, claim filed with the Real Property Assessment Division by September 30 before the tax year. No need to refile unless something changes.
hawaii.appeal_body: Honolulu Board of Review (Real Property Assessment Division)
hawaii.appeal_deadline: January 15 (notices of assessment mailed or posted by December 15)
hawaii.appeal_answer: In Honolulu, Hawaii, file an appeal with the Board of Review by January 15, online or on the city's form; the usual ground is that the assessed value exceeds market value by more than 10%, and you must bring evidence such as comparable sales.
hawaii.note: Article covers the City and County of Honolulu only. No annual cap on assessment increases in the pages read.

idaho.answer: Idaho's homeowner's exemption removes 50% of a home's market value, up to $125,000, from taxation, and property is assessed at market value as of January 1. In Boise's code area 01-1 the 2025 total levy is 0.9202%, and the appeal to the county Board of Equalization is due by 5:00 p.m. on the fourth Monday in June.
idaho.assessment_basis: County assessor assesses property at market value as of 12:01 a.m. January 1 of the levy year (Idaho Code 63-205). Tax = (assessed value minus exemptions) x total levy rate of all districts covering the parcel. Assessment notice mailed no later than the first Monday in June.
idaho.effective_rate_text: Boise (Ada County code area 01-1), 2025: total levy 0.9202% (0.009202233); Idaho State Tax Commission 2025 Ada County average 0.642%. $3,450.84 on a $500,000 home after the exemption.
idaho.homestead_exemption: Homeowner's exemption: the first $125,000 of the home's market value or 50% of it, whichever is less (63-602G). Owner-occupied primary dwelling plus up to one acre; apply once to the county assessor while the same owner lives in the same home; apply by the last business day of December to receive it for that year (after the second Monday in July it is granted as a tax cancellation). Separate Property Tax Reduction program (up to $1,500) for owner-occupants who are 65 or older, disabled, blind, widows or widowers etc. with income of $37,810 or less for 2025; apply January 1 to April 15.
idaho.assessment_cap: No cap on an individual assessment in the statutes read; taxing district budgets are capped at the highest of the previous three years plus up to 3% growth plus new construction and annexation (63-802), total increase generally not above 8%.
idaho.appeal_body: County Board of Equalization (Ada County), then Board of Tax Appeals or district court
idaho.appeal_deadline: 5:00 p.m. on the fourth Monday in June; next appeal within 30 days of the board's decision
idaho.appeal_answer: In Idaho (Ada County), file a written appeal with the county Board of Equalization by 5:00 p.m. on the fourth Monday in June, showing the assessed value is not the market value, and you can appeal the board's decision within 30 days.

illinois.answer: In Cook County, Illinois, a home is assessed at 10% of market value, multiplied by the state equalization factor (3.0300 for tax year 2025), and the General Homeowner Exemption subtracts $10,000. Chicago's average 2025 rate is 6.853%, and a Property Tax Appeal Board appeal is due within 30 days of the Board of Review notice.
illinois.assessment_basis: Cook County Assessor sets market value; assessed value is 10% of it for homes; the Illinois Department of Revenue equalization factor (3.0300 for 2025) is applied to give the equalized assessed value, then exemptions are subtracted. The Assessor reassesses one third of the county each year; Chicago was reassessed for tax year 2024 and next for tax year 2027.
illinois.effective_rate_text: Chicago average tax rate: 6.853% for 2025 (6.619% for 2024), per the Cook County Clerk. Example: $6,399.58 on a $341,200 median-value home with the $10,000 exemption (article's arithmetic; not the rate of any one parcel).
illinois.homestead_exemption: General homestead exemption: $10,000 off equalized assessed value in Cook County for tax year 2023 and after (35 ILCS 200/15-175) for owner-occupied homes. Senior (65 or older): additional $8,000 off EAV. Low-income senior assessment freeze (household income limit $65,000 through 2025, $75,000 for 2026). Veterans with a disability in specially adapted housing: assessed value up to $100,000 exempt. The Assessor decides who gets an exemption.
illinois.assessment_cap: No general cap on assessed value; the Low-Income Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze exemption freezes the base-year EAV for qualifying seniors. State limits (tax caps) can restrict the revenue a district extends.
illinois.appeal_body: Cook County Board of Review (township by township), then the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board
illinois.appeal_deadline: Board of Review: check your township's window (no date stated); Property Tax Appeal Board: within 30 days of the Board of Review notice, or 30 days after the Board transmits its final action on your township, whichever is later
illinois.appeal_answer: In Cook County, Illinois, appeal your assessment to the Board of Review during your township's filing window, and if the result disappoints you, appeal to the Property Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of the notice (35 ILCS 200/16-160); the PTAB reviews assessments only, not the tax bill or rate.
illinois.note: Board of Review filing dates by township are not given in the article. Article covers Cook County and Chicago.

indiana.answer: Indiana caps homestead property tax at 1% of gross assessed value, and for taxes payable in 2026 the standard homestead deduction is $48,000 plus a supplemental deduction of 40% of the remainder, with the standard deduction phasing out to $0 by 2031. 2026 bills are due May 11 and November 10, and an assessment appeal is due June 15 if the Form 11 notice was mailed before May 1.
indiana.assessment_basis: County assessor sets gross assessed value by mass appraisal, adjusted each year using sales data to track the market; the county auditor subtracts deductions to reach net assessed value. Tax = net assessed value / 100 x total rate, then credits come off. Assessment date is January 1.
indiana.effective_rate_text: Indianapolis Center Township (district 101), 2025 pay 2026: 2.7291 per $100 of net assessed value (seven Indianapolis districts range 2.6830 to 2.7291); estimated bill about $2,700 on a $300,000 home after the 1% cap and a $300 credit.
indiana.homestead_exemption: Standard deduction $48,000 for taxes payable 2026, then $40,000 (2027), $30,000 (2028), $20,000 (2029), $10,000 (2030), $0 (2031 and after), plus a supplemental deduction of 40% of the remainder for 2026 rising to 66.7% from 2031 (not above 75% of gross assessed value) under SEA 1 (2025); new supplemental homestead credit from 2026 of the lesser of 10% of the tax or $300. Principal residence (dwelling, garage, up to one acre); apply once with the county auditor on or before January 15; reapply only on sale or title change.
indiana.assessment_cap: Circuit breaker caps on tax as a share of gross assessed value: 1% for homesteads receiving the homestead standard deduction, 2% for other residential and agricultural land, 3% for other property; referendum taxes for building projects or school operating funds are exempt from the cap. Over 65 circuit breaker limits yearly increases to 2% for eligible seniors.
indiana.appeal_body: County assessor (informal), then the county property tax assessment board of appeals
indiana.appeal_deadline: June 15 if the Notice of Assessment (Form 11) was mailed before May 1; later if mailed on or after May 1 (check the Form 11)
indiana.appeal_answer: In Indiana, contact your county assessor and file your assessment appeal by June 15 if your Notice of Assessment (Form 11) was mailed before May 1; a notice mailed on or after May 1 carries a later deadline printed on the notice.
indiana.note: The article names the county assessor as the contact for appeals and does not name the next-level board.

iowa.answer: Iowa taxes a home's assessed market value after a state rollback, set at 44.5345% for residential property for the 2025 assessment year; in Des Moines the 2026-27 consolidated rate is $43.74496 per $1,000 of taxable value. File a written protest with the county board of review from April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year.
iowa.assessment_basis: Assessor sets actual value at fair market value (Iowa Code 441.21); real property is reassessed in odd-numbered years; the Department of Revenue certifies a residential percentage (rollback) each year, 47.4316% for 2024 and 44.5345% for 2025; taxable value = assessed value x percentage, minus exemptions. Taxes for an assessment year are billed two years later.
iowa.effective_rate_text: Des Moines city / Des Moines school district, 2026-27 consolidated rate: $43.74496 per $1,000 of taxable value (Polk County Auditor); $3,943.26 net tax on the $213,300 Census median value after the homestead credit.
iowa.homestead_exemption: Through assessment year 2025: credit equal to the levy on the first $4,850 of actual value (extra $6,500 taxable value exemption for owners 65 or older by January 1). From assessment year 2026 (SF 2472): exemption of 10% of taxable value, at least $5,500 and at most $20,000 (maximum inflation-adjusted from 2027); the 65+ exemption stays. File with the county assessor by July 1 of the year you first claim it; own and occupy the home on July 1; a buyer must refile after a sale.
iowa.assessment_cap: Growth of residential taxable value from revaluation is limited to 3% a year in total (Iowa Code 441.21(4)), implemented through the annual rollback percentage.
iowa.appeal_body: County board of review (then the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court)
iowa.appeal_deadline: April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year (assessor notifies of changed value by April 1); next appeal to the Property Assessment Appeal Board within 20 days after the board of review adjourns or by May 31, whichever is later
iowa.appeal_answer: In Iowa, file a written protest with the county board of review from April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year; if you lose, appeal to the Property Assessment Appeal Board within 20 days after the board of review adjourns or by May 31, whichever is later, or go to district court.

kansas.answer: Kansas assesses a home at 11.5% of appraised fair market value and applies the mills of every taxing unit, with $75,000 of a home's value exempt from the 20-mill statewide school levy. A $400,000 Overland Park home in USD 512 owes about $4,378 on 2025 Johnson County levies, and the informal appeal is due 30 days after the valuation notice is mailed.
kansas.assessment_basis: County appraiser sets fair market value as of January 1; residential property is assessed at 11.5% (vacant lots 12%, commercial 25%). Tax = assessed value x total mills / 1,000. Valuation notice mailed on or before March 1; the appraiser may not raise value solely for normal repair or maintenance (K.S.A. 79-1460(b)).
kansas.effective_rate_text: Overland Park, Johnson County, 2025: 48.043 mills for non-school units plus school-district mills (USD 512 total school 50.886); about $4,378.23 a year on a $400,000 home in USD 512, about 1.09% of value (USD 229 about $4,504; USD 233 about $4,887).
kansas.homestead_exemption: $75,000 of appraised value of residential property is exempt from the 20-mill statewide school levy for tax year 2024 and after (K.S.A. 79-201x), saving $172.50 a year; no application or age condition in the text. Separate refunds claimed January 1 to April 15 with the Department of Revenue: Homestead refund (K-40H) up to $700 (household income of $43,389 or less, home valued at no more than $350,000, 55 or older, disabled or other listed condition) and SAFESR (75% of taxes paid for owners 65+ with income of $25,380 or less).
kansas.appeal_body: County appraiser (informal appeal), then Kansas State Board of Tax Appeals
kansas.appeal_deadline: 30 days after the valuation notice was mailed (Johnson County lists March 31); appeal to the State Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days of the result
kansas.appeal_answer: In Kansas, file your informal appeal with the county appraiser within 30 days after the valuation notice is mailed (Johnson County lists March 31), and if you disagree with the result, appeal to the Kansas State Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days.
kansas.note: No statutory cap on yearly increases in appraised value found in the article. Appeal dates are from Johnson County.

kentucky.answer: Kentucky taxes real estate at fair cash value set by the county Property Valuation Administrator; the state rate is 10.3 cents per $100 for 2026, and Louisville's Urban Services District total for 2025 is $1.260 per $100. The $49,100 homestead exemption applies only to owners 65 or older or totally disabled, and you must request a PVA conference before appealing to the local board of assessment appeals.
kentucky.assessment_basis: County PVA values property at fair cash value as of January 1 (KRS 132.220); all real property can be revalued every year and each parcel must be physically inspected at least once every four years; homes are mostly valued by sales comparison. Tax = assessed value / 100 x rate.
kentucky.effective_rate_text: Louisville (Jefferson County), 2025: $1.260 per $100 inside the Urban Services District (state 0.106 + Metro 0.118 + school 0.717 + USD 0.319) and $0.941 outside it, before fire district or city rates. State rate 10.3 cents per $100 for 2026 (10.6 in 2025).
kentucky.homestead_exemption: $49,100 of assessed value for the 2025-2026 assessment years, only for owners who are 65 or older during the year or classified as totally disabled and who own and live in the home (KRS 132.810); adjusted every two years with the federal cost-of-living index; apply once with the county PVA (disability under 65 must reapply yearly); one per residential unit.
kentucky.assessment_cap: None per home found; taxing districts are limited under House Bill 44 (compensating rate, at most 4% more revenue, or a higher rate after a public hearing that voters can petition to recall).
kentucky.appeal_body: County Property Valuation Administrator conference (required first), then the local board of assessment appeals via the county clerk
kentucky.appeal_deadline: Jefferson County 2026: PVA online conference window April 24 to May 18; board of assessment appeals deadline June 12 (no later than one workday after the inspection period ends, or after an extension of up to 25 days); dates change each year
kentucky.appeal_answer: In Kentucky, request a conference with the county Property Valuation Administrator first (required under KRS 133.120), then appeal to the local board of assessment appeals by filing with the county clerk no later than one workday after the inspection period ends; in Jefferson County in 2026 the conference window ran April 24 to May 18 and the board deadline was June 12.
kentucky.note: Appeal dates are Jefferson County 2026; the article says dates change each year.

louisiana.answer: Louisiana assesses residential land and buildings at 10% of fair market value, and the homestead exemption removes $7,500 of assessed value ($75,000 of market value) from most taxes on a home you own and occupy. New Orleans's 2026 citywide millage is 121.20 mills, and complaints go to the board of review at least 7 days before its hearing, after the assessment list is open July 15 to August 15.
louisiana.assessment_basis: Assessor in each parish determines fair market value; land and residential improvements are each listed at 10% of fair market value (Art. VII, sec. 18(B)); property must be reappraised at intervals of no more than four years. Tax = taxable assessment minus exemptions, times millage.
louisiana.effective_rate_text: New Orleans, 2026: citywide millage 121.20 mills (120.48 exemption-eligible plus 11.51 mills police and fire charged without the exemption, per the article's table); $3,056.10 on a $300,000 house with the homestead exemption, before special district fees.
louisiana.homestead_exemption: $7,500 of assessed valuation ($75,000 of market value at the 10% ratio) off state, parish and special ad valorem taxes for a bona fide homestead up to 160 acres, owned and occupied as primary residence by a natural person; one per person in the state. In Orleans it covers state, general city, school, levee and levee district taxes but not police and fire millages (11.51 mills). August 1 status generally decides the following year; permanent registration with the assessor, no renewal while qualified.
louisiana.assessment_cap: Phase-in over four years if a reappraisal raises assessed value by more than 50% of the previous year's value (homestead owners; ends on sale). Special assessment-level freeze for owners 65 or older (and certain veterans, surviving spouses, permanently totally disabled) with prior-year adjusted gross income not above $100,000, adjusted for inflation from tax year 2026; ends on sale.
louisiana.appeal_body: Parish board of review (Orleans Parish), then the Louisiana Tax Commission
louisiana.appeal_deadline: Assessment list open for inspection July 15 to August 15; complaint to the board of review at least 7 days before its hearing; board decision final unless appealed to the Louisiana Tax Commission
louisiana.appeal_answer: In Orleans Parish, Louisiana, inspect the assessment list from July 15 to August 15 and file a complaint with the board of review at least 7 days before its hearing; the board's decision is final unless appealed to the Louisiana Tax Commission (R.S. 47:1992).
louisiana.note: Appeal calendar is for Orleans Parish. The article does not state a day-count deadline for the Tax Commission appeal.

maine.answer: Maine has no single state rate for home property tax: each town or city values property as of April 1 and sets its own rate. The homestead exemption takes $25,000 of just value off, you must apply by April 1, and you have 185 days from commitment to file a written abatement application with the assessors.
maine.assessment_basis: Municipal assessors record the nature, amount and value of each parcel as of April 1 (36 M.R.S. 708), with land valued separately from buildings, using cost, income and sales comparison approaches (701-A). Tax = (assessed value minus exemptions) x mill rate / 1,000. Each municipality sets its own rate, tax year and due dates; Portland says its assessments represent 100% of market value as of April 1, 2025.
maine.homestead_exemption: $25,000 of just value ($10,000 base plus $15,000 additional under 683; up to $25,000 under 683-A from April 1, 2027), multiplied by the municipality's certified assessment ratio. Must have owned a homestead in Maine for at least 12 months and occupy it as permanent residence on April 1; apply once to the local assessor on or before April 1 of the tax year. Veterans age 62+ or 100% disabled $6,000; veteran with specially adapted housing grant $50,000.
maine.appeal_body: Municipal assessors (abatement application), then the board of assessment review if the municipality has one, then Superior Court
maine.appeal_deadline: Written abatement application within 185 days from commitment; then 60 days after notice of the decision (or deemed denial) to appeal to the board of assessment review
maine.appeal_answer: In Maine, apply in writing to the municipal assessors for an abatement within 185 days from commitment, and if denied, appeal to the board of assessment review within 60 days after notice of the decision, then to Superior Court under Rule 80B.
maine.note: No statewide effective rate and no assessment cap in the article.

maryland.answer: Maryland property tax is local with a small state rate: for 2026-27 Baltimore City charges $2.248 per $100 of assessed value plus the State's $0.112, or $2.360 in total. The homestead credit caps yearly growth of the taxable assessment on a principal residence (4% in Baltimore City, 10% at most), and you have 45 days from the notice date to appeal.
maryland.assessment_basis: State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) values all real property once in every 3-year cycle (Tax-Property 8-104(b)); increases are phased in one-third a year over three years, so taxable assessment is often below the latest market value. Land and buildings valued separately. Bill = taxable assessment / 100 x combined rate, minus credits.
maryland.effective_rate_text: 2026-27: Baltimore City $2.2480 local plus $0.1120 State = $2.3600 per $100; Baltimore County $1.2120; Anne Arundel County $1.0800; Howard County $1.1560 combined per $100.
maryland.homestead_exemption: No homestead exemption; the Homestead Property Tax Credit limits yearly growth of taxable assessment on the principal residence (see cap). Apply once, by May 1 before the first tax year you want it; must live there by July 1 of the tax year; not granted if the home was sold for consideration during the previous tax year. Separate income-based Homeowners' Property Tax Credit.
maryland.assessment_cap: Homestead credit: local limit set by each county or municipality at 10% or less (2026-27: Baltimore City 4%, Baltimore County 4%, Anne Arundel County 2%, Howard County 5%); the State's share is always capped at 10%.
maryland.appeal_body: State Department of Assessments and Taxation (supervisor of assessments), then the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board, then the Maryland Tax Court
maryland.appeal_deadline: Within 45 days of the notice date (60 days from the transfer if you buy between January 1 and June 30 and the deed is recorded); then 30 days from the final notice to appeal to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board
maryland.appeal_answer: In Maryland, file your assessment appeal with the Department of Assessments and Taxation within 45 days of the notice date (60 days from the transfer if you bought between January 1 and June 30), then appeal to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days of the final notice.

massachusetts.answer: Massachusetts property tax is set city by city; in Boston the fiscal 2026 residential rate is $12.40 per $1,000 of assessed value, and owner-occupants can claim a residential exemption worth up to $4,353.74. To appeal, file an abatement application with the Boston Assessing Department after the third-quarter bill and by February 1, 2027 for fiscal 2027.
massachusetts.assessment_basis: Local assessors make a fair cash valuation of real property as of January 1 each year (G.L. c. 59, sec. 38 and 2A); the owner of record on January 1 is assessed. Cities may set different residential and commercial rates. Tax = (assessed value x rate / 1,000) minus exemptions.
massachusetts.effective_rate_text: Boston fiscal 2026 (July 2025 to June 2026): residential $12.40 per $1,000 (fiscal 2025 $11.58); commercial $26.96. $5,609.52 on an $800,000 home with the residential exemption and 1% Community Preservation surcharge.
massachusetts.homestead_exemption: Boston residential exemption (G.L. c. 59, sec. 5C): saved qualified owner-occupants up to $4,353.74 in fiscal 2026 (about $351,000 of value at $12.40 per $1,000); must own and live in the property as principal residence, one property only; fiscal 2027 application deadline April 1, 2027. Other exemptions (elderly, veteran, blind, hardship) exist; the one that saves the most applies.
massachusetts.assessment_cap: No cap on individual assessments. Proposition 2 1/2 limits a city's total levy to a 2.5% increase a year plus new growth (unless voters approve an override) and total taxes to 2.5% of full value; Boston says it does not limit year-to-year growth of individual assessments.
massachusetts.appeal_body: Boston Assessing Department (abatement application), then the Appellate Tax Board
massachusetts.appeal_deadline: For fiscal 2027: after the third-quarter bill and no later than February 1, 2027; the Department has three months to respond; if refused, three months from the decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board
massachusetts.appeal_answer: In Boston, Massachusetts, file an abatement application with the Assessing Department after the third-quarter bill and no later than February 1, 2027 for fiscal 2027; if it is denied, you have three months from the decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board, and filing does not delay payment.
massachusetts.note: Rates, exemption and appeal dates are Boston's. The article says the first two quarterly bills use the prior year's value and rate.

michigan.answer: Michigan assesses property at 50% of true cash value and caps yearly growth in taxable value at the lesser of inflation or 5% (2.7% for 2026) until the home is sold, and the principal residence exemption removes 18 mills of school operating tax. For a residential property, a Michigan Tax Tribunal petition is due July 31 of the tax year, after the required March Board of Review.
michigan.assessment_basis: Assessed value (state equalized value) is 50% of true cash value (MCL 211.27a(1)), fixed on December 31 of the year before (tax day). Taxable value is the lesser of the prior year's taxable value times the lesser of 1.05 or the inflation rate, plus additions, or the current assessed value. Tax = taxable value / 1,000 x total mills.
michigan.effective_rate_text: Detroit (Wayne County 2024 apportionment): 67.2737 mills total for a principal residence and 85.2737 mills for other property; $4,036.42 on $60,000 taxable value for a principal residence.
michigan.homestead_exemption: Principal residence exemption: exempt from the school operating tax, 18 mills (about $1,080 a year on $60,000 taxable value). Claim by affidavit with the local tax collecting unit by June 1 for the next summer levy or November 1 for the next winter levy; no similar exemption in another state; ends December 31 of the year of transfer and the buyer must file a new affidavit. Poverty exemption (25% to 100% reduction of taxable value) is heard by the Board of Review.
michigan.assessment_cap: Taxable value may rise by the lesser of 5% or the inflation rate multiplier each year (1.027, or 2.7%, for 2026); resets to assessed value the calendar year after a transfer of ownership.
michigan.appeal_body: Local March Board of Review (required), then the Michigan Tax Tribunal
michigan.appeal_deadline: Board of Review meets starting the second Monday in March (Detroit assessor review optional, February 1 to 22 in 2026); residential petition to the Michigan Tax Tribunal due July 31 of the tax year
michigan.appeal_answer: In Michigan, protest your assessment first at the March Board of Review, which meets starting the second Monday in March, then, for residential property, file a petition with the Michigan Tax Tribunal by July 31 of the tax year (MCL 205.735a).
michigan.note: Appeal steps are as listed by the City of Detroit. Rate figures are 2024, the most recent table the article read.

minnesota.answer: Minnesota values a home each year as of January 2 and taxes a share set by property class: a homestead is taxed at 1% of its first $500,000 of taxable value after a market value exclusion of up to $38,000. On a $400,000 Minneapolis homestead, Hennepin County's final 2025 rates give about $5,723 a year, and a Tax Court or district court petition is due by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.
minnesota.assessment_basis: County assessor sets market value as of January 2 each year (Minn. Stat. 273.01), reappraising each parcel at least every five years; state law converts market value to net tax capacity by class (homestead class 1a: 1% of the first $500,000, 1.25% above). Each taxing district applies a rate to net tax capacity; school referendum levies use a rate on market value.
minnesota.effective_rate_text: Minneapolis (Hennepin County, first taxing area), final 2025: total tax capacity rate 132.419% (range 132.419% to 134.575% across six Minneapolis areas) plus 0.14151% school referendum rate on market value; $5,723.10 on a $400,000 homestead, about 1.43% of market value.
minnesota.homestead_exemption: No flat exemption; a homestead market value exclusion of up to $38,000 applies: 40% of value for homes of $95,000 or less, $38,000 minus 9% of the value above $95,000 for $95,000 to $517,200, none at $517,200 or more (e.g. $28,550 at $200,000; $10,550 at $400,000). Must own, occupy and apply with the county assessor by December 31 (Hennepin County). Blind or disabled owners (class 1b): first $50,000 taxed at 0.45%. Senior deferral for owners 65+ with household income of $96,000 or less and five years in the home.
minnesota.appeal_body: Local board of appeal and equalization, then county board of appeal and equalization, or the Minnesota Tax Court
minnesota.appeal_deadline: Local board meets between April 1 and May 31 (valuation notice mailed March to April in Hennepin County); county board mid-June in Hennepin County; Tax Court or district court petition by April 30 of the year the tax is payable
minnesota.appeal_answer: In Minnesota, if you disagree with your valuation notice you can appeal to the local board of appeal and equalization (it meets between April 1 and May 31), then the county board (mid-June in Hennepin County), or petition the Tax Court or district court by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.
minnesota.note: The article read no cap on yearly increases in a home's market value. Board dates are as stated for Hennepin County.

mississippi.answer: Mississippi taxes an owner-occupied home at 10% of true value and applies local mills; the regular homestead exemption is a credit of up to $300, and owners 65 or older or totally disabled are exempt on the first $7,500 of assessed value. A Jackson home in Hinds County had 193.31 mills for 2024-25, and appeals go to the county Board of Supervisors, normally by the first Monday in August before taxes are due.
mississippi.assessment_basis: County tax assessor appraises property at true value; Class I single-family owner-occupied residential real property is assessed at 10% of true value (other real property 15%). Tax = true value x assessment ratio x millage rate. Assessors must revalue real property at least once every four years.
mississippi.effective_rate_text: Jackson (Hinds County, Jackson Public Schools), 2024-25: 193.31 mills (county 44.09 + city 63.03 + school 86.19); $2,899.65 on a $150,000 home before exemption.
mississippi.homestead_exemption: Tier 1 (under 65, not disabled): credit of up to $300 against taxes due, reaching the maximum at $7,350 to $7,500 of assessed value. Tier 2 (65 or older, or totally disabled, by January 1): exempt on the first $7,500 of assessed value. Tier 3: full exemption for veterans with a service-connected total disability, veterans 90 or older, and certain unremarried surviving spouses. Own and occupy as primary residence on January 1; apply with the county tax assessor between January 1 and April 1.
mississippi.assessment_cap: No limit on one home's assessed value found; MSU Extension describes a 10% cap on the increase in total tax receipts of a county or city, and says increases in assessed value after the first exemption year are exempt for owners 65 or older or disabled, with limits.
mississippi.appeal_body: County Board of Supervisors (hearing request); contact the county Chancery Clerk for the procedure
mississippi.appeal_deadline: Normally by the first Monday in August before the taxes are due (confirm with your chancery clerk)
mississippi.appeal_answer: In Mississippi, request a hearing with your county Board of Supervisors, normally by the first Monday in August before the taxes are due, and contact your county Chancery Clerk to confirm the procedure.
mississippi.note: Appeal details come from the Department of Revenue and are general; the article says to confirm date and procedure locally.

missouri.answer: Missouri assesses a home at 19% of market value and local districts apply their rates per $100 of assessed value; the City of St. Louis 2025 residential rate is $8.1867 per $100, about $3,336 a year on a $214,500 home. Missouri has no general homestead exemption in the statutes reviewed, and in St. Louis you can appeal to the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July.
missouri.assessment_basis: Residential property is assessed at 19% of true market value (farmland 12%, commercial 32%) under RSMo 137.115; new values are set as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year and carry into the even-numbered year except for new construction and improvements. Tax = market value x 19% x rate / 100.
missouri.effective_rate_text: City of St. Louis 2025 residential rate: $8.1867 per $100 of assessed value ($3,336.49 on a $214,500 home); Census-based rough ratios of median taxes to median value: about 1.02% (St. Louis), 0.79% (Missouri), 0.89% (U.S.), not official effective rates.
missouri.assessment_cap: No percentage cap; the assessor must physically inspect a home before raising its assessed value by more than 15% since the last assessment (excluding new construction), per RSMo 137.115.10. Credits instead: St. Louis Senior Property Tax Freeze Credit (age 62+, market value of $528,392 or less; freezes the City part only) and the state Property Tax Credit (up to $1,550 for the lowest income band).
missouri.appeal_body: Assessor (informal review), then Board of Equalization, then State Tax Commission
missouri.appeal_deadline: City of St. Louis: informal review May 1 to June 23; Board of Equalization appeal due by the second Monday in July; State Tax Commission by September 30 or 30 days after the Board's decision, whichever is later
missouri.appeal_answer: In the City of St. Louis, Missouri, ask for informal review with the Assessor from May 1 to June 23, appeal to the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July, and then appeal to the State Tax Commission by September 30 or 30 days after the Board's decision, whichever is later.
missouri.note: No general homestead exemption in the statutes reviewed. Appeal dates are the City of St. Louis calendar. An appeal does not postpone the bill.

montana.answer: Montana taxes a home on a state-set percentage of market value: for tax year 2026 an enrolled primary residence pays 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value, while a second home pays a flat 1.9%. You have 30 days from the date on your classification and appraisal notice to request an informal review or appeal to the county tax appeal board.
montana.assessment_basis: Department of Revenue appraises the property; taxable value is market value times the class four tax rate (MCA 15-6-134), then local mills apply. All class four real property is revalued every two years (2025-2026 cycle, valuation date January 1, 2024). Tiered rates for enrolled primary residence 2026: 0.76% to $378,000, 0.90% to $756,000, 1.10% to $1,511,999, 1.90% above.
montana.effective_rate_text: Billings example, tax year 2025: City of Billings 244.39 mills plus Yellowstone County countywide 140.95 mills on a taxable value of $3,040 (0.76% of $400,000) = $1,171.44 for those two pieces only; schools, state and special districts add more.
montana.homestead_exemption: No dollar exemption; the homestead reduced rate is a lower tax rate: 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value for 2026 versus a flat 1.9% for a second home. Must be principal residence at least seven months a year, owned by you or your revocable grantor trust, current on property taxes, and claimed on only one residence; must be enrolled (automatic if you got the 2025 rebate and live in the same home); application window for tax year 2027: May 4, 2026 to March 1, 2027. Property Tax Assistance Program multiplies the rate by 20%, 50% or 70% by income on the first $350,000.
montana.assessment_cap: No annual percentage cap on market value in the sources read; values are fixed for the two-year cycle (MCA 15-7-111) and local revenue growth is limited to one-half of the average inflation rate of the past three years plus new property.
montana.appeal_body: Department of Revenue (informal classification and appraisal review, Form AB-26) or directly the county tax appeal board; then Montana Tax Appeal Board and district court
montana.appeal_deadline: Within 30 days of the date on the notice (informal review or county tax appeal board via the county clerk and recorder)
montana.appeal_answer: In Montana, file a Request for Informal Classification and Appraisal Review (Form AB-26) with the Department of Revenue within 30 days of the date on your notice, or appeal directly to the county tax appeal board through the county clerk and recorder within 30 days of the notice date.

nebraska.answer: Nebraska taxes residential property at actual (market) value as of January 1; Douglas County's average rate for tax year 2025 was 2.0381%. There is no homestead exemption for every owner, and you protest your valuation with the county clerk by June 30.
nebraska.assessment_basis: County assessor values residential property at actual value (market value) as of January 1 (Neb. Rev. Stat. 77-201, 77-1301); farmland at 75% of actual value. Tax = taxable value / 100 x total rate of the taxing units covering the address.
nebraska.effective_rate_text: Douglas County average 2025: 2.0381% (2.0462% in 2024). A home in Omaha Public Schools paid 2.05683 per $100 in 2025 rates, $6,170.49 on a $300,000 assessed value, before the state credit.
nebraska.homestead_exemption: Targeted, not for every owner: owners 65 or older before January 1 (Category 1), certain disabled owners and veterans (Categories 2, 3, 6) and certain disabled veterans and surviving spouses (4V, 4S, 5, 7, with no income or value limit). Own and live in the home January 1 through August 15; apply to the county assessor after February 1 and by June 30. Exempt share depends on household income (2026: single owner 65+ gets 100% up to $37,000 and 0% from $54,301; married 100% up to $43,400 and 0% from $64,501); exempt amount capped at 100% of the county average value for Category 1 (Douglas County $302,282) and 120% for Categories 2, 3, 6.
nebraska.appeal_body: County board of equalization (protest filed with the county clerk), then the Tax Equalization and Review Commission
nebraska.appeal_deadline: File a protest with the county clerk by June 30 (one per parcel); appeal to the state commission by August 24 (September 10 if extended)
nebraska.appeal_answer: In Nebraska, file a protest with the county clerk by June 30, with your requested value and supporting documentation, and if the county board of equalization rules against you, appeal to the Tax Equalization and Review Commission by August 24 (September 10 if extended).
nebraska.note: No percentage cap on yearly value increases in the statutes read. State credit for tax year 2026: real property credit $118.87 per $100,000 of valuation plus a school district credit.

nevada.answer: Nevada taxes 35% of a home's taxable value, and in the City of Las Vegas the fiscal 2026-27 rate is $3.2782 per $100 of assessed value. A partial abatement under NRS 361.4723 limits the yearly increase in the tax bill on an owner-occupied home to 3%, and in Clark County you file an appeal with the County Board of Equalization by January 15.
nevada.assessment_basis: County assessor sets taxable value each year using the cost method (land at market value plus replacement cost of improvements, depreciated 1.5% a year up to 50 years); assessed value is 35% of taxable value; tax = assessed value x rate per $100. Combined rate capped at $3.64 per $100 (NRS 361.453), constitutional cap $5.00.
nevada.effective_rate_text: Fiscal 2026-27, per $100 of assessed value: City of Las Vegas $3.2782; Henderson $2.9613; North Las Vegas $3.3544; unincorporated Clark County areas $2.9328. Example: $4,015.80 before the cap on a $350,000 taxable value in Las Vegas.
nevada.assessment_cap: 3% a year on the tax bill (not the value) for an owner-occupied primary residence through a partial abatement under NRS 361.4723; qualifying rentals 3%; other residences, land and commercial property up to 8%. Recording a deed removes the abatement until the owner returns the Assessor's postcard; new construction or change of use gets no cap in the first year.
nevada.appeal_body: County Board of Equalization (Clark County), then State Board of Equalization and District Court
nevada.appeal_deadline: Forms available in December; file by January 15 (next business day if on a weekend or holiday)
nevada.appeal_answer: In Clark County, Nevada, file an appeal with the County Board of Equalization by January 15, after talking to an Assessor appraiser, and if the board upholds the value you can go to the State Board of Equalization and then District Court.
nevada.note: No general homestead exemption; only exemptions for surviving spouses, veterans, disabled veterans and blind owners (amounts in assessed value, apply by June 15). Appeal details are from Clark County.

new-hampshire.answer: New Hampshire property tax is set locally and property is taxed at market value as of April 1; in Manchester the 2025 rate is $20.24 per $1,000 of assessed value. To challenge an assessment, apply to the Board of Assessors for an abatement by March 1 after the notice of tax.
new-hampshire.assessment_basis: Assessors appraise most property at market value (full and true value) as of April 1 each year (RSA 75:1, 74:1); the tax year runs April 1 to March 31; Manchester uses sales comparison and cost approaches (income approach only for rental property). Tax = assessed value x rate / 1,000.
new-hampshire.effective_rate_text: Manchester 2025: $20.24 per $1,000 of assessed value (municipal $10.04 + local education $7.33 + state education $1.51 + county $1.36); $7,084.00 on a $350,000 assessment with no exemption.
new-hampshire.appeal_body: Board of Assessors (abatement application), then the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or Superior Court
new-hampshire.appeal_deadline: Abatement application received or postmarked by March 1 after the notice of tax; board decides by July 1; appeal by September 1
new-hampshire.appeal_answer: In New Hampshire, apply to your Board of Assessors for an abatement by March 1 after the notice of tax (RSA 76:16); if it is denied or not answered by July 1, appeal by September 1 to the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to Superior Court.
new-hampshire.note: No general homestead exemption; Manchester lists blind, disabled, elderly (e.g. $156,000 deduction at ages 65 to 74, with income and asset limits), solar, veterans and deferral programs. No assessment cap in the article. Appeal details are from Manchester. The article cites a 2025 ratio of 64.8% without explaining it.

new-jersey.answer: New Jersey taxes real property at assessed value times a local general tax rate; in Newark the 2025 rate is $3.999 per $100 of assessed value, and the average residential bill was $7,641. You can appeal your assessment to the County Board of Taxation by April 1.
new-jersey.assessment_basis: Full and fair (market) value assessed as of October 1 of the year before the tax year; after a municipal revaluation assessments must be at 100% of true market value, and between revaluations the Division tracks an average ratio (Newark 35.83% for tax year 2027, common level range 30.46% to 41.20%). Tax = assessed value x rate / 100.
new-jersey.effective_rate_text: Newark 2025: general tax rate $3.999 per $100 of assessed value (effective rate 1.845, for comparing towns only, not for bills); average residential assessment $191,065 and average residential bill $7,641. Essex County general rates range from $1.862 (Roseland) to $4.157 (Belleville).
new-jersey.appeal_body: County Board of Taxation (Essex County for Newark); Tax Court directly if assessed over $1,000,000
new-jersey.appeal_deadline: April 1, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of assessment notices, or May 1 if the municipality did a revaluation or reassessment; county board judgment appealed to the Tax Court within 45 days
new-jersey.appeal_answer: In New Jersey, file your assessment appeal with the County Board of Taxation by April 1 (or May 1 if the municipality did a revaluation, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of notices), and appeal a county board judgment to the Tax Court within 45 days; properties assessed over $1,000,000 can go straight to Tax Court.
new-jersey.note: No general homestead exemption: small deductions ($250 senior or disabled, $250 veteran, 100% for disabled veterans) plus state ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ benefits (2025 application deadline November 2, 2026). No cap on a single owner's assessment found; municipal and county budgets are capped (2% cost-of-living adjustment for 2026).

new-mexico.answer: New Mexico taxes one-third of a home's market value; Albuquerque's 2026 residential rate is 48.313 mills, about $6,357 a year on a $400,000 home after the $2,000 head-of-family exemption. Residential value can rise only 3% a year until the home is sold, and you protest within 30 days of the valuation notice.
new-mexico.assessment_basis: County assessor values the home at market value (7-36-15), subject to the residential limit; taxable value is one-third (33 1/3%) of that value (7-37-3); net taxable value is taxable value minus exemptions. Notice of valuation mailed by April 1. Tax = net taxable value x mills / 1,000.
new-mexico.effective_rate_text: Albuquerque (Bernalillo County district 12 IN R) 2026: 48.313 mills total (2025: 48.323); about $6,357 a year on a $400,000 home, about 1.6% of market value.
new-mexico.homestead_exemption: Head-of-family exemption: up to $2,000 of taxable value for a New Mexico resident who is the head of a family (7-37-4), one person per household in one county; worth about $84 a year at the Albuquerque rate; applied automatically once allowed, but a buyer must claim it within 30 days of the first notice of valuation. Veteran exemption $10,000 of taxable value (2025, inflation-adjusted from 2026). Value freeze for owners 65 or older or disabled with modified gross income of $44,200 or less (apply within 30 days of the notice).
new-mexico.assessment_cap: Residential value cannot exceed the higher of 103% of last year's value or 106.1% of the value two years earlier (7-36-21.2), summarized as 3% a year; does not apply to new improvements or change in use or zoning; resets to market value after a sale. It limits value, not the tax bill.
new-mexico.appeal_body: Assessor (protest), then the county valuation protests board, then district court
new-mexico.appeal_deadline: Within 30 days of the notice of valuation (some counties mail it with the prior bill; then the later of April 1 or 30 days)
new-mexico.appeal_answer: In New Mexico, file a protest with the county assessor within 30 days of the notice of valuation (mailed by April 1), the county valuation protests board hears it, and you can appeal its decision to district court; you can instead pay first and file a refund claim, but you must choose one route.

new-york.answer: New York has no single property tax system: outside New York City, local assessors set values and local governments and school districts set rates, with STAR credits for primary residences, while in the city a one- to three-family home is Class 1, assessed at 6% of market value and taxed at 19.843% for tax year 2026. Outside the city, file a grievance by Grievance Day (usually the fourth Tuesday in May); in the city, Class 1 complaints are due by March 15.
new-york.assessment_basis: Outside NYC, each municipality may assess at market value or at a fraction of it, uniformly; the state measures the level of assessment with an equalization rate. In NYC, the Department of Finance values one- to three-unit homes by statistical modeling of similar sales in the prior three years and applies a 6% assessment ratio for Class 1 (45% for Classes 2, 3 and 4).
new-york.effective_rate_text: NYC tax year 2026: Class 1 19.843% (2025: 20.085%); Class 2 12.439%; Class 3 11.108%; Class 4 10.848%. Outside NYC no single official statewide figure exists, and the article gives no typical rate.
new-york.homestead_exemption: No homestead exemption as such; STAR (School Tax Relief) lowers school taxes on a primary residence. Basic STAR: owners of a primary residence of any age, income $500,000 or less for the STAR credit ($250,000 or less for the exemption). Enhanced STAR: at least one resident owner 65 or older by December 31 of the benefit year, income $110,750 or less for 2026 benefits ($113,550 for 2027). New homeowners get the credit, not the exemption; register once with the Tax Department.
new-york.assessment_cap: Outside NYC the state Property Tax Cap limits total local levies to the lower of 2% or inflation (not an individual bill; a 60% vote can override). In NYC Class 1 assessed value can rise at most 6% a year and 20% over five years, unless from new construction or renovation.
new-york.appeal_body: Outside NYC: assessor or board of assessment review (grievance, Form RP-524), then Small Claims Assessment Review or tax certiorari in State Supreme Court; in NYC: NYC Tax Commission
new-york.appeal_deadline: Outside NYC: Grievance Day, usually the fourth Tuesday in May (Suffolk towns third Tuesday in May, Westchester towns third Tuesday in June, assessing villages often the third Tuesday in February); NYC: March 15 for Class 1 properties and March 1 for all others
new-york.appeal_answer: In New York outside New York City, file Form RP-524 with your assessor or board of assessment review by Grievance Day, usually the fourth Tuesday in May, and in New York City file with the NYC Tax Commission by March 15 for Class 1 properties (March 1 for all others); missing the deadline loses review for that year.
new-york.note: Dates and rules differ outside NYC and in NYC; confirm the date with your assessor or the Tax Commission.

north-carolina.answer: North Carolina property tax is set locally: in Charlotte the 2025-26 combined rate is 76.68 cents per $100 of value (49.27 Mecklenburg County plus 27.41 City of Charlotte). There is no general homestead exemption in the NCDOR forms, and after the local board of equalization and review you appeal to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days of the board's decision.
north-carolina.assessment_basis: County assessor appraises property at value as of January 1; counties must reappraise at least every eight years (a growing number every four); Mecklenburg last reappraised effective January 1, 2023, next scheduled 2027. Between reappraisals value may change only in listed cases. Tax = value / 100 x combined rate.
north-carolina.effective_rate_text: Charlotte 2025-26: combined 0.7668 per $100 (Mecklenburg County 0.4927 + City of Charlotte 0.2741); effective combined rate 0.6808 (adjusted by the 2025 sales assessment ratio 0.8878). $3,311.81 on a $431,900 value; special district charges excluded.
north-carolina.assessment_cap: No separate annual percentage cap in the material read; between reappraisals an assessor may change a home's value only in listed cases (G.S. 105-287), such as correcting an error or a change in the property.
north-carolina.appeal_body: County Board of Equalization and Review, then the Property Tax Commission
north-carolina.appeal_deadline: Local board deliberates from about the first week of April (earliest start the first Monday in April; in a reappraisal year it must stop taking new appeals by December 1); Property Tax Commission appeal within 30 days after the local board mails its decision
north-carolina.appeal_answer: In North Carolina, appeal your value to the county Board of Equalization and Review, which begins deliberating around the first week of April, and if you disagree, appeal to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days after the local board mails its decision (G.S. 105-290(e)).
north-carolina.note: No general homestead exemption; state relief is the elderly or disabled exclusion (greater of $25,000 or 50% of appraised value, income at or below $38,800 for 2026; $39,900 for 2027), the disabled veteran exclusion (first $45,000) and a circuit breaker deferment, filed on Form AV-9 with the county assessor by June 1; one program per owner.

north-dakota.answer: A North Dakota home is taxed on 4.5% of its true and full value (50% assessed value times a 9% residential factor), and Cass County, which includes Fargo, averaged 292.90 mills for 2025. Owners can apply each year for a Primary Residence Credit of up to $1,600, and formal appeals go to the city board of equalization (first 15 days of April), then the county board (first 10 days of June).
north-dakota.assessment_basis: Assessor sets true and full value; assessed valuation is 50% of that (57-02-01) and the taxable valuation of residential property is 9% of assessed value (57-02-27), together 4.5% of market value. Tax = taxable value x mill levy.
north-dakota.effective_rate_text: Cass County (Fargo) 2025 average: 292.90 mills, about 1.32% of market value before credits (0.045 x mills / 1,000); $4,613 gross tax on a $350,000 home before the $1,600 credit. Rate varies by city and school district.
north-dakota.homestead_exemption: Primary Residence Credit: up to $1,600 a year (not more than the tax due) for any owner who lives in the home as a primary residence, no age or income limit; apply online only from January 1 to April 1; one per household. Homestead credit for owners 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled with income up to $70,000: reduces taxable value by up to $9,000 (100% at income up to $40,000) or up to $4,500 (50% at $40,001 to $70,000); apply to the local assessor by April 1.
north-dakota.assessment_cap: No cap on an individual home's assessed value in the statutes read; a taxing district's levy in dollars may not exceed its base-year levy increased by 3% (57-15-01.2) unless voters approve more or an exception applies.
north-dakota.appeal_body: City board of equalization, then county board of equalization, then State Board of Equalization (informal review with the assessor first; abatement is a separate route)
north-dakota.appeal_deadline: City board of equalization meets in the first 15 days of April; county board in the first 10 days of June; abatement application by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent
north-dakota.appeal_answer: In North Dakota, ask the assessor for an informal review, then appeal formally to the city board of equalization, which meets in the first 15 days of April, and then the county board of equalization, which meets in the first 10 days of June; to reach the State Board of Equalization you must have appeared at both.
north-dakota.note: Appeal details are from the City of Fargo and the Century Code.

ohio.answer: Ohio taxes 35% of a home's market value; in the City of Columbus tax district the Franklin County Auditor's 2025 file shows a 49.78-mill effective residential rate (115.89 mills full rate). The homestead credit is means-tested (low-income seniors and disabled owners, credit on $29,700 of value for tax year 2026), and you file a Board of Revision complaint by March 31, 2027 for tax year 2026.
ohio.assessment_basis: County auditor values each home as of January 1 and sets taxable value at 35% of market value; auditors reappraise every property once every six years with a sales-based update in the third year (Franklin County 2026 triennial update tentative values posted June 9, 2026, about 10% higher). Tax = taxable value x full rate, reduced by a reduction factor, then credits.
ohio.effective_rate_text: City of Columbus district 010, 2025: full rate 115.89 mills, effective rate 49.775 mills after the reduction factor (Columbus in Hilliard schools full rate 127.78; in Worthington schools 147.07); $4,726.95 a year on a $300,000 home, about 1.58% of market value.
ohio.homestead_exemption: Means-tested credit, not for every owner: low-income senior (65 by December 31 of the application year) or permanently and totally disabled owner gets a credit on $29,000 of value for 2025 and $29,700 for 2026 (disabled veterans $58,000 and $59,400, no income limit); income limit $40,000 for 2025 and $41,000 for 2026 (Ohio modified adjusted gross income). Own and occupy as principal residence on January 1; apply to the county auditor on or before December 31 of the year for which you seek it (form DTE 105A); reapply at a new address.
ohio.assessment_cap: No cap on one home's taxable value or tax found; after a reappraisal each levy's rate is adjusted for the change in value of the whole taxing district, which mostly disappears when a school district is at the 20-mill floor.
ohio.appeal_deadline: Complaint filed between August 25, 2026 and March 31, 2027 for tax year 2026; 30 days to appeal the board's decision
ohio.appeal_answer: In Ohio (Franklin County), file a complaint with the Board of Revision between August 25, 2026 and March 31, 2027 for tax year 2026, and if you disagree with the decision you have 30 days to appeal.
ohio.note: Appeal and due-date details are from Franklin County.

oklahoma.answer: Oklahoma taxes real property at 11% of fair cash value and applies a local millage rate; for 2025 the combined rate for a home in Oklahoma City and the Oklahoma City school district is 122.90 mills, about $3,257 on a $250,000 home after the $1,000 homestead exemption. If the assessor raises your value, you have 30 calendar days from the mailing date to file a written protest with the county assessor.
oklahoma.assessment_basis: County assessor sets fair cash value (visits all properties at least once every four years); assessed value is 11% of fair cash value (the Constitution allows 11% to 13.5%); taxable value is assessed value minus exemptions; tax = taxable value x millage. A mill is $1 per $1,000.
oklahoma.effective_rate_text: Oklahoma County tax district 200 (Oklahoma City, OKCPS #89), 2025: 122.90 mills (city 15.16, schools 65.49, technology centers 19.11, county 23.14); $3,256.85 on a $250,000 home, about 1.30% of value. Edmond district 712: 120.32 mills; county rates vary from about 75 to 134 mills.
oklahoma.homestead_exemption: First $1,000 of assessed value of a homestead (68 O.S. 2889), worth about $123 at 122.90 mills; must own and live in the home on January 1 with the deed on record by February 1. Additional $1,000 for a head of household with gross household income of $30,000 or less last year. Apply by March 15 or within 30 days after a valuation increase notice, whichever is later. Valuation freeze for owners 65 and older within the county's HUD median income; 100% disabled veteran exemption.
oklahoma.assessment_cap: Fair cash value cannot rise more than 5% a year (Art. X, sec. 8B); 3% for property with a homestead exemption and for agricultural land; does not apply in a year when title changes hands or improvements are made.
oklahoma.appeal_body: County assessor (written protest), then the county board of equalization, then district court
oklahoma.appeal_deadline: 30 calendar days from the mailing date of a valuation increase notice (or by the first Monday in April if the value did not change); 15 calendar days to appeal to the county board of equalization after the assessor's written decision; 30 calendar days from the board's order to appeal to district court
oklahoma.appeal_answer: In Oklahoma, file a written protest with the county assessor within 30 calendar days of the mailing date of your valuation increase notice (or by the first Monday in April if your value did not change), then appeal to the county board of equalization within 15 calendar days of the assessor's decision and to district court within 30 calendar days of the board's order.

oregon.answer: Oregon taxes a home's assessed value, not its market value, and under Measure 50 assessed value can rise at most 3% a year and does not reset when you buy; in Multnomah County code area 001 (Portland) the 2025-26 rate was $26.9199 per $1,000 of assessed value. Oregon has no statewide general homestead exemption, and you petition the county property value appeals board after the tax statement is mailed and by December 31.
oregon.assessment_basis: Three values: real market value (RMV), maximum assessed value (MAV, grows 3% a year after the first year: 103% of prior assessed value or 100% of prior maximum, whichever is greater) and assessed value (AV, the lesser of MAV and RMV, which is taxed). Bill is the lower of AV x code area rate or RMV x Measure 5 limits ($5 per $1,000 education, $10 general government) plus taxes outside the limits. Value set as of January 1; tax year July 1 to June 30.
oregon.effective_rate_text: Multnomah County levy code area 001 (City of Portland, Portland Public Schools), 2025-26: $26.9199 per $1,000 of assessed value (education 7.8507 + general government 14.9515 + bonds 4.1177); $8,075.97 on $300,000 AV (RMV $500,000), 1.62% of market value.
oregon.assessment_cap: Measure 50 (Art. XI, sec. 11): maximum assessed value grows at most 3% a year, assessed value cannot exceed real market value; a sale does not reset it, but new improvements, partitions, rezoning, loss of an exemption and other listed events can. The tax itself is not limited to 3%.
oregon.appeal_deadline: After the tax statements are mailed and by December 31 of that year (ORS 309.100); the board meets from the first Monday in February and must finish by April 15
oregon.appeal_answer: In Oregon, file a petition with the county property value appeals board after the tax statement is mailed (by October 25) and by December 31 of that year; the board hears petitions from February and must finish by April 15.
oregon.note: Oregon has no statewide general homestead exemption (Department of Revenue); relief is a senior and disabled deferral (age 62+, household income under $70,000, net worth under $500,000, claim by April 15) and a disabled veteran exemption.

pennsylvania.answer: Pennsylvania's property tax is local, set by the county, municipality and school district; in Philadelphia the 2025 rate is 1.3998% of assessed value, and the Homestead Exemption removes $100,000 of assessed value, saving most owners up to $1,399 a year. Outside Philadelphia appeals to the county board of assessment appeals are due by September 1 (or a county date no earlier than August 1); in Philadelphia, by the first Monday in October.
pennsylvania.assessment_basis: The county assessment office sets assessed value (in Philadelphia, the Office of Property Assessment); the new bill follows the assessment, not the sale price. Philadelphia mailed its 2027 revaluation notices in summer 2026. The article does not state a statewide assessment fraction or reassessment frequency.
pennsylvania.effective_rate_text: Philadelphia tax year 2025: 1.3998% of assessed value (0.6159% city + 0.7839% school district); $3,550 on a $253,600 assessment without exemption and $2,150 with the Homestead Exemption.
pennsylvania.homestead_exemption: Philadelphia Homestead Exemption: removes $100,000 from assessed value of an owner-occupied home (mortgage allowed), saving most owners up to $1,399 a year from 2025; apply by December 1 (by October 1 to see it on the bill); no reapplication unless the deed changes; not available with a 10-year residential tax abatement. State law lets a local governing body exclude a fixed dollar amount of assessed value of each homestead and farmstead (apply to the assessor by March 1). Philadelphia also has the LOOP program and a senior tax freeze.
pennsylvania.assessment_cap: No general cap; Philadelphia's Longtime Owner Occupants Program caps the assessment for owners whose assessment rose at least 50% in one year or 75% over five years, with 10 years of residence and an income limit (applications due September 30); Senior Citizen Real Estate Tax Freeze for owners 65+ with income of $33,500 or less (single) or $41,500 (married).
pennsylvania.appeal_body: Outside Philadelphia: county board of assessment appeals; in Philadelphia: Board of Revision of Taxes (or a First Level Review)
pennsylvania.appeal_deadline: Outside Philadelphia: September 1, or a date set by the county commissioners no earlier than August 1 (40 days from the date of a notice of changed assessment); in Philadelphia: the first Monday in October
pennsylvania.appeal_answer: In Pennsylvania outside Philadelphia, appeal to the county board of assessment appeals by September 1 (or the county's date, no earlier than August 1; 40 days from a changed-assessment notice), and in Philadelphia appeal to the Board of Revision of Taxes by the first Monday in October.
pennsylvania.note: Rates, exemption and Philadelphia appeal details are for Philadelphia; the county deadline is the state-law default (53 Pa.C.S. 8844).

rhode-island.answer: In Rhode Island each city or town assesses and taxes property; Providence's 2025 rate is $8.40 per $1,000 of assessed value for an owner-occupied single-family home ($14.60 non-owner-occupied), or $3,360 a year on a $400,000 assessment. To appeal, file with the local assessor on or before November 15 (R.I. Gen. Laws 44-5-26).
rhode-island.assessment_basis: Assessors value property at full and fair cash value as of December 31 in the year of the last revaluation, statistical revaluation or update, or at a uniform percentage not above 100% (44-5-12); no market adjustment between those years. Providence says the law requires a full revaluation every nine years with updates every three years.
rhode-island.effective_rate_text: Providence 2025: $8.40 per $1,000 for owner-occupied 1 family ($14.60 not owner-occupied; $7.55 and $14.00 for 2 to 5 families); $3,360 a year on a $400,000 assessment, owner-occupied.
rhode-island.assessment_cap: A city or town may levy no more than 4% above the prior year's levy (44-5-2(b)), with statutory exceptions; this caps the city's total levy, not each bill.
rhode-island.appeal_body: Local tax assessor, then the local tax board of review, then Superior Court
rhode-island.appeal_deadline: On or before November 15 (not less than 90 days after the first tax payment is due) with the assessor; board of review within 30 days of the assessor's decision (or by January 31 if no decision); Superior Court within 30 days of the board's written decision
rhode-island.appeal_answer: In Rhode Island, file your assessment appeal with the local assessor on or before November 15 and not less than 90 days after the first tax payment is due (R.I. Gen. Laws 44-5-26), then appeal to the local tax board of review within 30 days of the assessor's decision, and to Superior Court within 30 days of the board's decision.
rhode-island.note: No state-set homestead exemption in the sources; Providence uses a lower owner-occupied rate and lists fixed exemptions (elderly $750, veteran $306, service-disabled veteran $614, Social Security age 62 to 64 $460, Social Security disability $499, blind $921; apply by March 15). Providence's FAQ also cites a 90-day window; confirm with the Assessor.

south-carolina.answer: In South Carolina a home you own and live in as your legal residence is assessed at 4% of fair market value (other real estate 6%) and is exempt from school operating taxes; in the City of Greenville the 2025 millage is 331.5 mills. You have 90 days from the mailing of the assessment notice to give the assessor written notice of objection.
south-carolina.assessment_basis: County assessor sets fair market value; legal residence (up to five contiguous acres) is assessed at 4% and other real property at 6% (S.C. Code 12-43-220); the 4% ratio must be applied for and a new owner must apply again. Counties must reappraise every fifth year (Greenville's next is 2030). A sale triggers reappraisal at fair market value. Tax = fair market value x ratio x millage / 1,000.
south-carolina.effective_rate_text: City of Greenville 2025: 331.5 mills on the county sheet (county 60.1 + schools 141.2 operations and 48.5 debt + city 81.4 + other 0.3); owner-occupied 4% homes owe on 190.3 mills (school operations exempt), $3,044.80 on a $400,000 home, about 0.76% of value.
south-carolina.homestead_exemption: Homestead exemption for older and disabled owners: first $50,000 of fair market value exempt from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes for owners who have lived in South Carolina at least one year and are 65 or older by December 31, are totally and permanently disabled, or are legally blind; hold fee simple or a life estate; apply to the county auditor before July 16 of the tax year. Separately, the 4% legal-residence ratio and school operating tax exemption must be applied for.
south-carolina.assessment_cap: Any increase in value from a countywide reappraisal is limited to 15% within a five-year period (12-37-3140(B)); does not apply to new additions and improvements or in the year of a sale; limits value, not the tax bill.
south-carolina.appeal_body: County assessor (written objection), then a conference and written protest, then the county board of assessment appeals
south-carolina.appeal_deadline: 90 days from the mailing of the assessment notice; in years without a notice, in writing before the first penalty date
south-carolina.appeal_answer: In South Carolina, give the county assessor written notice of objection within 90 days of the mailing of your assessment notice (S.C. Code 12-60-2510), then request a conference, file a written protest within 30 days if it fails, and appeal to the county board of assessment appeals within 30 days of the assessor's answer.

south-dakota.answer: South Dakota has no state property tax; counties, cities and school districts levy it on market value equalized to 85%, and owner-occupied homes get a lower school general fund levy. For taxes payable in 2026 a $400,000 Sioux Falls owner-occupied home owes $5,205, and you must appeal first to the local board of equalization (March 12 in 2026).
south-dakota.assessment_basis: County director of equalization values every parcel at full and true (market) value as of November 1 of the year before the assessment year (SDCL 10-6-105), reassessed every year, with notices by March 1. State law requires equalization to 85%, so assessed value is multiplied by an annual county factor (0.947 in Minnehaha County for taxes payable in 2026). Tax = taxable value x total levy / 1,000.
south-dakota.effective_rate_text: Minnehaha County, Sioux Falls school district 49-5, 2025 taxes payable in 2026: total levy 13.742 per $1,000 of taxable value owner-occupied (16.893 for other property); $5,205 on a $400,000 home, about 1.3% of assessed value.
south-dakota.homestead_exemption: No dollar homestead exemption. Owner-occupied classification gives a reduced school general fund levy (7.129 versus 10.280 per $1,000 in Sioux Falls, about $1,194 less on a $400,000 home); file a certificate with the county director of equalization by March 15; stays until sale or change of use. South Dakota's 'homestead exemption' is a deferral for people 70 or older (apply by April 1). Also an assessment freeze for age 65+ or disabled (income under $56,595 one person, $66,885 household; home value below $514,500; April 1).
south-dakota.assessment_cap: No cap on a single home in effect; S.B. 216 (2025) caps annual increases in each county's total owner-occupied valuation at 3% and limits local budget growth to 3% a year for five years starting with taxes payable in 2027. Assessment freeze program for seniors and disabled owners.
south-dakota.appeal_body: Local board of equalization first, then county board of equalization, then the Office of Hearing Examiners, then circuit court
south-dakota.appeal_deadline: 2026 calendar: written appeal to the local board March 12; county board April 7; Office of Hearing Examiners May 15; circuit court within 30 days of the decision (dates change slightly each year; assessment notices mailed by March 1)
south-dakota.appeal_answer: In South Dakota, you must appeal first to the local board of equalization (written appeal due March 12 in 2026), then to the county board (April 7 in 2026), then the Office of Hearing Examiners (May 15), or you lose your rights to the later boards; circuit court is available within 30 days of the decision.

tennessee.answer: Tennessee assesses homes at 25% of appraised value; in Nashville-Davidson County the 2025 rate is $2.814 per $100 of assessed value in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District, or $2,814 a year on a $400,000 home in the USD. In Davidson County, informal review was due April 17, 2026 and the Metropolitan Board of Equalization deadline to schedule was June 26, 2026.
tennessee.assessment_basis: County assessor sets appraised value as of January 1; residential and farm property assessed at 25% of appraised value (commercial and industrial 40%). Tax = assessed value / 100 x rate. Davidson County's last reappraisal was in 2025, on a four-year cycle; a Certified Tax Rate is required after each reappraisal.
tennessee.effective_rate_text: Nashville-Davidson County 2025: $2.814 per $100 of assessed value in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District (2024: $3.254 and $2.922); $2,814 a year on a $400,000 home in the USD, about 0.70% of appraised value.
tennessee.appeal_body: Assessor (informal review), then the Metropolitan Board of Equalization, then the State Board of Equalization
tennessee.appeal_deadline: Davidson County 2026: informal review April 17, 2026; Metropolitan Board of Equalization deadline to schedule June 26, 2026; State Board of Equalization generally by August 1 or within 45 days of the county board's notice, whichever is later; deadlines move each year
tennessee.appeal_answer: In Nashville-Davidson County, Tennessee, the 2026 deadline for informal review with the Assessor was April 17 and for the Metropolitan Board of Equalization was June 26, and you can appeal to the State Board of Equalization generally by August 1 or within 45 days of the county board's notice, whichever is later.
tennessee.note: No homestead exemption: Tennessee offers a state tax relief reimbursement (income limit $38,470 for 2026) and a tax freeze for owners 65+ (income under $63,470; apply to the Davidson County Trustee by April 5, 2027 for tax year 2026). No cap on appraised-value increases in the sources read.
