texas.answer: Texas has no state property tax; local units apply their rates to appraised value minus exemptions, and since the 2025 tax year school districts must exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value. A homestead's appraised value can rise at most 10% a year, and you file a protest with the Appraisal Review Board by May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered, whichever is later.
texas.assessment_basis: County appraisal district appraises property at market value as of January 1 (Tax Code 23.01) and decides exemptions; each taxing unit sets a rate per $100 of taxable value. Tax = (appraised value minus exemptions) x rate / 100, summed over all units. Notice of appraised value by April 1 for a homestead.
texas.effective_rate_text: Dallas 2026 rates: total 2.250760 per $100 of taxable value for a homestead in the units listed (county 0.248650, Parkland 0.212000, Dallas College 0.106575, City 0.697800, Dallas ISD 0.985735); $6,216.70 on a $400,000 home with exemptions (about 1.55%), $9,003.04 without.
texas.homestead_exemption: School districts must exempt $140,000 of appraised value of a residence homestead from the 2025 tax year (Tax Code 11.13(b)), plus $60,000 more for owners 65 or older or disabled. Optional local exemptions: up to 20% of appraised value (minimum $5,000) and at least $3,000 for 65+ or disabled. Must own and occupy as principal residence; apply once on Form 50-114 with the appraisal district before May 1 (late filing allowed up to two years after the delinquency date); stays until the home changes owners.
texas.assessment_cap: 10% a year on appraised value of a homestead over the prior year's appraised value plus new improvements (Tax Code 23.23); starts January 1 of the year after the first year of the exemption and ends when the home no longer qualifies. School tax on a homestead of an owner 65+ or disabled generally cannot increase while it remains the homestead.
texas.appeal_deadline: By May 15 or 30 days after the notice of appraised value was delivered, whichever is later
texas.appeal_answer: In Texas, file a written notice of protest with your county Appraisal Review Board by May 15 or within 30 days after your notice of appraised value was delivered, whichever is later; any written notice that identifies the property and your disagreement is enough, and you may ask for an informal conference first.

utah.answer: Utah values property at fair market value as of January 1, and a primary residence gets a 45% exemption so owners pay tax on 55% of the value; in Salt Lake City tax area 01A the 2025 rate is 0.924% of taxable value, or $2,541 on a $500,000 home. Apply to the county board of equalization by the later of September 15 or 45 days after the valuation notice.
utah.assessment_basis: County assessor values property each year at fair market value as of January 1 (Utah Code 59-2-103); taxable value is market value minus the residential exemption; each taxing entity sets a rate by tax area; the county auditor mails a Notice of Valuation and Tax Changes by July 22.
utah.effective_rate_text: Salt Lake City tax area 01A, 2025: 0.924% (0.009240) of taxable value; $2,541.00 on a $500,000 home after the 45% exemption (taxable value $275,000), $4,620.00 without it.
utah.homestead_exemption: 45% exemption of the value of residential property, so 55% is taxed (Utah Code 59-2-103(3)); one primary residence per household (a tenant's home can also qualify for the owner), up to one acre per residential unit, part-year homes qualify if used as residential for 183 or more consecutive days. After a change of ownership return a signed Residential Property Declaration within 90 days of the notice; first application deadline the later of September 15 or 45 days after the valuation notice; some counties require an application first.
utah.assessment_cap: None found in the sources read; Utah limits each taxing entity's revenue (certified rates raise about the same revenue as the prior year apart from new growth, and entities that want more must hold a Truth in Taxation hearing).
utah.appeal_body: County board of equalization, then the State Tax Commission
utah.appeal_deadline: On or before the later of September 15 or the last day of the 45-day period beginning on the valuation notice date (notice mailed by July 22); the board decides within 60 days
utah.appeal_answer: In Utah, apply to the county board of equalization on or before the later of September 15 or the last day of the 45-day period beginning on the date of your Notice of Valuation and Tax Changes (mailed by July 22), including your estimate of market value and evidence; the board must decide within 60 days, and you can go on to the State Tax Commission.

vermont.answer: A Vermont property tax bill adds a municipal tax and a statewide education tax, and filing a homestead declaration each year gives your principal home the lower homestead education rate; in Burlington for FY2027 the rates are 1.5489 (homestead education) and 0.9097 (municipal) per $100 of listed value. In Burlington, file a written grievance with the Assessor's Office by May 15, then appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals within 14 days of the decision letter.
vermont.assessment_basis: Local listers or an assessor appraise each property at fair market value as of April 1 (Burlington's listed values were set as of April 1, 2021, so listed values can differ from sale prices). Tax = listed value / 100 x (education rate + municipal rate + local agreement). Fiscal years run July 1 to June 30.
vermont.effective_rate_text: Burlington FY2027 per $100 of listed value: education homestead 1.5489 (nonhomestead 1.5154), municipal 0.9097, local agreement 0.0004; $9,836.00 on a $400,000 homestead, about 2.459% of listed value. Statewide nonhomestead education rate $1.643 for FY2027.
vermont.appeal_body: Municipal Board of Assessors (written grievance to the Assessor's Office in Burlington), then the Board of Tax Appeals, then the Vermont Department of Taxes or Superior Court
vermont.appeal_deadline: Burlington: grievance by May 15, 2026 (online form reopens February 2027); 14 days from the date of the decision letter to appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals; then 30 days to appeal to the Department of Taxes or Superior Court
vermont.appeal_answer: In Burlington, Vermont, file a written grievance with the Assessor's Office by May 15 (the 2026 deadline), and if the Board of Assessors rules against you, appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals within 14 days of the decision letter and then to the Vermont Department of Taxes or the Superior Court within 30 days.
vermont.note: No fixed-dollar homestead exemption in the sources read: a homestead declaration (Form HS-122, due April 15; late to October 15 with a penalty of up to 3% or 8% of the education tax) gives the homestead education rate, plus an income-based property tax credit (up to $5,600 education and $2,400 municipal; income under $115,400 for tax year 2025). No statewide assessment cap found.

virginia.answer: Virginia requires real estate to be assessed at 100% of fair market value, and each county and city sets its own rate; Arlington County's rate is $1.053 per $100 of assessed value, about $9,297 a year on the county's $882,900 average residential assessment. In Arlington, request a department review by March 1 and a Board of Equalization hearing by April 15.
virginia.assessment_basis: Real estate must be assessed at 100% of fair market value (Va. Const. art. X, sec. 2; Code 58.1-3201); Arlington assesses every property each year as of January 1 and mails notices each January. Tax = assessed value / 100 x rate.
virginia.effective_rate_text: Arlington County: $1.053 per $100 of assessed value adopted April 22, 2026 (up from $1.033); about $9,297 a year on the $882,900 average residential assessment, billed in two installments due June 15 and October 5.
virginia.assessment_cap: No limit on one home's assessment found; when assessments would raise a locality's total real estate tax by 1 percent or more, the locality must lower its rate so the levy rises no more than 1 percent unless it holds a separate public hearing (58.1-3321); new construction excluded.
virginia.appeal_body: Arlington Department of Real Estate Assessments (review), then the Board of Equalization, then Circuit Court
virginia.appeal_deadline: Arlington: March 1 (March 2 in 2026) for department review; April 15 for the Board of Equalization; court application within three years of the last day of the tax year or within one year of the assessment, whichever is later
virginia.appeal_answer: In Arlington, Virginia, file for a department review by March 1 (or the next business day) and for a Board of Equalization hearing by April 15, with the 2027 dates on your January notice; if you disagree with the Board you may apply to Circuit Court within three years of the last day of the tax year or one year of the assessment, whichever is later.
virginia.note: No general homestead exemption on the Arlington pages; targeted programs exist (Real Estate Tax Relief Program for owners 65+ or disabled, income limit $105,937 for 2025, file by November 15; disabled veterans; surviving spouses of service members killed in action). Appeal details are for Arlington.

washington.answer: Washington counties value homes at 100% of market value as of January 1 and there is no general homestead exemption; in Seattle the King County Assessor's 2026 rate is $9.90845 per $1,000 of assessed value, or $8,253.74 on the $833,000 median home. File a petition with the county Board of Equalization by July 1 or 30 days after the notice, whichever is later.
washington.assessment_basis: County assessor values property at 100% of true and fair value as of January 1 each year (RCW 84.40.020, 84.40.030), using sales of the property or similar properties within the past five years and cost or income methods in some cases. Tax = assessed value / 1,000 x total levy rate.
washington.effective_rate_text: Seattle (King County levy code 0010) 2026: $9.90845 per $1,000 of assessed value, $8,253.74 on the $833,000 median assessed value, about 0.99% (2025: $7,943.77).
washington.assessment_cap: No cap on assessed value; combined levies may not exceed 1% of true and fair value unless voters approve more (RCW 84.52.050), and a district's regular levy may grow by the limit factor (101% or 100% plus inflation, whichever is lower, for districts of 10,000 or more) plus new construction (RCW 84.55.010); this limits district revenue, not an individual bill.
washington.appeal_deadline: July 1 or 30 days after the notice, whichever is later (a county may allow up to 60 days); King County 2026 calendar lists July 1
washington.appeal_answer: In Washington, file a petition on a Department of Revenue form with the county Board of Equalization by July 1 or within 30 days after the assessment notice, whichever is later (a county may allow up to 60 days); King County's 2026 calendar lists July 1.
washington.note: No general homestead exemption: senior, disabled and certain veteran exemptions (age 61+, income thresholds by county; King County 2024-2026 thresholds $60,000, $72,000, $84,000, rising for 2027-2029) and deferrals (age 60+) exist; apply through the county assessor.

west-virginia.answer: West Virginia assesses homes at 60% of market value, set each year as of July 1, and owner-occupied homes are Class II; for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2027 the Class II levy in Charleston is $1.609 per $100 of assessed value. Owners 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled can exempt the first $20,000 of assessed value (apply to the assessor before December 1), and you must appear before the Board of Equalization and Review, which sits by February 1.
west-virginia.assessment_basis: County assessor estimates market value and multiplies by 60% to get the assessed value, set each year as of July 1 (W. Va. Code 11-3-1); homes are reassessed every year. Tax = market value x 60% x levy rate / 100. Class II (owner-occupied residential) is two times Class I; levies are set by the Legislature, county board of education, county commission and city council.
west-virginia.effective_rate_text: Charleston (Kanawha County) Class II, fiscal year ending June 30, 2027: $1.609 per $100 of assessed value (160.90 cents); $1,930.80 on a $200,000 home, about 0.97% of market value. Statewide average Class II levy for tax year 2025: $1.21 per $100.
west-virginia.homestead_exemption: First $20,000 of assessed value exempt for owner-occupants 65 or older (age reached on or before June 30 after the July 1 assessment date) or permanently and totally disabled, with two years of West Virginia residency (11-6B-3); veterans rated 90% to 100% disabled may qualify. Apply to the county assessor before December 1 to qualify for the next tax year; carries over unless status changes; removed on sale unless the new owner qualifies.
west-virginia.assessment_cap: No percentage cap on assessed value; the owner must be notified by January 15 when the assessor raises the assessed value by more than 110% of last year's and by more than $1,000, but a missed notice does not void the increase.
west-virginia.appeal_body: County commission sitting as the Board of Equalization and Review, then the Office of Tax Appeals
west-virginia.appeal_deadline: Board sits no later than February 1 and adjourns no later than the end of February (11-3-24); a taxpayer who fails to apply there waives the right to challenge that year's list except by appeal to the Office of Tax Appeals
west-virginia.appeal_answer: In West Virginia, appear before the county commission sitting as the Board of Equalization and Review, which meets no later than February 1 and adjourns by the end of February; if you had a hearing, you may appeal the board's order to the Office of Tax Appeals, and you must keep paying taxes before they become delinquent.

wisconsin.answer: Wisconsin assessors value homes at full market value as of January 1; for the 2025 levy the Department of Revenue reports an average effective rate of 2.078% in the city of Milwaukee versus 1.338% statewide. Give the board of review notice at least 48 hours before its first meeting, which falls in a 45-day period starting the fourth Monday of April, then file a written objection within the first two hours of that meeting.
wisconsin.assessment_basis: Assessor values real property at full value ordinarily obtained at private sale, using recent arm's-length sales of the property and comparable property (70.32), as of the close of January 1 each year (70.10); the owner must be notified of a changed assessment. Each taxing body then levies its share.
wisconsin.effective_rate_text: City of Milwaukee 2025 levy: gross rate 2.239%, effective rate 2.078% after the school levy credit (Milwaukee County 1.896%; Wisconsin statewide 1.338%); about $4,320.16 on the $207,900 median home value (Census), a DOR average rate.
wisconsin.appeal_body: Municipal board of review, then excessive assessment claim with the municipality and court
wisconsin.appeal_deadline: Board meets once a year during a 45-day period beginning the fourth Monday of April (April 27 in 2026); notice to the clerk at least 48 hours before its first meeting; written objection within the first two hours of the first meeting; excessive assessment claim served by January 31 of the year the tax is payable
wisconsin.appeal_answer: In Wisconsin, give the municipal clerk notice at least 48 hours before the board of review's first meeting (it meets during a 45-day period beginning the fourth Monday of April) and file a written objection within the first two hours of that meeting; if you still disagree, serve an excessive assessment claim by January 31 of the year the tax is payable.
wisconsin.note: No homestead exemption on assessed value in the sections read; relief comes as credits on the bill (school levy credit, first dollar credit, lottery and gaming credit for owner-occupied principal dwellings, apply by January 31 to the treasurer) and an income-tax homestead credit (household income under $24,680 for 2025, maximum $1,168). No assessment cap in the article.

wyoming.answer: Wyoming values each home at market value every year and taxes 9.5% of it; the Laramie County 2025 sheet gives 70.54 mills for Cheyenne's main school district, and owner-occupants can claim a 25% exemption on the first $1 million of value. Appeal by filing a statement of reasons with the county assessor within 30 days of the date on your assessment schedule.
wyoming.assessment_basis: County assessor values property each year as of January 1 at fair market value (W.S. 39-13-103); taxable value is 9.5% of fair market value for homes. Tax = fair market value x 9.5% x mills / 1,000. Assessment schedules mailed on or before the fourth Monday in April.
wyoming.effective_rate_text: Cheyenne (Laramie County main school district 0150), 2025: 70.54 mills (17.54 county general); $2,680.52 on a $400,000 home without exemption (about 0.67% of market value) and $2,010.39 with the 25% exemption (about 0.50%).
wyoming.homestead_exemption: Homeowner exemption (W.S. 39-11-105(a)(xlvi)): 25% of fair market value of a single-family home and improved land, on the first $1,000,000 of value; must live there at least 8 months a year (from tax year 2026); file the Wyoming Residential Owner-Occupied Affidavit online with the Department of Revenue. Long-term homeowner exemption: 50% on the first $3,000,000 for owners 65 or older who paid Wyoming residential property tax for 25 years (repealed effective July 1, 2027); claim date March 1; not both exemptions in the same year.
wyoming.assessment_cap: Increase limit exemption: any assessed-value increase above the prior year's value plus 4% is exempt (W.S. 39-11-105(a)(xliii)-(xliv)); does not apply to new construction or additions or if you acquired the property during the prior calendar year.
wyoming.appeal_body: County assessor (statement of reasons), then the county board of equalization
wyoming.appeal_deadline: Within 30 days of the date on the assessment schedule; county board gives written findings by October 1
wyoming.appeal_answer: In Wyoming, file a statement of reasons with the county assessor within 30 days of the date on your assessment schedule (W.S. 39-13-109(b)(i)); appeals go to the county board of equalization, which issues written findings by October 1.

alabama.answer: No Alabama statute says a buyer or seller must hire an attorney to close, but under Ala. Code 34-3-6 only a lawyer may prepare deeds and mortgages for others for pay, so an attorney normally prepares or supervises the legal documents even when a title company runs the table.
alabama.rule: No Alabama statute read requires an attorney at closing, but Ala. Code 34-3-6 makes drawing deeds and mortgages for others for pay the practice of law and bars title companies from preparing them. Alabama State Bar Formal Opinion RO-94-01 lets non-lawyers run only the ministerial steps of a closing.
alabama.who_closes: Attorney prepares the documents; a title company or attorney may run the signing table (ministerial steps only)
alabama.note: Opinion RO-94-01 (1994) may have been superseded; the source page does not say. No fee figure given.

alaska.answer: Alaska does not require an attorney to buy or sell a home: a title insurance company may hold the escrow and run the closing (AS 21.66.180), and licensed real estate agents may prepare purchase contracts (AS 08.88.405).
alaska.rule: No Alaska statute requires an attorney for a home sale. AS 21.66.180 lets a title insurance company hold the escrow and run the closing, and AS 08.88.405 lets real estate licensees prepare purchase contracts.
alaska.who_closes: Title insurance company (escrow, settlement and closing)
alaska.note: No typical attorney fee found. Title companies must file a schedule of escrow and closing charges (AS 21.66.460).

arizona.answer: Arizona law does not require an attorney to buy or sell a home; instead an escrow agent must hold a state license (A.R.S. 6-813), and a licensed broker or salesperson handles most transactions.
arizona.rule: No Arizona statute read requires an attorney. Escrow agents must hold a state license (A.R.S. 6-813); attorneys licensed in Arizona are exempt if not actively conducting an escrow business (6-811(A)(1)).
arizona.note: The article says no source gives how often each party closes, and no fee figure. Escrow company as typical closer is inferred from the licensing structure; the article does not state market share.

arkansas.answer: No Arkansas statute or rule read requires an attorney to attend or conduct a residential closing, but agents may fill in blanks only on attorney-approved forms for simple transactions (17 CAR 220-1009(c), Pope County Bar Association v. Suggs).
arkansas.rule: No Arkansas statute or Real Estate Commission rule read requires an attorney to attend or conduct a residential closing. Under Pope County Bar Association v. Suggs (1981) and 17 CAR 220-1009(c), agents may fill in blanks only on attorney-approved forms for simple transactions.
arkansas.note: Article gives no usual closing party and no typical attorney fee. The Suggs summary is secondary (court opinion not opened).

california.answer: No. California home sales close through escrow, and the Escrow Law lets licensed escrow companies, title insurers, banks, brokers and attorneys hold escrows, so no attorney is required; a written fee contract is required if a lawyer is hired and fees will exceed $1,000 (Bus. & Prof. Code 6148).
california.rule: California home sales close through escrow under the Escrow Law (Financial Code 17000 ff.). Licensed escrow companies, title insurers, banks, brokers and attorneys may hold escrows (Fin. Code 17006); the law does not make an attorney part of the closing. Only State Bar licensees may practice law (Bus. & Prof. Code 6125).
california.who_closes: Escrow (licensed independent escrow company, or a title insurer, broker or attorney acting as controlled escrow)
california.typical_fee_text: No official fee figure. A written contract is required when total fees will exceed $1,000 (Bus. & Prof. Code 6148).
california.note: No typical attorney fee given by any official source.

colorado.answer: No Colorado statute read requires a buyer or seller to hire an attorney to close; closings are normally run by a title insurance company or agent that provides closing and settlement services (C.R.S. 10-11-102).
colorado.rule: No Colorado statute read (Titles 10, 12, 38) requires an attorney to close. Title insurance companies and agents provide closing and settlement services (C.R.S. 10-11-102(3.5)). Brokers must advise clients to consult legal counsel before signing standard forms (12-10-403(4)(c)).
colorado.note: No typical fee found. H.B. 26-1426 (new 12-10-408.5, listed as effective August 12, 2026) requires brokers to advise seeking legal advice when a principal supplies its own purchase contract.

connecticut.answer: Yes. Under Conn. Gen. Stat. 51-88a, no one may conduct a real estate closing in Connecticut unless admitted as an attorney in the state and in good standing; violating this is a class D felony in the ordinary case.
connecticut.rule: Conn. Gen. Stat. 51-88a: no one may conduct a real estate closing unless admitted as an attorney in Connecticut and in good standing. Violation is unauthorized practice of law under 51-88, a class D felony in the ordinary case.
connecticut.note: The statute does not define conduct and the article does not list which tasks that covers. No fee figure.

delaware.answer: Yes. In Matter of Mid-Atlantic Settlement Services (Del. 2000), the Delaware Supreme Court held that a Delaware-licensed attorney must conduct the closing of a sale or refinance of Delaware real property.
delaware.rule: Matter of Mid-Atlantic Settlement Services, Inc. (Del. Supreme Court, May 31, 2000): a Delaware-licensed attorney must conduct the closing of a sale or refinance of Delaware real property and be involved in drafting or reviewing documents affecting title. The rule comes from the Court, not a statute.
delaware.note: Rule is judicial, not statutory. One exception: a home equity loan where the lender acts on its own behalf. No fee figure.

florida.answer: No. As of October 2026 no Florida statute requires a lawyer at a home closing; a title insurance agent licensed by the Department of Financial Services can close and hold escrow funds (Fla. Stat. 626.8417, 626.8473).
florida.rule: No Florida statute requires a lawyer at a home closing. A DFS-licensed title insurance agent may conduct closing services and hold escrow (Fla. Stat. 626.8417, 626.8473, 627.7711). Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 89-5 notes the Florida Supreme Court permits title companies to conduct closings.
florida.who_closes: Title insurance agent or agency (or attorney)
florida.note: No typical attorney fee; fee is not regulated. Title premium is set by rule (627.782) but closing fees are separate.

georgia.answer: Yes. In In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 (277 Ga. 472, 2003) the Supreme Court of Georgia held that only a licensed Georgia attorney may prepare or facilitate execution of a deed of conveyance, so closing a transaction for a seller, borrower or lender is unauthorized practice of law for non-lawyers.
georgia.rule: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, 277 Ga. 472 (Ga. 2003): only a licensed Georgia attorney may prepare or facilitate execution of a deed of conveyance, and closing a real estate transaction for a seller, borrower or lender is unauthorized practice of law for anyone else. Parties may handle their own transaction pro se. Witness-only closings are rejected.
georgia.who_closes: Attorney (licensed Georgia attorney in control of the closing; staff only under direct, constant supervision)
georgia.note: Rule is judicial; parties may act pro se in their own transaction. FAO 23-1 (Jan. 23, 2025) allows the attorney to meet duties by video conference. No fee figure.

hawaii.answer: The Hawaii statutes read do not require a buyer or seller to hire an attorney to close; only a licensed escrow depository corporation may act as escrow for a fee (HRS 449-5), while attorneys and brokers may hold escrow only with no escrow fee (HRS 449-3).
hawaii.rule: No Hawaii statute read requires an attorney to close. HRS 449-5 allows only a licensed escrow depository corporation to act as escrow for a fee; a licensed attorney or broker may hold escrow only if no escrow fee is charged (449-3).
hawaii.note: The article says this is a finding about the texts read, not about all Hawaii law. No fee figure.

idaho.answer: None of the Idaho statutes read requires a buyer or seller to hire an attorney to close; Idaho instead regulates title insurance agents who handle escrow and closings, with a state license and a bond of $10,000 to $50,000 (Idaho Code 41-2704, 41-2711).
idaho.rule: No Idaho statute read requires an attorney to close. The title insurance chapter puts escrow and closing work inside the title business (Idaho Code 41-2704(3)); title agents are licensed, bonded $10,000 to $50,000 and file escrow fees with the Department of Insurance (41-2705, 41-2710, 41-2711).
idaho.who_closes: Licensed title insurance agent or insurer (title company)
idaho.note: The article says this reflects the texts read, not every court rule or bar opinion. No fee figure.

illinois.answer: No Illinois statute read requires a buyer or seller to hire an attorney to close a home sale; a title company or registered agent may handle the escrow and closing if it issues closing protection letters (215 ILCS 155/16.1).
illinois.rule: No Illinois statute read requires an attorney to close. Only licensed attorneys may be paid for legal services (705 ILCS 205/1); a title insurance company or registered agent may handle escrow and closing if it issues closing protection letters (215 ILCS 155/16.1).
illinois.who_closes: Title insurance company or registered title agent may hold escrow and close; attorney optional (article does not say which is usual)
illinois.note: The article states it found no official source on how often attorneys or title companies run closings, so who_closes reflects what the law allows, not market practice. No fee figure.

indiana.answer: The Indiana statutes read do not require an attorney to close a home sale, although engaging in the business of a practicing lawyer without admission is a Class B misdemeanor (IC 33-43-2-1) and a lender or contract may still require one.
indiana.rule: No Indiana statute read requires an attorney at closing. IC 33-43-2-1 reserves the practice of law to admitted attorneys (Class B misdemeanor otherwise). Every recorded deed must name who prepared it (IC 36-2-11-15), but not necessarily a lawyer.
indiana.note: The article says the texts do not say who must conduct the closing. No fee figure. No Indiana court decision or bar opinion on point was found.

iowa.answer: No Iowa statute or court rule read requires an attorney at closing, but nonlawyers may not prepare deeds (Iowa Court Rule 37.5) and a title guaranty requires a title opinion from a participating attorney (Iowa Code 16.91(6)).
iowa.rule: No Iowa statute or court rule read requires an attorney at closing, but Iowa Court Rule 37.5 bars nonlawyers from preparing deeds, and Iowa Code 16.91(6) requires a title opinion from a participating attorney for a title guaranty.

iowa.note: List of participating closers comes from a June 2021 program manual, which the article calls a few years old. No fee figure.

kansas.rule: No Kansas statute read requires a real estate attorney at closing. K.S.A. 40-1137 lets title insurance agents operate as escrow, settlement or closing agents if they hold client funds in separate fiduciary trust accounts.

kansas.note: No Kansas court rule or opinion was read. No fee figure.

kentucky.answer: No Kentucky statute or court rule read requires an attorney to attend a home closing, but a non-lawyer drafting a deed for another person is the practice of law (KBA U-63) and every recorded deed must show who prepared it (KRS 382.335).
kentucky.rule: No Kentucky statute or court rule read requires an attorney to attend a closing. KBA opinion U-63 lists drafting a deed for another person as unauthorized practice of law by a non-lawyer, and KRS 382.335 requires every recorded deed to show the name, address and signature of its preparer. KBA U-31 (1981) allowed ministerial closings by lay people; U-58 (1999) was vacated in 2003 (Countrywide v. KBA, 113 S.W.3d 105).
kentucky.who_closes: Attorney or title company (article says it depends on the contract and lender)
kentucky.note: Sources give a mixed picture on who may run the closing; the court decision vacating U-58 was not opened. No fee figure.

louisiana.answer: No Louisiana statute read orders buyers or sellers to hire a lawyer, but R.S. 37:212 treats preparing acts of sale for pay and giving title opinions as the practice of law, so a Louisiana attorney is built into a normal closing before a notary and two witnesses.
louisiana.rule: A Louisiana home sale is normally passed by act of sale before a notary and two witnesses (Civil Code art. 1833, 1839, 2440). No statute read orders parties to hire a lawyer, but R.S. 37:212 makes drafting acts of sale for pay and giving title opinions the practice of law, and title insurance must rest on a Louisiana attorney opinion (R.S. 37:212(B)).
louisiana.who_closes: Notary public (may or may not be a lawyer) for the act; licensed Louisiana attorney drafts the act and certifies title
louisiana.note: Parties may sign their own sale. No fee figure.

maine.rule: No Maine statute read requires an attorney to prepare the deed, run the closing or attend. 4 M.R.S. 807 reserves the practice of law to lawyers admitted in Maine (Class E crime otherwise).
maine.note: The article found no official source on who typically closes. No fee figure.

maryland.answer: No Maryland law read requires a buyer or seller to hire an attorney to close, but a deed cannot be recorded without a certification that an attorney or a party prepared it (Real Property 3-104(f)), and only licensed producers can conduct settlements.
maryland.rule: No Maryland law read requires an attorney to close. Preparing a deed is the practice of law (Bus. Occ. & Prof. 10-101(h)(2)(ii)), and a deed cannot be recorded without a certification that a Maryland attorney or a party to the deed prepared it (Real Prop. 3-104(f)). The Maryland Insurance Administration says only licensed producers can conduct settlements.
maryland.who_closes: Title company (licensed producer) conducts the settlement
maryland.note: The article found no source on the share of closings involving an attorney. Title company fees are not regulated; premiums are. No attorney fee figure.

massachusetts.rule: None of the Massachusetts General Laws sections read says a lawyer must attend a home closing. M.G.L. c. 221, 46A reserves the practice of law to members of the Massachusetts bar.
massachusetts.note: The statutes read do not say who must run the closing table, so attorney_required "no" means no requirement was found in those texts, not a confirmed absence. No fee figure.

michigan.rule: No Michigan statute read requires an attorney. Only persons licensed in Michigan may practice law (MCL 600.916), and a recorded instrument must carry the name and business address of its drafter (MCL 565.201). State Bar opinion RI-298 says a lawyer may not be named as drafter without drafting or reviewing the deed.
michigan.note: The article says the laws read do not name who must run a closing (title company, lender or attorney). No fee figure.

minnesota.answer: Minnesota does not require an attorney at a home closing: Minn. Stat. 507.45 lets a licensed attorney, real estate broker, salesperson or real estate closing agent provide closing services for a fee, with the fee disclosed in writing at least five business days before closing.
minnesota.rule: Minn. Stat. 507.45 lets a licensed attorney, real estate broker, salesperson or licensed closing agent provide residential closing services for a fee. Brokers, salespersons and closing agents may not give opinions on the legal effect of closing documents (507.45, subd. 3(a)).
minnesota.who_closes: Attorney, real estate broker, salesperson or licensed real estate closing agent (the statutes do not pick one)
minnesota.typical_fee_text: No fee schedule set. A closing agent must disclose its fee in writing at least five business days before closing (507.45, subd. 2). Closing agent initial license fee is $85 (82.57).
minnesota.note: No typical attorney fee found. The $85 figure is the closing agent license fee, not a closing fee.

mississippi.answer: No Mississippi statute or Bar material read says a buyer or seller must hire an attorney to close, but anyone who writes a deed, deed of trust or mortgage for a fee is practicing law (Miss. Code 73-3-55), so those documents must come from a Mississippi-licensed lawyer.
mississippi.rule: Miss. Code 73-3-55: anyone who writes a deed of conveyance, deed of trust or mortgage for a fee is practicing law. A broker may not practice law, give legal advice or prepare documents fixing the parties legal rights (73-35-21(2)). No text read says a buyer must have a lawyer or that a lawyer must attend closing.
mississippi.who_closes: Licensed Mississippi attorney prepares deeds and deeds of trust; title companies certify titles only through a licensed attorney agent (or as a chartered abstract company)
mississippi.note: Only two sources. The Bar notes courts ultimately decide what the practice of law is. No fee figure.

missouri.answer: None of the Missouri statutes read requires a buyer or seller to hire a real estate attorney; a title company usually runs the closing under RSMo 381.022, and only a lawyer may give legal advice or draft custom documents (RSMo 484.010).
missouri.rule: No Missouri statute read requires an attorney. RSMo 381.022 lets a title insurer, agency or agent act as closing agent only if a title commitment and closing protection letters are issued. nevada.rule: No Nevada rule read requires a buyer or seller to hire an attorney. Anyone administering escrows for pay must be licensed as an escrow agent or agency (NRS 645A.015, as quoted by the Division of Mortgage Lending). Licensees may not give legal advice.

north-carolina.answer: In North Carolina the State Bar says a nonlawyer may not handle a residential real estate closing (Authorized Practice Advisory Opinion 2002-1), and the Real Estate Commission says the closing will probably be handled by an attorney chosen by the buyer.

south-carolina.answer: Yes. The South Carolina Supreme Court has held that all real estate and mortgage loan closings must be supervised by a licensed attorney (Matrix Financial Services Corp. v. Frazer, 2011).
south-carolina.rule: South Carolina Supreme Court: all real estate and mortgage loan closings must be supervised by an attorney (Matrix Financial Services Corp. v. Frazer, 2011; Doe v. McMaster, 2003; State v. Buyers Service Co., 1987). The rule comes from the Court power to regulate the practice of law, not from a statute.
south-carolina.who_closes: Attorney (licensed South Carolina attorney supervises; title companies may assist only under attorney supervision)
south-carolina.note: Rule is judicial, not statutory. The attorney need not personally do every clerical task (Boone v. Quicken Loans, 2017). No fee figure.

south-dakota.answer: None of the South Dakota statutes read says a buyer or seller must hire an attorney to close, but only an active State Bar member may practice law (SDCL 16-18-1) and a licensed agent may draft only five kinds of documents (SDCL 36-21A-71).
south-dakota.rule: No South Dakota statute read says a buyer or seller must hire an attorney to close. SDCL 16-18-1 reserves the practice of law to active State Bar members, and a licensed agent may draft only five kinds of documents (SDCL 36-21A-71).
south-dakota.note: The article says a requirement elsewhere in the code, a court rule or a lender instruction cannot be ruled out. The statutes do not say who runs a given closing. No fee figure.

tennessee.answer: None of the Tennessee sources read requires a lawyer at a home closing; a 2007 Attorney General opinion (07-88) says preparing deeds, deeds of trust and sale contracts is not the practice of law, though it can be law business when it takes a lawyer professional judgment.
tennessee.rule: No Tennessee statute or court rule read requires a lawyer at closing. Attorney General Opinion 07-88 (2007) says preparing deeds, deeds of trust and sale contracts is not the practice of law (Tenn. Code 23-3-101(2)) but can be law business when it takes a lawyer professional judgment (23-3-101(1)).
tennessee.note: The Attorney General opinion is advisory and dates from 2007. The article says the sources do not describe who conducts closings. No fee figure.

texas.answer: No. No Texas statute requires an attorney to close a home sale; a title insurance agent and its licensed escrow officer, regulated by the Texas Department of Insurance, can handle the closing, and TDI says you may also have an attorney attend.
texas.rule: No Texas statute requires an attorney to close a home sale. Title insurance agents and licensed escrow officers regulated by TDI (Insurance Code ch. 2651-2652) can handle the closing; an attorney may perform escrow officer duties without an escrow license (2652.003). Drafting legal documents for others is the practice of law (Gov. Code 81.101).
texas.who_closes: Title company (title insurance agent and licensed escrow officer)
texas.note: No official fee figure. Title premium is set by TDI; escrow fees differ between agents.

utah.answer: In the Utah statutes and state purchase contract read, no rule requires a buyer or seller to hire a real estate attorney to close; closings are handled by a title insurance agency with an escrow license (Utah Code 31A-23a-406).
utah.rule: No Utah statute or state purchase contract read requires a real estate attorney to close. A title insurance producer holding the title line and escrow subline may do escrow involving real property transactions (Utah Code 31A-23a-406). Licensees may fill out only forms approved by the commission and attorney general (61-2f-306).
utah.who_closes: Title insurance agency with an escrow license (escrow/closing office)
utah.note: The Utah Supreme Court practice-of-law rule could not be opened, so the article does not say where that line falls. No fee figure.

vermont.answer: None of the Vermont statutes read says a home sale must be closed by an attorney; a deed must be signed, acknowledged before a notary and recorded in the town clerk office (27 V.S.A. 341).
vermont.rule: No Vermont statute read says a home sale must be closed by an attorney. A deed must be signed, acknowledged before a notary and recorded in the town clerk office (27 V.S.A. 341). Practicing law without a license is prohibited (Administrative Order 41, section 1).
vermont.note: The article says the statutes do not say who must run the closing and do not list which closing tasks count as practicing law. No fee figure.

virginia.answer: No Virginia statute read requires a buyer or seller to hire a lawyer; Code of Virginia 55.1-1003 limits who may run a closing to six kinds of settlement agent, one of which is a Virginia-licensed attorney, and only an attorney can give legal advice at the table.
virginia.rule: No Virginia statute read requires a buyer or seller to hire a lawyer. Code of Virginia 55.1-1003 limits who may act as settlement agent to six kinds, one of which is a Virginia-licensed attorney (others: title insurer, title agent, licensed real estate broker, financial institution, its affiliate).
virginia.who_closes: Settlement agent: attorney, title insurance company or agent, licensed real estate broker, or financial institution (buyer chooses)
virginia.note: The statute does not say how often each type is used. Settlement agents other than banks and title insurers need $250,000 E&O and a $200,000 surety bond (55.1-1004). No fee figure.

washington.answer: The Washington statutes and court rules read do not require a buyer or seller to hire an attorney to close; escrow agents need a license from the Department of Financial Institutions unless exempt, such as a bank, a title insurer or agent, or a lawyer (RCW 18.44.021).
washington.rule: No Washington statute or court rule read requires an attorney. Escrow agents need a Department of Financial Institutions license unless exempt, including banks, title insurers and agents, and lawyers (RCW 18.44.021). Limited practice officers may complete approved closing forms under Admission and Practice Rule 12.
washington.who_closes: Licensed escrow company, title company, bank or attorney office (the statute does not say which)

west-virginia.answer: In West Virginia the State Bar Unlawful Practice of Law Committee says conducting a title examination and a real estate closing is the practice of law, so a non-lawyer may do it only under a lawyer direct supervision and control, although no statute read says a buyer or seller must hire an attorney.
west-virginia.rule: No West Virginia statute read says a buyer or seller must hire an attorney, but the State Bar Unlawful Practice of Law Committee (Advisory Opinion 2010-002 Amended) says conducting a title examination and a real estate closing is the practice of law; a non-lawyer may do it only under a lawyer direct supervision and control. Individuals may represent themselves.
west-virginia.who_closes: Attorney, or a lay person under the attorney direct supervision and control
west-virginia.note: The requirement comes from a State Bar advisory opinion (last amended 2015), not a statute. The 2010 Brooke County order was not read. No fee figure.

wisconsin.answer: None of the Wisconsin statutes read requires a lawyer to buy or sell a home, but a real estate licensee may not advise on the legal effect of a specific contract or conveyance or on title (Wis. Stat. 452.40).
wisconsin.rule: No Wisconsin statute read (chapters 452, 709, 757, 846) requires a lawyer to buy or sell a home. Wis. Stat. 452.40 lets licensees fill in approved forms but bars them from advising on the legal effect of a specific contract or conveyance or on title.
wisconsin.note: The article says the statutes do not name who must run a closing, and its finding is limited to the texts read. No fee figure.

wyoming.answer: No Wyoming statute read requires an attorney to buy or sell a home; the Wyoming Title Insurance Act lets a licensed title insurer or title agent run escrow, settlement and closing (W.S. 26-23-314) but does not authorize anyone to practice law.
wyoming.rule: No Wyoming statute read requires an attorney to buy or sell a home. The Wyoming Title Insurance Act lets a licensed title insurer or title agent engage in escrow, settlement and closing (W.S. 26-23-314) and does not authorize anyone to practice law (26-23-302(c)).
wyoming.who_closes: Licensed title insurer or title agent
wyoming.note: The Wyoming State Bar website could not be read. No fee figure.

alabama.answer: Alabama does not require a home seller to deliver a disclosure form in the statutes reviewed. The written duty falls on licensed agents, who must disclose known latent structural defects (Code of Alabama 34-27-36), with fines of $100 to $5,000; fraud statutes apply to all sellers.
alabama.buyer_remedy: No statutory cancellation period. Fraud claim for willful or reckless misrepresentation of a material fact (6-5-101); Real Estate Commission Recovery Fund for violations by a licensee (34-27-31).
alabama.note: Article found no statutory seller form. Rule applies to agents (and licensees selling their own property), not to private sellers. Federal lead-paint rule applies to pre-1978 homes.

alaska.answer: An Alaska seller must deliver a completed written disclosure statement (form 08-4229) before the buyer makes a written offer (AS 34.70.010). If it arrives after the offer, the buyer may withdraw within 3 days, or 6 days if mailed.
alaska.form_name: Residential Real Property Transfer Disclosure Statement, form 08-4229 (Rev. 05/2024)
alaska.covers: Property type and year built, construction and foundation, known defects in appliances and structural parts (roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical, heating, sewage, windows), documents held, utility costs, and yes/no/unknown questions on legal actions, HOA dues, zoning, easements, water and sewer systems, flooding, erosion, permafrost, permits, pests, and environmental hazards. Also asks about a murder or suicide in the past 3 years and smoking inside.
alaska.buyer_remedy: If the statement is delivered after the offer, buyer may withdraw within 3 days of delivery (6 days if mailed). A transfer is not invalidated by non-compliance. Negligent violation: actual damages. Willful violation: up to 3 times actual damages (AS 34.70.090), plus costs and attorney fees.
alaska.note: Exemptions: first transfer of a never-occupied home (AS 34.70.120, form 08-4894) and written waiver by both parties (AS 34.70.110). Unclear whether a bank selling a foreclosed home must use the form.

arizona.answer: Arizona has no statewide seller disclosure form in the statutes reviewed. A.R.S. 32-2156 bars lawsuits over failure to disclose a death, felony, HIV or AIDS exposure, or a nearby sex offender; specific disclosures apply only in certain cases such as HOA documents and rural parcels.
arizona.covers: Case-specific items only: affidavit of disclosure for 5 or fewer parcels in an unincorporated county area (33-422); HOA documents within 10 days of an accepted offer (33-1806); military airport noise notice recorded by the commissioner (32-2113).
arizona.buyer_remedy: Only where a statute says so: for 5 or fewer unincorporated parcels, buyer may rescind within 5 days after receiving the affidavit (33-422). No general statutory penalty found; agent may face license discipline (32-2153).
arizona.note: Article notes a Seller's Property Disclosure Statement (SPDS) may be used in practice but is not prescribed by the statutes read. Federal lead-paint rule applies to pre-1978 homes.

arkansas.answer: Arkansas has no disclosure statute for individual owner-sellers, according to the Arkansas Real Estate Commission, so no state law requires a seller to deliver a condition report. Licensed agents must disclose material facts they know or should know (Ark. Code 17-42-316).
arkansas.statute: Ark. Code 17-42-316 and 17 CAR 220-1005 (agents); no owner-seller statute
arkansas.buyer_remedy: No statutory remedy found for owner silence. Untrue statements in a signed form or in answer to a direct question may be actionable under contract and general misrepresentation law.
arkansas.note: Many sellers use a voluntary Realtor trade association form. Article says it could not open Ark. Code 17-10-101 itself; the Commission column (undated) says a homicide, suicide or felony at the property is not a material fact that must be disclosed.

california.answer: A California seller must deliver a Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement (Civil Code 1102.6) and a Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement (1103.2). If either arrives after the offer, the buyer may cancel within 3 days of in-person delivery or 5 days if mailed or sent electronically.
california.form_name: Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement (TDS); Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement (NHD)
california.covers: The TDS covers the seller's and agent's disclosures on the home's condition. The NHD asks whether the property is in a FEMA flood zone, dam inundation area, high fire hazard zone, wildland fire area, earthquake fault zone, or seismic hazard zone. Separate notices cover Megan's Law, smoke alarms, carbon monoxide devices, water heater bracing, pre-1960 earthquake hazards, fire hardening, defensible space, supplemental tax bills, and Mello-Roos.
california.buyer_remedy: Buyer may terminate in writing within 3 days of in-person delivery or 5 days of mailing or electronic delivery (1102.3, 1103.3). Seller who willfully or negligently fails to disclose is liable for actual damages (1102.13, 1103.13). Smoke alarm and carbon monoxide violations: actual damages up to $100 plus costs and fees.
california.note: The form cannot be waived, including in an as-is sale (1102, 1102.1). Exemptions in 1102.2 include probate, foreclosure, and transfers between spouses or close relatives. A death more than 3 years before the offer need not be disclosed (1710.2).

colorado.answer: Colorado has no single statute requiring every seller to complete one condition form. C.R.S. Title 38, Article 35.7 requires specific disclosures, including special taxing districts, elevated radon, water source, and past methamphetamine use.
colorado.form_name: Colorado Real Estate Commission approved seller's property disclosure (referred to by several statutes)
colorado.covers: Named items only: special taxing districts, HOA notice, methamphetamine lab use, drinking water source (well or provider), transportation projects, oil, gas and mineral estate, new construction in a metro district, metro district website, and known radon test results and mitigation.
colorado.buyer_remedy: Remedies are set item by item: special taxing district notice, buyer may claim all damages plus costs (38-35.7-101); HOA notice, actual damages plus costs (38-35.7-102); meth lab known and undisclosed, seller liable for remediation, health injuries and attorney fees, suit within 3 years after closing (38-35.7-103).
colorado.note: Article could not open the Commission's current form. A death, felony or occupant HIV or AIDS status is not a material fact subject to disclosure (38-35.5-101). A cleaned-up meth lab with compliance certificates need not be disclosed.

connecticut.answer: A Connecticut seller of a one- to four-unit home must give the buyer a written residential condition report before the buyer signs a binder or contract (Conn. Gen. Stat. 20-327b). If the seller does not, the buyer gets a $500 credit at closing.
connecticut.covers: General information (year built, easements, flood hazard, wetlands, dam, assessments, historic district), leased equipment, mechanical and utility systems, water and sewage, asbestos and lead, and building and structure (foundation, pyrrhotite, roof, water damage, pests, radon). Answers are to the seller's best knowledge.
connecticut.buyer_remedy: $500 credit at closing if the report is not furnished (20-327c(a)). Buyer may also sue for actual damages for a defect within the seller's actual knowledge that significantly impairs value, health or safety, or useful life (20-327c).
connecticut.note: Exemptions include transfers between co-owners, to a spouse or close relative, new homes under the implied warranty, fiduciary sales, and most foreclosure sales; in crumbling-foundation towns a foreclosure owner gives a shorter Residential Foundation Condition Report.

delaware.answer: A Delaware seller of a one- to four-family home must disclose all known material defects in writing before signing the listing agreement (6 Del. C. 2572). The seller must give the buyer the Real Estate Commission's condition report before the buyer makes an offer, plus a separate radon disclosure.
delaware.form_name: Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report (effective August 1, 2026); Radon Disclosure form
delaware.covers: Occupancy and rentals, deed restrictions, HOA and condo fees and assessments, title and zoning, environmental concerns (underground tanks, asbestos, lead, mold, methamphetamine), flood zone and drainage, insurance claims in the past 5 years, structure, roof, termites, plumbing, septic, heating, electrical, and who pays to repave the street. The radon form covers known radon and tests.
delaware.note: No fixed cancellation window and no penalty stated in the sections read; the statute lists when a buyer cannot sue (2575). Exemptions in 2577 include court-ordered sales, foreclosure, fiduciary sales, and transfers to a spouse or relative. Psychologically impacted property is not a material fact (24 Del. C. 2927).

florida.answer: Florida has no statewide seller condition form, but a 1985 Florida Supreme Court ruling (Johnson v. Davis) requires sellers to disclose known, hidden facts that materially affect value. Statutes add written notices, including a flood disclosure under 689.302 required since October 1, 2024.
florida.covers: Flood disclosure form: flooding that damaged the property during the seller's ownership, flood insurance claims including NFIP, and flood assistance including FEMA. Also radon notice, property tax summary, HOA disclosure summary, condo documents, coastal construction control line statement, and known sewer lateral defects.
florida.buyer_remedy: Missing HOA summary: buyer may cancel within 3 days of receiving it or before closing (720.401). Condo documents delivered late: buyer may cancel within 7 days. Hidden material defects: buyer may sue under the duty set by case law.
florida.note: Duty applies even in an as-is sale of residential property. A homicide, suicide or death, and HIV or AIDS, are not material facts that must be disclosed (689.25). Coastal statement missing does not void the contract (161.57(4)).

georgia.answer: Georgia has no mandatory state seller-disclosure form in the statutes reviewed; caveat emptor is the general rule for used homes. A seller who knows of a serious hidden defect and stays silent can be sued for fraud.
georgia.statute: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5(b) (brokers); 44-1-16; fraud case law (Dennis v. Wohlgemuth, 2022)
georgia.buyer_remedy: Buyer who proves fraud may affirm the contract and sue for damages, or promptly rescind and sue in tort. Reliance is hard to prove if inspection or the form flagged the problem.
georgia.note: Seller forms arise from the purchase contract, not statute. Broker must disclose known adverse physical conditions on the property and within one mile (10-6A-5(b)). Flood disclosure bill HB 618 did not become law. Death or disease facts need not be volunteered but questions must be answered truthfully (44-1-16).

hawaii.answer: Hawaii has a mandatory seller-disclosure law, chapter 508D of the Hawaii Revised Statutes. The sources reviewed do not state its deadlines, form contents or buyer remedies.
hawaii.note: Article could not open the text of chapter 508D, so form name, contents, deadline and remedies are not stated. Reviewed sources only cross-reference the chapter. Federal lead-paint rule applies to pre-1978 homes.

idaho.answer: An Idaho seller of a home with one to four dwelling units must complete the statutory disclosure form and deliver it within 10 days after accepting the buyer's offer (Idaho Code 55-2504, 55-2509). The buyer may rescind within 3 business days of receiving it.
idaho.statute: Idaho Code 55-2501 to 55-2518 (Property Condition Disclosure Act)
idaho.covers: Annexation and city services, appliances and systems not working, problems with basement water, foundation, roof, well, septic, plumbing, drainage, electrical and heating, title conditions (encroachments, easements, zoning violations, lot line disputes), hazardous materials or pests, additions without a permit, and any other known problem.
idaho.buyer_remedy: If the form arrives after the purchase agreement is signed, buyer may rescind in writing within 3 business days of receipt, with deposit returned (55-2515). A transfer is not invalidated by non-compliance; a willful or negligent violation makes the seller liable for actual damages (55-2517).
idaho.note: Section 55-2505 lists 16 exempt transfers, including foreclosure and bank resales, estates, family transfers, and new homes never inhabited. The form is not a warranty (55-2507).

illinois.answer: An Illinois seller of one to four units, a condo or a co-op must complete the 24-item disclosure report and deliver it before the contract is signed (765 ILCS 77). If it arrives after signing, the buyer may cancel within 5 business days and get the earnest money back.
illinois.form_name: Residential Real Property Disclosure Report (form set in 765 ILCS 77/35); Disclosure of Information on Radon Hazards
illinois.covers: 24 yes/no/not applicable statements, including basement flooding or leaks, floodplain, roof, foundation, wall, electrical, plumbing and heating defects, radon, asbestos, lead paint and lead pipes, termites, underground fuel tanks, mine subsidence, boundary disputes, code violations, and methamphetamine production. Answers reflect only actual knowledge.
illinois.buyer_remedy: Report with a material defect delivered after signing: cancel within 5 business days of receipt, earnest money returned (77/40). No report before conveyance: right to terminate (77/55). Knowing violation: actual damages and court costs, possibly attorney fees; suit within one year (77/55, 77/60).
illinois.note: Separate radon pamphlet and form required before the buyer is bound. Exemptions in Section 15 include court-ordered and fiduciary transfers, family transfers, foreclosure transfers and never-occupied new homes. The Act does not limit fraud remedies.

indiana.answer: An Indiana owner of a one-to-four-unit home must complete and sign the state disclosure form and give it to the buyer before an offer is accepted (IC 32-21-5-10). If a defect is disclosed only after acceptance, the buyer has two business days to cancel in writing.
indiana.form_name: Real Estate Seller's Disclosure Form (State Form 46234)
indiana.covers: Known condition of the foundation, mechanical systems, roof, structure, water and sewer systems; also uncertified methamphetamine contamination, nearby airport, military installation, FEMA flood plain, historic district, conservation easement, and certain redevelopment liens.
indiana.buyer_remedy: If a form or amended form disclosing a defect arrives after the offer is accepted, buyer may cancel within two business days by written rescission and get deposits back (32-21-5-13). Failure to deliver the form does not by itself invalidate a completed sale.
indiana.note: An accepted offer is not enforceable against the buyer until both sign the form. Exemptions in 32-21-5-1(b) include court-ordered, foreclosure, fiduciary, family and never-inhabited new-construction transfers. HOA documents due 10 days before closing (32-21-5-8.5).

Real Estate Licensing Information, with State Form 46234, Real Estate Seller's Disclosure Form (Indiana Professional Licensing Agency)

iowa.answer: An Iowa seller of a home with one to four units must give the buyer a written disclosure statement before making or accepting a written offer (Iowa Code 558A.2). If it is late, the buyer may withdraw within 3 days of personal delivery or 5 days of mail or electronic delivery.
iowa.form_name: Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement (Real Estate Commission sample form)
iowa.statute: Iowa Code chapter 558A; Iowa Administrative Code 481-2014
iowa.covers: 20 numbered yes/no items: basement or foundation water, roof, sewer, heating, cooling, plumbing and electrical, infestation and structural damage, asbestos, radon tests, lead-based paint, flood plain, lead water service lines, zoning and covenants, HOA, settling and drainage problems, well and septic. Seller also acknowledges the Iowa radon fact sheet.
iowa.buyer_remedy: Late statement: buyer may withdraw the offer or revoke acceptance without liability within 3 days of personal delivery or 5 days of mail or electronic delivery. Violator is liable for actual damages (558A.6). A transfer is not invalidated solely for non-compliance (558A.8).
iowa.note: Iowa does not force one exact form; the Commission rule lists minimum content and recommends a sample. Exemptions in 558A.1(7) include court-ordered, foreclosure, fiduciary, family and divorce transfers. No exemption for new construction or as-is sales.

kansas.answer: No Kansas statute in the sources reviewed prescribes a seller disclosure form. Licensed agents must disclose adverse material facts they actually know (K.S.A. 58-30,106(d)(1)), and every residential sales contract must carry a radon notice (K.S.A. 58-3078a).
kansas.buyer_remedy: No penalty for a silent seller found in the statutes reviewed. Court decisions on hidden-defect claims were not read.
kansas.note: Duty is on licensees, not on a seller who sells without an agent. Radon notice says Kansas law requires sellers to disclose known elevated radon information. Federal lead-paint rule applies to pre-1978 homes.

K.S.A. 58-3062, Prohibited acts (Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes)

kentucky.answer: Kentucky requires a written seller's disclosure on single-family homes when a licensed agent is paid in the sale (KRS 324.360). The seller completes KREC Form 402, and the listing agent must give the buyer a copy within 72 hours of receiving a signed offer.
kentucky.form_name: KREC Form 402, Seller's Disclosure of Property Condition (12/2022)
kentucky.covers: 13 topics on yes/no/unknown/not applicable: rental use and vacancy, plumbing, electrical, appliances, heating, cooling, water heater, structure and foundation, roof, land and drainage including flood hazard area, boundaries, water and sewer or septic, remodeling and permits, HOA and condo status, hazardous conditions (underground tanks, lead paint, radon, methamphetamine), and miscellaneous items.
kentucky.buyer_remedy: No set penalty or cancellation right found in KRS 324.360 or 201 KAR 11:121. A seller may refuse to complete the form, and the agent must then tell the buyer in writing. The form warns that undisclosed methamphetamine contamination left undecontaminated is a Class D felony.
kentucky.note: Statute applies only where a licensee is paid; a sale by owner with no licensee is outside it. Exempt: new homes with a warranty, auctions, court-supervised foreclosures (KRS 324.360(7)). The form is not a warranty.

KREC Form 402, Seller's Disclosure of Property Condition, 12/2022 (Kentucky Real Estate Commission)

louisiana.answer: A Louisiana seller of residential property with one to four dwelling units must complete a property disclosure document and deliver it no later than the time the buyer makes an offer (R.S. 9:3198). If it arrives after the offer, the buyer may cancel within 72 hours with the deposit returned.
louisiana.form_name: Property Disclosure Document (Louisiana Real Estate Commission, 2026 form)
louisiana.covers: Known defects (conditions that substantially hurt value, significantly impair health or safety, or significantly shorten life), homeowners' association and restrictive covenants, illegal methamphetamine laboratory, salt-dome cavity and solution-mining injection well within 2,640 feet, and commercial or industrial zoning.
louisiana.buyer_remedy: If delivered after the offer, buyer may cancel the contract or withdraw the offer within 72 hours of receipt (weekends and holidays excluded), deposit promptly returned; right expires at transfer of title or occupancy (9:3198(B)(3)). Separately, redhibition under Civil Code art. 2520, 2545: a seller who knew of an undeclared defect owes the price back with interest, expenses, damages and reasonable attorney fees.
louisiana.note: Exempt transfers in 9:3197(B) include court-ordered and foreclosure sales, estates, never-occupied new construction and family transfers. A transfer is not invalidated by non-compliance. Act 708 of 2026 extends the chapter to vacant residential land from January 1, 2027.

maine.answer: A Maine seller of a home with one to four residential units must give the buyer a written property disclosure statement no later than the offer (33 M.R.S. 173, 174). If it arrives after the offer, the buyer has 72 hours to withdraw without penalty.
maine.covers: Water supply (including water test results and PFAS), heating, waste disposal and septic, hazardous materials (asbestos, lead paint, radon, underground oil tanks, methamphetamine), known defects, access and private road maintenance, flood zone and flood history, and shoreland zoning violations. Seller also hands over state arsenic information.
maine.buyer_remedy: Form delivered after the offer: buyer may end the contract or withdraw within 72 hours of receiving it, deposit promptly returned; right lapses at settlement or occupancy (174). A transfer is not invalidated solely for non-compliance; common-law fraud duties remain (178).
maine.note: The statute lists contents but the sections read set no single mandatory form. Exemptions in 172 include foreclosure sales, estates, family transfers, and government transfers. Seller must supplement in writing if an error is learned before settlement (175).

Maine Revised Statutes, Title 33, §§ 174-178, delivery, changes, liability (Maine Legislature)

maryland.answer: A Maryland seller of a home with four or fewer units must give the buyer either a disclosure statement or an as-is disclaimer statement, on the Real Estate Commission's form, on or before the contract (Real Property 10-702). A buyer who gets it late may rescind within 5 days after receiving it.
maryland.form_name: Maryland Residential Property Disclosure and Disclaimer Statement
maryland.covers: Seller either lists defects actually known or states the sale is as-is. Topics: water and sewer, insulation, structural systems, plumbing, electrical, heating and air conditioning, wood-destroying insects, land use, hazardous materials (asbestos, lead paint, radon, underground tanks, landfills), smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms, and other material defects.
maryland.buyer_remedy: If not received by the contract date, buyer may rescind before receiving it or within 5 days after receiving it, with immediate refund of deposits (10-702(h)). Right ends at closing or occupancy, or at mortgage application if the lender gave written notice. The text lists no fines.
maryland.note: Even an as-is seller must disclose known latent defects (10-702(d)). Exemptions include first sale of never-occupied homes, foreclosure and fiduciary sales, and transfers exempt from transfer tax. A revised form was reported approved at the August 19, 2026 Commission meeting.

massachusetts.answer: Massachusetts does not require a general property condition form. A seller must give the buyer the state lead notice before the purchase and sale agreement is signed (M.G.L. c. 111, 197A), with a penalty of up to $1,000 for failing to do so.
massachusetts.form_name: State lead notification form (Massachusetts lead program)
massachusetts.covers: Lead notice and known information about dangerous lead levels; smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms on sale (fire department inspection); federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 homes.
massachusetts.buyer_remedy: Failure to give the lead notice: liability for all damages caused plus a civil penalty of up to $1,000, and a c. 93A unfair or deceptive practice claim. False statements about the house can support a c. 93A claim even without a form. Federal rule gives a 10-day lead inspection window.
massachusetts.note: A psychologically impacted property (felony, suicide, homicide, HIV or AIDS, alleged supernatural event) need not be disclosed, but a seller may not lie when asked (c. 93, 114). Article could not read the Title 5 septic text and states no septic inspection rule.

michigan.answer: A Michigan seller of 1 to 4 residential units must give the buyer a signed disclosure form before the buyer signs a binding purchase agreement (Seller Disclosure Act, MCL 565.954). If it arrives later, the buyer may cancel within 72 hours in person or 120 hours by registered mail.
michigan.form_name: Statutory seller disclosure statement (form written into MCL 565.957)
michigan.covers: Appliances and systems, water in basement, roof leaks, well and septic, infestation, flood insurance, mineral rights, environmental problems (asbestos, radon, lead paint, tanks, contaminated soil), shared walls, easements, zoning violations, HOA, work without permits, settling, flooding, fire or wind damage, nearby landfills or airports, unpaid assessments, and litigation.
michigan.buyer_remedy: If delivered after a binding agreement, buyer may terminate within 72 hours (in person) or 120 hours (registered mail); right ends at transfer of title (565.954). A sale is not invalidated solely for non-compliance (565.964). Fraud and misrepresentation remedies remain (565.961).
michigan.note: Exemptions in 565.953 include court-ordered and foreclosure sales, fiduciary transfers, family transfers, and a builder's first sale of never-occupied new homes. Local governments may require extra disclosures (565.959).

minnesota.answer: A Minnesota seller of residential property must give the buyer a written disclosure of all material facts the seller knows before signing the sale agreement (Minn. Stat. 513.55). A buyer harmed by a missed disclosure has two years after closing to sue.
minnesota.covers: All material facts the seller knows that could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment. Separate required items: radon tests, reports, mitigation and state booklet; wells; sewage system; and known methamphetamine production.
minnesota.buyer_remedy: Seller who knew and failed to disclose is liable for damages and equitable relief; suit within two years after closing (513.57). No automatic right to cancel; a court may order rescission (513.59). Hidden private sewage system: cost of compliance plus attorney fees (115.55).
minnesota.note: Sections read do not prescribe an official form. Deaths, suicide, HIV or AIDS, and paranormal activity need not be disclosed (513.56). Buyer and seller may waive the written disclosure in writing (513.60). Exemptions in 513.54 include foreclosure, family transfers and new homes.

mississippi.answer: A Mississippi seller of a home with one to four dwelling units must give the buyer a Property Condition Disclosure Statement when a licensed broker or salesperson is involved (Miss. Code 89-1-501 to 89-1-523). If it arrives after the offer, the buyer has 3 days after in-person delivery or 5 days after mailing to terminate.
mississippi.form_name: Property Condition Disclosure Statement (Mississippi Real Estate Commission form)
mississippi.statute: Miss. Code 89-1-501 to 89-1-523 (as amended by House Bill 1271, 2024)
mississippi.covers: Appliances and systems, roof age and leaks, past flooding and flood insurance, foundation repairs, termite and other infestation history, easements, major fire, wind or flood damage, hazards such as asbestos, radon or underground tanks, and other needed repairs.
mississippi.buyer_remedy: If the statement or a material amendment arrives after the offer, buyer may terminate by written notice within 3 days of in-person delivery or 5 days of mailing (89-1-503(1)). If a statement is not delivered or left blank, the buyer is presumed to be on notice to inquire (89-1-503(2)). A transfer is not invalidated solely for non-compliance.
mississippi.note: Law applies only to transfers made with a licensee's aid. Article could not open the Commission's current form, so the contents list reflects the 1997 statute form. 2024 law says a licensee has no duty under the Act and cannot be disciplined for the disclosure. Exemptions in 89-1-501(2) include foreclosure, fiduciary and family transfers.

missouri.answer: No Missouri statute reviewed requires a seller to deliver a general property-condition form. Specific duties apply to methamphetamine production (RSMo 442.606) and landfills on the property (RSMo 260.213), and concealing a material fact can still create liability.
missouri.covers: Written disclosure of known methamphetamine production, meth-related convictions of a resident or storage or lab use if the seller knew or should have known, and a permitted or unpermitted landfill or solid waste site on the land.
missouri.buyer_remedy: No single statutory remedy set in the sections read. Possible claims under the Merchandising Practices Act (RSMo 407.020, 407.025) if the sale falls within it, under the specific meth and landfill statutes, and under the contract.
missouri.note: Many sales use a seller's condition form as a contract document, not a state-mandated one. A homicide, felony, suicide or occupant HIV or AIDS is not a material fact that must be disclosed (442.600). Agents must disclose adverse material facts they knew or should have known (339.730).
