new-york.answer: New York State taxes every deed at $2 per $500 of price, or 0.4%, and the seller pays. New York City adds its own tax of 1% up to $500,000 and 1.425% above it on homes, and the buyer pays a 1% mansion tax on residential sales of $1 million or more.
new-york.tax_name: Real estate transfer tax (Tax Law 1402), plus mansion tax (1402-a)
new-york.rate_text: $2 per $500 of consideration, or fraction of $500 (0.4%), when consideration is over $500

calc.explain: Divide consideration by $500, round up to the next whole unit, multiply by $2. Applies when consideration is more than $500. The 1% mansion tax (buyer) on residential sales of $1,000,000 or more is separate and not included.

new-york.local_taxes: New York City RPTT on sales above $25,000: 1% up to $500,000 and 1.425% above for 1-3 family houses, condos and co-ops; other property 1.425% up to $500,000 and 2.625% above. In NYC, additional base tax of $1.25 per $500 (0.25%) on residential conveyances of $3 million or more ($2 million for non-residential), and a buyer-paid supplemental tax on residential sales of $2 million or more rising from 0.25% to 2.9% of the whole price.
new-york.who_pays_text: State base tax and additional base tax: seller (grantor), with the buyer liable if the seller fails to pay or is exempt. Mansion tax and NYC supplemental tax: buyer. NYC RPTT: the city page does not assign it to one side, so the contract controls.
new-york.mortgage_tax: The sources say New York taxes the recording of a mortgage separately and it is not a transfer tax; no rate is given.
new-york.exemptions: Tax Law 1405 exempts conveyances to the United States, New York State or agencies, deeds that only secure a debt, gifts and other transfers without consideration, changes of form with no change in beneficial ownership, partition deeds, and certain contracts or options under $200,000 on a personal residence. NYC lists its own exemptions; a sale by an executor is taxable.
new-york.note: The mansion tax is a cliff: $999,999 pays none and $1,000,000 pays $10,000. File Form TP-584 (or TP-584-NYC in the city); tax is due by the 15th day after delivery.

north-carolina.answer: North Carolina charges a state excise tax on deeds of $1 for each $500, or fraction of $500, of the price or value conveyed, which is $864 on a $431,900 home. The seller owes it and pays the county Register of Deeds before the deed is recorded.
north-carolina.tax_name: Excise stamp tax on conveyances (G.S. 105 Article 8E)
north-carolina.rate_text: $1 for each $500, or fractional part, of consideration or value (0.2%)

calc.explain: Divide the consideration or value by $500, round up to the next whole unit, multiply by $1.

north-carolina.local_taxes: Only seven counties levy a local excise tax: Camden, Chowan, Currituck, Dare, Pasquotank, Perquimans and Washington. It is $1 per $100 or fraction (about 1%) on top of the state tax. Mecklenburg County is not one of them, though its own Register of Deeds pages could not be opened.
north-carolina.who_pays_text: By law the transferor (seller) pays the Register of Deeds before the deed is recorded. Buyers and sellers can bargain over costs in the contract.
north-carolina.exemptions: The state statute listing exemptions could not be read, so the state exemptions are not stated. For the local tax in the seven counties: deeds of gift, foreclosure deeds or deeds in lieu to the mortgage holder, government deeds, and transfers with no consideration.
north-carolina.note: The local exemption list does not prove the state tax works the same way. NCDOR's allocation table dates from the mid-2000s. The deed of trust has a recording fee, not the excise tax.

north-dakota.answer: North Dakota has no real estate transfer tax: Title 57 of the Century Code has no chapter on one and the Tax Commissioner's list of state taxes shows none. A recording fee of $20 applies to a deed of one to six pages, and the buyer must certify the full sale price on the deed.
north-dakota.rate_text: None; recording fee only ($20 for a deed of 1 to 6 pages, N.D.C.C. 11-18-05)

calc.explain: No tax is calculated on the price. Recording fees depend on page count.

north-dakota.local_taxes: None found. The sources read do not cover local taxes in detail; ask the county recorder or title company. The recorder fee schedule is the same in every county.
north-dakota.who_pays_text: No transfer tax. The statute does not say whether buyer or seller bears the recording fee; the purchase agreement and closing statement decide.
north-dakota.exemptions: No tax to exempt from. The grantee certifies the full consideration or an exemption from the price statement, which covers family sales, estate settlements, forced sales and foreclosures, nonprofit sales, quitclaim deeds and others.
north-dakota.note: The Cass County recorder's own fee page was not available.

ohio.answer: Ohio does not call it a transfer tax; counties collect a conveyance fee when a deed is presented to the auditor. Franklin County's calculator shows $3 per $1,000 of the price, made of $1 set by the State of Ohio and $2 set by the county commissioners, plus a $0.50 transfer tax.
ohio.tax_name: Conveyance fee (collected by the county auditor)
ohio.rate_text: Franklin County: $3 per $1,000 of price, of which $1 is the state share and $2 is the county share; $1 per $1,000 if the seller receives the homestead exemption

calc.explain: State share only: round the sale amount up to the nearest $100, then $1 per $1,000 ($0.10 per $100). Franklin County adds $2 per $1,000 set by the county commissioners (waived if the grantor has the homestead exemption), a $3 minimum conveyance fee and a $0.50 transfer tax on every non-exempt transfer.

ohio.local_taxes: Counties set their own local portion. Franklin County: $2 per $1,000 (last updated August 2019) plus a $0.50 transfer tax; no additional Columbus city charge was found in the sources.
ohio.who_pays_text: The sources do not say who must pay; the contract controls. The reduced homestead rate refers to the grantor (seller), which points to the seller as the party charged.
ohio.exemptions: Transfers to or from governments, transfers solely securing or releasing a debt (affidavit required), corrective deeds, gifts between spouses or parent and child (or child's spouse), delinquent tax sales, transfers with no consideration that are not gifts (affidavit), transfers to or from a revocable trust, and transfers among heirs when no money is paid. An exempt transfer still pays the $0.50 transfer tax and is reported on form DTE 100EX.
ohio.note: Based on the Franklin County Auditor's calculator as read in October 2026; another county can differ.

oklahoma.answer: Oklahoma has no transfer tax by that name but taxes deeds through a documentary stamp tax of $0.75 for each $500 of consideration, or part of $500, which is $375 on a $250,000 sale. It applies only when the value exceeds $100, and stamps must be on the deed before recording.
oklahoma.rate_text: $0.75 for each $500 of consideration, or fractional part of $500 ($1.50 per $1,000, 0.15%)

calc.explain: Divide consideration (minus any lien that stays on the property) by $500, round up to the next whole unit, multiply by $0.75. Applies only when the net consideration is more than $100. Consideration includes any debt the buyer assumes.

oklahoma.local_taxes: None found. The sources read for Oklahoma County show only the state stamp tax; ask the closing company to confirm no local charge.
oklahoma.who_pays_text: The statute puts the tax on any person who makes, signs, issues or sells the deed, or for whose benefit it is made, which points first at the seller in a normal sale. It does not say whether a contract can move the cost. On a foreclosure deed to a non-lender grantee, the purchaser pays.
oklahoma.mortgage_tax: A separate real estate mortgage tax (68 O.S. 1904): $0.10 per $100 of principal for a mortgage of five years or more, with lower rates for shorter terms, plus a $10 county treasurer certification fee.
oklahoma.exemptions: Deeds between spouses, parent and child, or relatives within the second degree with no actual consideration; to or from a person's express revocable trust; to a family-owned entity (tax due if an interest passes to a non-family member within one year); deeds securing or releasing a debt; corrective deeds; to a mortgage holder in foreclosure or in lieu (except cash paid); tax deeds; and certain government deeds. The exemption must be written on the deed.
oklahoma.note: A note that the price is under $100 no longer works as an exemption. Federal transfers to or from national banks and federal savings and loans are not exempt.

oregon.answer: Oregon has no state transfer tax. Article IX, Section 15 of the Oregon Constitution bars the state, cities and counties from taxing the transfer of real property or measuring a tax by its price, except taxes in effect on December 31, 2009. In Multnomah County a deed costs $86 to record for the first page and $5 per extra page.
oregon.rate_text: None; recording fee only (Multnomah County: $86 first page, $5 each extra page)

calc.explain: No tax is calculated on the price. Recording fees do not rise with the price.

oregon.local_taxes: None in Multnomah County's fee schedule. The Constitution exempts only local taxes already in force on December 31, 2009 (ORS 306.815 uses March 31, 1997 for local taxes on fee estates); the sources do not name which governments had one, so ask the county assessment and taxation office or title company elsewhere.
oregon.who_pays_text: No transfer tax to assign. Who pays the recording fees is a term of the purchase agreement.
oregon.exemptions: No tax to exempt from. Recording fees are not treated as a tax on the transfer.
oregon.note: Conclusion rests on the Constitution and ORS 306.815; the constitutional text read does not list which pre-2010 taxes survive.

ORS 306.815, tax on transfer of real property prohibited; exceptions (Oregon Legislature)

pennsylvania.answer: Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1% of the value of the property, and counties and municipalities add a local tax; Philadelphia adds 3.578% for a total of 4.578%. Both buyer and seller are liable to the state, and in Philadelphia the tax is usually split evenly.
pennsylvania.rate_text: 1% of the value of the property

calc.explain: 1% of the value of the real estate, including contracted-for improvements, plus assumed debt. For transfers with no sale price, such as gifts or foreclosures, the base is assessed value times the Department of Revenue's Common Level Ratio factor for the county.

pennsylvania.local_taxes: Local rates are set by each jurisdiction (county, municipality, school district); ask the Recorder of Deeds. Philadelphia: 3.578% city share (raised from 3.278% on July 1, 2025), total 4.578% with the state.
pennsylvania.who_pays_text: The state holds seller and buyer jointly and severally liable. In Philadelphia the tax is usually split evenly but this is not required, and the city can collect 100% from either party; the contract decides the split.
pennsylvania.exemptions: Certain transfers among family members, transfers to governmental units, between religious organizations, to shareholders or partners, deeds to burial sites, and property passed by will or intestate succession. Philadelphia adds most transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings, with documentation. Buying from an estate is not exempt.
pennsylvania.note: In Philadelphia payment is due within 30 days after the Department of Records receives the document; misrepresentation or failure to record can bring penalties up to 50% of the tax.

rhode-island.answer: Rhode Island taxes real estate sales through its conveyance tax of $3.75 for each $500 of the price, or part of it, which is $3,000 on a $400,000 home. Unless the parties agree otherwise the seller pays, and residential sales above $800,000 owe a second layer.
rhode-island.tax_name: Real estate conveyance tax (R.I. Gen. Laws 44-25-1)
rhode-island.rate_text: $3.75 for each $500 of price or fractional part of $500; residential property adds a second $3.75 per $500 on the part above $800,000 (threshold indexed to inflation from 2026)

calc.explain: Basic tax = $3.75 x number of $500 blocks (fraction rounds up) on the whole price, including any lien that stays on the property; applies to deeds for more than $100. For residential property, add a second tax of $3.75 per $500 block on the part of the price above $800,000. The statute adjusts the $800,000 threshold with CPI-U from tax years beginning January 1, 2026 and the adjusted figure is not in the statute; check with the Division of Taxation. Example at $900,000 with an $800,000 threshold: $6,750 + $750 = $7,500.

rhode-island.local_taxes: None found. Providence has no separate conveyance tax in the statute read; the municipality keeps $1.80 of each $3.75 of the state tax it collects.
rhode-island.who_pays_text: By law, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, the seller (grantor) pays (44-25-1(a)); the purchase contract can shift the cost.
rhode-island.exemptions: Documents securing a debt such as a mortgage, deeds where the United States, Rhode Island or a political subdivision is the grantor, certain sales of manufactured home communities to a resident-owned organization, and some transfers among owners of affordable housing companies financed with federal low-income housing tax credits.
rhode-island.note: The Division of Taxation's pages could not be opened, so the current indexed threshold is unknown. Rate as amended effective October 1, 2025.

sources.title: R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-25-1, Tax imposed, payment, burden (Rhode Island General Assembly)
R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-25-2, Exemptions (Rhode Island General Assembly)

south-carolina.answer: South Carolina has no tax called a transfer tax but charges a deed recording fee of $1.85 per $500 of value, or $3.70 per $1,000 ($2.60 state and $1.10 county), which is $1,480 on a $400,000 sale. By law the seller owes it.
south-carolina.rate_text: $1.85 per $500 of value, or fractional part of $500 ($3.70 per $1,000): $1.30 per $500 state and $0.55 per $500 county

calc.explain: Divide value by $500, round up to the next whole unit, multiply by $1.85 (state $1.30 plus county $0.55, both set by statute). Value is what was paid, including debt assumed, minus any prior lien that stays on the property; the parties may elect the property tax fair market value.

south-carolina.local_taxes: The county part ($0.55 per $500) is included in the $1.85. Greenville County's schedule shows no city component. Flat filing fees of $15 for a deed and $25 for a mortgage apply regardless of price.
south-carolina.who_pays_text: The statute puts the fee on the grantor (seller), jointly and severally if several; the buyer is only secondarily liable. For deeds from a master-in-equity, governments or a tax-exempt retirement plan, the grantee owes it.
south-carolina.exemptions: Deeds of $100 or less, transfers to governments including school districts, transfers with no gain or loss recognized under IRC 1041 (spouses and certain divorce transfers), partition deeds, corrective or quitclaim deeds with no consideration, deeds to a mortgagee in lieu of foreclosure or in foreclosure, and certain no-consideration transfers involving corporations, partnerships and trusts. A deed of distribution from an estate is not taxable.
south-carolina.note: The statute calls it a recording fee, but in effect it works as a transfer tax on most sales. An affidavit stating the value or the exemption must be filed with the deed.

sources.title: S.C. Code Title 12, Chapter 24, Deed Recording Fee, §§ 12-24-10 to 12-24-160 (South Carolina Legislature)
Recording Requirements & Fees (Greenville County Register of Deeds)

south-dakota.answer: South Dakota imposes a real estate transfer fee of $0.50 for each $500 of value, or fraction, which is 0.1% or $400 on a $400,000 sale. The statute makes the grantor, the seller, pay it, and the county register of deeds collects it at recording.
south-dakota.rate_text: $0.50 for each $500 of value, or fraction of $500 (0.1%)

calc.explain: Divide the declared value by $500, round up to a whole number, multiply by $0.50. The statute sets no minimum or maximum.

south-dakota.local_taxes: None. The sources show one transfer fee, the same in every county, credited to the county general fund; the Minnehaha County schedule shows no separate city charge.
south-dakota.who_pays_text: By law the grantor pays (SDCL 43-4-21), which is the seller in a sale; the purchase contract could shift the cost by agreement.
south-dakota.exemptions: Transfers to or by governments, transfers solely securing a debt, corrective deeds, spouse or parent-child transfers for nominal consideration, tax sales, sheriff's, foreclosure and in-lieu deeds, partition, estate decrees of distribution, absolute gifts, divorce decrees, and transfers for no consideration. SDCL 43-4-22 lists 19 exemptions; the deed must say 'exempt from transfer fee' and name the subdivision.
south-dakota.note: A certificate of real estate value must accompany the deed; a false value or false exemption claim is a Class 1 misdemeanor.

SDCL 43-4-22, exemptions from real estate transfer fee (South Dakota Legislature)

tennessee.answer: Tennessee taxes both the deed and the loan: the realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price and the mortgage tax is $0.115 per $100 of debt with the first $2,000 exempt. By the Department of Revenue's rules the buyer pays the first and the borrower the second.
tennessee.tax_name: Realty transfer tax (recordation tax, Tenn. Code Ann. 67-4-409)

calc.explain: Price divided by $100, times $0.37. The base for a typical sale is the greater of the price paid or the value of the property at transfer. The sources do not say how a fraction of $100 is handled.

tennessee.local_taxes: None found. The Department's and Davidson County Register's materials show only the state tax; ask the Register of Deeds.
tennessee.who_pays_text: The Department's manual says the grantee (buyer named on the deed) pays the realty transfer tax and the mortgagor pays the mortgage tax; the manual does not discuss private agreements, so check the purchase contract.
tennessee.mortgage_tax: Mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 of principal indebtedness, with the first $2,000 of the debt exempt; interest and collection costs are not taxed; paid by the borrower. Lines of credit are taxed on the stated maximum.
tennessee.exemptions: Leasehold transfers, spouse transfers creating or dissolving a tenancy by the entirety, transfers of property formerly held as tenants in common, deeds carrying out a will, deeds under divorce decrees, transfers into or out of a revocable living trust by the same owner or spouse, and transfers to a government entity. A deed of trust assigned to THDA or FHA is exempt from mortgage tax; Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are not.
tennessee.note: A quitclaim deed is taxed on the consideration given. A lower stated value than the assessor's base is subject to audit. Davidson County's recording fee page was last updated in August 2021.

sources.title: Recordation Tax Due Date and Tax Rates (Tennessee Department of Revenue)
Recordation Tax Manual, June 2026 (Tennessee Department of Revenue)

texas.answer: Texas has no real estate transfer tax. Article VIII, Section 29 of the Texas Constitution, added November 3, 2015, says no law enacted after January 1, 2016 may impose a transfer tax on a transaction that conveys fee simple title to real property.
texas.rate_text: None; the Constitution bars a transfer tax on conveyances of fee simple title

calc.explain: No transfer tax exists. Buyers pay county recording fees and a state-set title insurance premium.

texas.local_taxes: None. The constitutional ban covers any law imposing a transfer tax on such a conveyance; removing it would take a constitutional amendment approved by voters.
texas.who_pays_text: No transfer tax to assign. Recording fees and the title insurance premium appear on the closing statement.
texas.exemptions: No tax to exempt from. The ban does not cover a general business tax, a minerals production tax, a tax on the issuance of title insurance, or a change in rate of a tax that existed on January 1, 2016.
texas.note: County recording fee base under Local Government Code 118.011: $5 first page, $4 each additional page, plus optional county fees. Dallas County charges $25 for the first page and $4 per extra page. Title insurance premiums are set by the state and based on price.

sources.title: Texas Constitution, Article VIII, Section 29 (Texas Legislature)
Texas Local Government Code § 118.011, county clerk fee schedule (Texas Legislature)

utah.answer: Utah has no state transfer tax in the official sources read. Recording a deed costs a flat $40 per document under Utah Code 17-71-407, and Utah is a non-disclosure state where deeds do not state the sale price.
utah.rate_text: None found; flat recording fee of $40 per document (Utah Code 17-71-407)

calc.explain: No tax is calculated on the price. The recording fee is flat per instrument.

utah.local_taxes: None found. No source read lists a city or county transfer tax in Utah; the Salt Lake County Recorder's schedule lists only recording and copy fees.
utah.who_pays_text: No transfer tax. The recording fee is owed by whoever submits the document; the state purchase contract does not assign recording fees, so closing instructions and the loan decide.
utah.exemptions: No tax to exempt from; the recording fee applies to each instrument regardless of price.
utah.note: S.J.R. 2 (2024), a proposed constitutional ban on new transfer taxes, did not pass. The conclusion rests on the county fee schedule and the cited statute, not on a statement that no tax exists anywhere.

sources.title: Utah Code § 17-71-407, county recorder fees (Utah Legislature)
Requirements & Fees (Salt Lake County Recorder)

vermont.answer: Vermont taxes the transfer of a deed: for a principal residence, 0.5% on the first $200,000 and 1.25% above that plus a 0.22% Clean Water Surcharge above $200,000, while a year-round home that is not a primary residence or long-term rental pays 3.4% plus 0.22%. The buyer owes the tax unless the parties agree otherwise.
vermont.tax_name: Property transfer tax (32 V.S.A. 9602) and Clean Water Surcharge
vermont.rate_text: Principal residence: 0.5% on the first $200,000, 1.25% above plus 0.22% surcharge (1.47% total); other year-round homes 3.4% plus 0.22% (3.62% total); long-term rentals, land and 5+ unit buildings 1.25% plus 0.22%

calc.explain: Principal residence only: 0.5% on the first $200,000 and 1.47% (1.25% plus the 0.22% Clean Water Surcharge) on the value above $200,000. A principal residence bought with a VHFA, USDA Rural Development direct, or VHCB homeland-grant loan owes no tax on the first $250,000 (1.47% above). A year-round home that is neither a primary residence nor a long-term rental pays 3.62% on the whole value. Long-term rental, land, non-year-round home, and buildings with five or more units pay 1.47%. The general tax is 1.25% of value or $1.00, whichever is greater.

vermont.local_taxes: None found; the sources describe only the state tax. The clerk charges $15 per page to record and $15 to file the return.
vermont.who_pays_text: By statute the tax is the buyer's liability unless fixed otherwise by agreement of the parties (9604). It is due within 30 days after the transfer.
vermont.exemptions: Transfers between spouses, parent and child (or child's spouse), or grandparent and grandchild (or spouse) without actual consideration, divorce transfers under a court judgment, transfers securing a debt and releases, foreclosure or deed in lieu between borrower and lender, corrective transfers, and certain abandoned municipal dwellings. Section 9603 lists 28 exemptions; exempt transfers still need a return stating the basis.
vermont.note: Act 164 of 2026 (signed June 18, 2026) lets the Commissioner assess the 3.4% rate if a landlord certificate is filed without a bona fide landlord-tenant relationship. A buyer from a nonresident seller must withhold 2.5% for income tax; the land gains tax is separate.

virginia.answer: Virginia has no tax called a transfer tax but taxes the recording of the deed: a state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100 and a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 paid by the seller. Northern Virginia adds two regional fees of 10 cents per $100 each, and counties such as Arlington add a local recordation tax.
virginia.tax_name: Recordation tax (Va. Code 58.1-801) and grantor tax (58.1-802)
virginia.rate_text: State recordation tax $0.25 per $100 or fraction; grantor tax $0.50 per $500 or fraction

calc.explain: Recordation tax = $0.25 per $100 (or fraction) of the greater of price or the most recent property tax assessment. Grantor tax = $0.50 per $500 (or fraction) of the greater of price or value, excluding any lien that stays on the property; the state keeps half and the locality half. Total state-level cost on a sale = both added. Regional fees in Northern Virginia are extra.

virginia.local_taxes: A county may add a recordation tax of one-third of the state tax (about $0.083 per $100); Arlington County does. Northern Virginia members of the Northern Virginia Transportation Authority, including Arlington, also pay a regional WMATA capital fee of $0.10 per $100 and a regional congestion relief fee of $0.10 per $100 (the latter has a contingent-expiration note).
virginia.who_pays_text: The grantor tax and the two regional fees are the grantor's (seller's) by statute unless the parties agree otherwise. The sections read do not say who pays the state and county recordation tax; the contract and loan documents decide.
virginia.mortgage_tax: The same state recordation tax applies to a deed of trust: $0.25 per $100 of the amount secured. A refinance of a debt on which the tax was already paid is taxed on a lower schedule starting at $0.18 per $100.
virginia.exemptions: Deeds to the United States, the Commonwealth or a locality, partition deeds among co-owners, and deeds under a divorce decree; a deed of gift or quitclaim deed with no consideration owes no recordation tax if it says so on its face. Several exemptions also remove the grantor tax and regional fees. Deeds of trust are not subject to the grantor tax.
virginia.note: The 2026 General Assembly changed some exemption code citations effective July 1, 2026; documents must show the updated section on the first page or be rejected (Prince William County clerk).

sources.title: Code of Virginia § 58.1-801, Deeds generally (Virginia General Assembly)
Code of Virginia § 58.1-802, Additional tax paid by grantor (Virginia General Assembly)
Code of Virginia § 58.1-803, Deeds of trust or mortgages (Virginia General Assembly)

washington.answer: Washington taxes each sale with a graduated state real estate excise tax of 1.1% on the first $525,000, 1.28% up to $1,525,000, 2.75% up to $3,025,000 and 3% above that for sales through December 31, 2026, plus a local tax such as Seattle's 0.5%. The law makes it the seller's obligation.
washington.rate_text: Sales through Dec 31, 2026: 1.10% up to $525,000, 1.28% from $525,000 to $1,525,000, 2.75% from $1,525,000 to $3,025,000, 3.00% above; farm, agricultural and timber land pay a flat 1.28%

calc.explain: Graduated like an income tax: each rate applies only to the slice of the price inside its bracket. These thresholds apply to sales dated through December 31, 2026; from January 1, 2027 they become $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. Farm, agricultural and timber land pay a flat 1.28%. The sale date decides which column applies.

washington.local_taxes: Cities and counties add a local REET, a flat percentage of the whole price added to the state tax (up to 0.25% each under RCW 82.46.010 and 82.46.035 for a city planning under the Growth Management Act). Seattle and most King County cities: 0.50%; Skykomish 0.25% (rates effective May 1, 2026).
washington.who_pays_text: The law makes the tax the obligation of the seller (RCW 82.45.080). If the seller does not pay, the buyer is responsible and unpaid tax can become a lien on the property.
washington.exemptions: Gifts and inheritances, community property transfers and transfers under a divorce, separation or invalidity decree, foreclosure, deed in lieu and contract forfeiture, transfers to or from tenants in common and joint tenants, and certain affordable-housing, low-income and self-help housing transfers. The full list is in WAC 458-61A; the exemption code is written on the affidavit.
washington.note: Price is the full consideration including the loan balance. Tax is due on the date of sale. Penalties of 5%, 5% and 10% (20% in all) apply if unpaid after one, two and three months, plus interest.

RCW 82.45.060, tax on sale of property (Washington Legislature)

west-virginia.answer: West Virginia taxes the transfer of real estate at $1.10 for each $500 of value plus a county tax of 55 cents per $500 or more, up to $1.65, and a $20 housing fee on sales. By law the grantor, usually the seller, pays.
west-virginia.tax_name: Excise tax on the privilege of transferring title to real estate (W. Va. Code 11-22-2)
west-virginia.rate_text: $1.10 per $500 of value or fraction, plus a county tax of $0.55 per $500 (up to $1.65 by county vote), plus a $20 flat housing fee

calc.explain: Divide the value (full consideration including any lien assumed) by $500, round up to the next whole unit, multiply by $1.10. The county tax of $0.55 per $500 (up to $1.65) and the $20 flat housing fee on transfers for consideration are added. Since July 1, 2025 counties keep the $1.10 tax.

west-virginia.local_taxes: County tax of 55 cents per $500, which a county commission may raise by majority vote up to $1.65. Kanawha County's current rate was not found on an official page.
west-virginia.who_pays_text: By statute the tax is paid by the grantor, the seller, unless the buyer accepts the deed without the tax paid; for tax sales the grantee pays. The sales contract can shift the cost.
west-virginia.exemptions: Transfers where the value is $1,000 or less, transfers between spouses and, without consideration, between parent and child, grandparent and grandchild or siblings, deeds into or out of trusts, partition deeds and wills, certain no-consideration deeds to wholly owned LLCs, corrective deeds, transfers to or from governments, and mortgages and deeds of trust.
west-virginia.note: Only one state-level tax and one county tax are paid on any one document, in the county where the deed is first recorded.

sources.title: W. Va. Code § 11-22-2, rate of tax and county tax (West Virginia Legislature)
W. Va. Code § 11-22-1, definitions and exempt documents (West Virginia Legislature)

wisconsin.answer: Wisconsin charges a real estate transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value, or $3 per $1,000, and the law puts it on the grantor, the seller. On a $207,900 sale it is $623.70, collected by the register of deeds at recording.
wisconsin.rate_text: $0.30 per $100 of value or fraction of $100 ($3 per $1,000)

calc.explain: Divide the value (full price including any lien) by $100, round up to the next whole unit, multiply by $0.30. The county keeps 20% and sends 80% to the state.

wisconsin.local_taxes: None. Section 77.256 bars any city, village, town or county from charging a fee on a conveyance that is exempt from the state fee; no separate Milwaukee city or county fee was found.
wisconsin.who_pays_text: By statute the fee is imposed on the grantor, the seller; the purchase contract may say otherwise.
wisconsin.exemptions: Transfers of value $1,000 or less, between spouses or domestic partners, between parent and child and similar pairs for nominal or no consideration, by will, descent or survivorship and transfer-on-death, to a trust if a transfer to the beneficiary would be exempt, foreclosure or deed in lieu to the mortgage holder, deeds solely securing a debt, partition among co-owners, and corrective deeds for nominal or no consideration. The exemption subsection of 77.25 is cited on the deed.
wisconsin.note: The fee is on the whole price, not the cash netted after a mortgage payoff. An electronic transfer return must be filed first. Understating value by 25% or more brings a penalty of $25 or 25% of the added fee, whichever is greater.

sources.title: Wisconsin Statutes § 77.22, imposition of real estate transfer fee (Wisconsin Legislature)
Wisconsin Statutes § 77.25, exemptions from fee (Wisconsin Legislature)
Wisconsin Real Estate Transfer Return (RETR) Overview, R. 5-26 (Wisconsin Department of Revenue)

wyoming.answer: In the Wyoming statutes read (Titles 34 and 39, compiled May 2026), no state, county or city tax is charged on recording a deed. Recording costs $12 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, and the buyer must file a sworn statement of the price.
wyoming.rate_text: None found; recording fee only ($12 first page, $3 each additional page, W.S. 18-3-402)

calc.explain: No tax is calculated on the price. Recording fees depend on page count.

wyoming.local_taxes: None found. The statutes authorize no county or city transfer tax that the article found; local ordinances were not reviewed one by one.
wyoming.who_pays_text: No transfer tax. No statute read assigns the recording fee to buyer or seller; the purchase contract decides.
wyoming.exemptions: No tax to exempt from. Some transfers may omit the price on the sworn statement, such as corrective deeds, gifts of more than half the value, spouse or parent-child transfers for nominal consideration, and foreclosure sales.
wyoming.note: The sworn statement of consideration (W.S. 34-1-142) is not a tax return; it is confidential and used for sales-price ratio statistics. Private transfer fee obligations recorded on or after April 1, 2012 are unenforceable (W.S. 34-28-102).

sources.title: Wyoming Statutes, Title 39 (Taxation and Revenue) (Wyoming Legislative Service Office, compilation of May 2026)

guides.title: 1031 exchange for investment property: 45 and 180 days
guides.description: A 1031 exchange defers tax on investment real estate if you identify a replacement in 45 days and close in 180. It does not apply to your home.

guides.title: Buyer agreements after the 2024 NAR settlement
guides.description: Since August 17, 2024, MLS agents must sign a written agreement with you before touring a home, stating a set fee. What it must say; what VA buyers can pay.

guides.title: Buying land: costs, financing and checks
guides.description: Federal loan programs fund land mostly with a home or a farm: FHA, VA, Fannie Mae and FSA rules compared. FSA direct farm loans go up to $600,000.

guides.title: Capital gains on a home sale: the $250,000 / $500,000 exclusion
guides.description: Sell your main home and exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for joint filers) if you owned and lived in it 2 of the last 5 years.
guides.query: capital gains tax on home sale exclusion

guides.title: Closing costs explained: what each line means
guides.description: Read the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure line by line. Some costs cannot rise, recording fees may rise 10 percent as a group, others have no cap.

guides.title: Conventional loans: requirements and 2026 limits
guides.description: The 2026 conforming loan limit is $832,750 for one unit, up to $1,249,125 in high-cost areas. Down payment, credit, DTI and mortgage insurance rules.

guides.title: Credit score and mortgage rates: what lenders look at
guides.description: Lenders usually price on the middle of your three scores. Fannie Mae sets 620 as the floor for manual fixed-rate loans; its automated system has no minimum.
guides.query: credit score needed for a mortgage

guides.title: Debt-to-income ratio: the limits mortgage lenders use
guides.description: Fannie Mae allows a DTI up to 50% on loans run through its system, 36% to 45% on manual ones. Federal rules require lenders to check DTI. How it is counted.
guides.query: debt to income ratio mortgage limit

guides.title: How much down payment do you need to buy a home?
guides.description: FHA needs 3.5% down, Fannie Mae's HomeReady 3%, VA and USDA 0%. On a $400,000 home that is $14,000, $12,000 or $0, plus 2% to 5% for closing costs.
guides.query: how much down payment do you need

guides.title: Earnest money: how much and when you get it back
guides.description: Earnest money is a good-faith deposit on a signed contract. No federal rule sets the amount or the refund: your contract does. Know what protects the deposit.

guides.title: Escrow accounts for taxes and insurance: your rights
guides.description: Under Regulation X a servicer may hold a cushion of at most one-sixth of annual bills and must send a yearly statement within 30 days. Shortages, refunds.
guides.query: mortgage escrow account how does it work

guides.title: FHA loans: requirements, 2026 limits and mortgage insurance
guides.description: FHA loans need 3.5% down with a 580 credit score. Upfront mortgage insurance is 1.75% and the annual premium is 0.55% at 96.5% LTV. 2026 limits inside.

guides.title: Flood insurance and the NFIP: rules, limits and cost
guides.description: Federally regulated lenders must require flood insurance in high-risk zones. NFIP covers up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for contents.

guides.title: Home appraisal cost and how it works
guides.description: VA single-family appraisal fees run $650 to $1,500 by county (May 2026). Lenders must give you the appraisal promptly or 3 business days before closing.

guides.title: Steps to buy a home in the United States
guides.description: The CFPB splits home buying into four steps. Your lender must send a Loan Estimate within 3 business days of your application. Here is the order, step by step.

guides.title: How long does it take to buy a home?
guides.description: No official source gives an average. Federal rules set the clock: Loan Estimate in 3 business days, Closing Disclosure 3 business days before closing.
guides.query: how long does it take to buy a home

guides.title: Home inspection cost and what it covers
guides.description: No federal agency sets or publishes a home inspection price. HUD says FHA performs none, and EPA says fix radon at 4 pCi/L or more. What drives the cost.

guides.title: Homeowners insurance: what lenders require and what it covers
guides.description: Fannie Mae caps the deductible at 5% of coverage: $20,000 on $400,000. What a lender-required policy must include, and why flood is not covered.

guides.title: Land survey cost and when you need one
guides.description: No federal agency publishes survey prices. Lenders, VA rules and FEMA elevation certificates decide when one is needed; a purchase survey adds to tax basis.

guides.title: Mortgage interest deduction: the $750,000 limit in 2026
guides.description: You can deduct interest on up to $750,000 of mortgage debt ($375,000 if married filing separately). Mortgage insurance premiums are deductible again for 2026.

guides.title: Mortgage preapproval: what lenders check and how long it lasts
guides.description: A preapproval letter typically lasts 30 to 60 days, and mortgage credit checks within 45 days count as one inquiry. What lenders check, with a DTI example.

guides.title: How mortgage rates are set: rate, APR, points and locks
guides.description: Your rate follows long-term market yields, then credit, down payment and term adjust it. One point costs 1% of the loan. How APR and locks work.

guides.title: Private mortgage insurance (PMI): how to remove it
guides.description: Federal law lets you ask to cancel PMI when your balance is scheduled to reach 80% of the original value, and ends it at 78%. The rules and a worked example.
guides.query: how to remove private mortgage insurance

guides.title: Property tax deduction and the SALT cap in 2026: $40,400
guides.description: For 2026 the SALT cap is $40,400 ($20,200 if married filing separately), shrinking above $505,000 of income to a $10,000 floor.

guides.title: Real estate commission: how agents are paid now
guides.description: Commissions are negotiable and not set by law. Since August 17, 2024, offers of compensation are banned from the MLS and buyers sign a written agreement first.

guides.title: Refinancing a mortgage: costs, break-even and your rights
guides.description: A refinance brings new closing costs. Example: a $197 monthly saving repays $6,000 of costs in about 31 months. Your rescission rights and tax notes.

guides.title: Selling a home without an agent (FSBO)
guides.description: FSBO sellers keep federal duties: lead-paint disclosure for pre-1978 homes, fair housing ad rules, the $250,000 gain exclusion. FHA caps seller help at 6%.
guides.query: selling a home without an agent

guides.title: Title insurance explained
guides.description: Lender's title insurance is usually required, owner's is optional. In a CFPB example, $2,568 and $1,175 premiums cost $2,768 together at a simultaneous rate.

guides.title: USDA loans: eligible areas, income limits and fees
guides.description: USDA guaranteed loans need no down payment in eligible rural areas. For fiscal year 2027 the upfront guarantee fee is 1.00% and the annual fee 0.35%.

guides.title: VA loans: eligibility and funding fee
guides.description: VA loans need no down payment or monthly mortgage insurance. The funding fee is 2.15% on a first use with under 5% down, 1.25% with 10% down.
